To address this gap, we developed Biotin-Operated Ligand Trapping (BOLT), which combines a HaloTag-fused POI with a streptavidin trap. Desthiobiotin-conjugated Janelia Fluor HaloTag ligands enable POI visualization, trapping, and biotin-operated release. We demonstrate BOLT's capacity in synchronized secretory cargo release, microtubule-directed organelle movement and hitchhiking, and ectopically localizing nuclear transcription factor. Importantly, pulse-chase BOLT further reveals bidirectional endoplasmic reticulum-Golgi trafficking of an endogenous Golgi enzyme and distinguishes recycled from newly synthesized enzyme populations using distinct HTLs. Altogether, BOLT provides an all-in-one platform to interrogate how subcellular localization regulates protein function across HaloTag-compatible systems.

Title: SroA links SigS-dependent stress signaling to metabolic remodeling in Staphylococcus aureus
Authors: Alqahtani, S. A.; Pasham, S.; Alsulami, J.; Al Ali, A.; Aubee, J. I.; Tomlinson, B. R.; Kennedy, S.; Felton, E. A.; Shaw, L. N.; Thompson, K. M.
Abstract: Staphylococcus aureus encounters diverse environmental conditions during colonization and infection, including fluctuations in nutrient availability, oxidative stress, and oxygen limitation. Adaptation to these environments requires regulatory systems that coordinate stress responses with metabolic physiology. The extracytoplasmic function sigma factor SigS contributes to stress adaptation and virulence in S. aureus and directly activates expression of the sroAB operon, which encodes the small proteins SroA and SroB. Previous work demonstrated that SroA participates in feedback regulation of sigS expression, but the broader physiological role of SroA has remained unclear. To further define the regulatory functions of SroA, we performed RNA sequencing following inducible overexpression of sroA in S. aureus. Transcriptome analysis identified altered expression of genes associated with nitrate respiration, nucleotide biosynthesis, stress responses, and nutrient acquisition. Northern blot and quantitative RT-PCR analysis confirmed repression of narG and narJ transcripts following SroA overexpression. Consistent with these transcriptional changes, SroA overexpression impaired nitrate reduction and produced a modest but significant growth disadvantage under anaerobic conditions in chemically defined medium supplemented with glucose and nitrate. In addition to repression of nitrate respiration genes, SroA overexpression reduced expression of genes involved in de novo purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis, while transcripts associated with stress responses and nutrient acquisition, including sosA and pstS, were increased. Together, these findings support a role for SroA in modulating nitrate respiration-associated pathways and growth under conditions supporting anaerobic respiration, linking SigS-dependent stress signaling to metabolic adaptation in S. aureus.

Title: Lactate epigenetically shapes tumor cell states in H3K27M diffuse midline gliomas
Authors: Lum, J.; Nuechterlein, N.; Sliger, S.; Eyunni, S.; Tamrazi, B.; Bluml, S.; Tian, W.; Deogharkar, A.; Sweha, S. R.; Mota, M.; Bayliss, J.; Peterson, E.; Ji, S.; Wittwer, M.; Bhat, K.; Mott, B. T.; Hamanishi, E. T.; Merkuri, F.; Azambuja, A.; Conceicao, H.; Su, F.; Cao, X.; Pandey, R.; Ljare, O. B.; Parolia, A.; Yadav, V. N.; Wahl, D. R.; Koschmann, C.; Simoes-Costa, M.; Pichumani, K.; Wang, S.; Chinnaiyan, A. M.; Venneti, S.
Abstract: H3K27M diffuse midline gliomas (DMGs) are lethal and lack treatment options. These tumors exhibit tumor heterogeneity with aggressive oligodendrocyte precursor (OPC)- and mesenchymal (MES)-like cell states. Because all tumor cells bear H3K27M, tumor heterogeneity has been attributed to microenvironmental cues that remain obscure. H3K27M DMGs exhibit increased glycolysis and the Warburg effect to produce lactate. Lactate can directly modify histone lysines including H3K27Lac, and we hypothesized that lactate epigenetically regulates tumor cell states in H3K27M DMGs. We undertook a comprehensive and integrated analysis of H3K27M DMG cell lines, animal models, tumor tissues, and magnetic resonance spectroscopy in patients to decipher the epigenetic roles of lactate. Here, we report that H3K27M cells uniquely exhibit elevation of the activating mark H3K27Lac. We observed significant heterogeneity in lactate levels within tumors, and the addition of exogenous lactate resulted in marked increases in H3K27Lac and the expression of critical OPC- and MES- like gene signature genes, which correlates with poorer patient outcomes. Our therapeutic approach leverages the inhibition of CBP/p300, which deposits both H3K27Lac and H3K27ac. Targeting CBP/p300 effectively reduces both H3K27Lac and H3K27ac levels, suppresses key OPC- and MES-like signatures, and shows efficacy in preclinical models. Collectively, our findings identify lactate as a key player in the epigenetic regulation of tumor cell state heterogeneity and suggest that targeting this pathway offers promise for addressing the heterogeneous complexities of H3K27M DMGs.

Title: Dual regulation of chemical stress-induced DDI2/3 expression by a transcription factor Fzf1 and nucleosome in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
Authors: Du, Y.; Lin, A.; Brown, J. A. R.; Howe, L.; Xao, W.
Abstract: DDI2 and DDI3 (DDI2/3) are duplicated genes in Saccharomyces cerevisiae that exhibit strong induction by a transcription factor Fzf1 in response to chemical treatments like cyanamide (CY) and methyl methanesulfonate (MMS). Although, like DDI2/3, SSU1, YHB1 and YNR064C also contain an Fzf1-binding consensus sequence CS2 and are coordinately regulated by Fzf1, these genes are only modestly induced by CY and MMS. To identify additional cis-acting elements in the DDI2/3 promoter, we made DDI2/3 promoter deletions in a reporter system and identified upstream repressing sequences (URS) spanning 480 nucleotides. To test a hypothesis that the chromatin structure constitutes the URS, we utilized a yeast strain capable of histone H3/H4 depletion by shifting carbon sources. Following histone depletion, DDI2/3 were strongly induced in an Fzf1 dependent manner, while YHB1 was repressed. Interestingly, under histone depletion conditions, CY or MMS treatment further increased expression of all Fzf1-regulated genes to comparable levels in an Fzf1 dependent manner. A genome-wide MNase-seq analysis showed that CY treatment reduced the nucleosome occupancy at the mapped DDI2/3 URS region in wild-type cells, but not in in fzf1{Delta} cells. These findings collectively indicate that Fzf1 plays dual roles in regulating the DDI2/3 response to CY. Firstly, it binds CS2 and serves as a transcription activator. Secondly, it is required for the chromatin remodeling at URS. This two-tier regulation at the DDI2/3 promoter helps to explain why DDI2/3 achieve much higher fold induction by CY and MMS than other Fzf1-regulated genes, suggesting Fzf1 to be a candidate pioneer transcription factor.

Title: Metatranscriptomic Identification of Co- and Incidental Infections in Marine Turtles Reveals Complex Disease Aetiologies
Authors: Lim, L.; Lang, B.; Fenton, H.; Rose, K. C.; Hall, J.; Holmes, E. C.
Abstract: Traditional veterinary pathology investigations on wild animals generally conclude a primary cause of death based on a combination of observed clinical signs, gross and microscopic lesions, microbial culture and PCR. However, these methods may fail to capture the broader microbial community of the host. We employed metatranscriptomic sequencing to characterise the potential pathobiome of necropsied marine turtles, comparing these findings with corresponding veterinary pathology reports. Tissue samples were collected from 76 individuals spanning three species of marine turtles -- the green turtle (Chelonia mydas), the hawksbill turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata), and the loggerhead turtle (Caretta caretta) -- across the coastline of New South Wales, Australia. Reported causes of mortality ranged from infectious disease to trauma. We identified a diverse range of parasites within the genera Neospirochis, Hapalotrema, Paraorgymatobothrium, Eimeria and Callitetrarhynchus, and bacteria including the genera Aeromonas, Clostridium, and Vibrio. Novel viruses of the families Astroviridae, Caliciviridae, Hepaciviridae, Hepeviridae, Nyamivirdae, Orthomyxoviridae, Picobirnaviridae and Rhabdoviridae were also identified. In cases where infectious disease was noted in the pathology report, we frequently observed high pathogen read counts consistent with the listed primary diagnoses. However, we also detected a range of incidental infections involving eukaryotic parasites, bacteria, and viruses. The diversity of infectious agents detected in marine turtles suggests that the observed disease outcomes are unlikely to be driven by a single causative agent, but rather by complex interactions between host health, the pathobiome, and environmental stressors. We discuss the potential implications for turtle health and conservation.

Title: Patronin condensation integrates recognition, protection and organization of microtubule minus ends
Authors: Zhang, B.; Yang, J.; Yu, S.; Zhou, K.; He, L.; Huang, L.; Liang, X.; Wang, H.; Chen, J.
Abstract: Microtubule minus ends are central to non-centrosomal microtubule organization, yet how their recognition, protection and molecular organization are integrated remains unclear. Here we show that Drosophila Patronin forms dynamic condensates at microtubule minus ends through a prion-like domain (PrLD). PrLD-mediated condensation cooperates with the CKK domain and a second CKK-independent recognition region to convert weak or broadly distributed microtubule-binding activities into persistent minus-end recognition and tracking. Replacing the PrLD with a heterologous phase-separating HNRNPA1 IDR restores minus-end targeting, indicating that condensation capacity rather than PrLD primary sequence is critical. Patronin condensates further form a protective cap that resists minus-end depolymerization and recruit the cytoskeletal regulators Sas-4, Katanin and Ena. Disrupting PrLD multivalency impairs Patronin localization at multiple developmental sites and causes early organismal lethality. Thus, Patronin condensation creates a physiologically essential microtubule minus-end compartment coupling end recognition, stabilization and cytoskeletal organization.

Title: A dsRNA Virus Converts Early Endosomes into Stable Replication Organelles Through Maturation Arrest and Retrograde Transport
Authors: Gimenez, M. C.; Ferrero, D.; Issa, M.; Moussaoui, S.; Cabrini, M.; Reboucas Paixao, A.; Liu, L.; Ganesan, S.; Acharya, D.; Boermel, M.; Zaremberg, V.; Verdaguer, N.; Terebiznik, M.
Abstract: Infectious bursal disease virus (IBDV) and infectious pancreatic necrosis virus (IPNV) are major animal pathogens that impose a heavy burden on the poultry and aquaculture industries. Yet, major aspects of their unique replication program remain unknown. IBDV is unusual among double-stranded RNA viruses in that it replicates in association with host endosomes. We previously demonstrated this association to be orchestrated by the viral protein VP3 and the early endosomal lipid phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate [PtdIns(3)P], suggesting an essential role for VP3 in forming birnaviruses specialized replication compartments. Here, combining high-resolution fluorescence and correlative light-electron microscopy with diverse molecular and biochemical analyses, we define how the IBDV protein VP3 targets and remodels host endosomes, and establish that endosome-associated replication is conserved in members of the Birnaviridae family. We show that IBDV VP3 targets early endosomes via the PtdIns(3)P effector Early Endosomal Antigen 1 (EEA1) to arrest their maturation and prompt their association with the Golgi complex via ESCPE-1-mediated retrograde transport. We further show that IPNV also exploits endosomal membranes for replication in a PtdIns(3)P dependent manner, although for this virus VP3 engages endosomes through an EEA1-independent mechanism yet to be determined. This work uncovers how birnaviruses exploit a single viral protein to orchestrate endosome remodeling and intracellular trafficking to establish specialized replication compartments while revealing both conserved and host-adapted features of birnaviruses replication.

Title: ESX-1 remodels the Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigen storage compartment in macrophages
Authors: Luk, C. H.; Auchynnikava, T.; Fearns, A.; Ortiz Canseco, J.; Lockwood, P. K.; Charoy, C.; Gutierrez, M. G.
Abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) secretes antigenic proteins that drive protective T cell responses, yet how Mtb intracellular localization affects the trafficking and spatiotemporal distribution of mycobacterial antigens in macrophages remains elusive. Here, we developed a split fluorescent protein reporter to monitor the dynamics of the TB vaccine lead antigen Ag85B in infected human macrophages. We discovered that Mtb triggers the formation and remodeling of two distinct types of Mtb Antigen Storage Compartment (MASC) that retains Ag85 within macrophage membranes. Using subcellular spatial proteomics, we profiled the composition of the MASC, identifying both the Mtb and macrophage proteins that constitute these compartments. Unexpectedly, MASCs are defined by metabolic compartmentalization and rewiring to lipid metabolism in both the macrophage and Mtb. Thus, Mtb builds via the ESX-1 system a metabolically distinct antigen storage compartment in immune cells, with potential implications for antigen selection and delivery in TB vaccine development.

Title: Targeted tumor desialylation by engineered probiotic reprograms the tumor microenvironment to potentiate immunotherapy
Authors: Wang, J.; Wang, J.; OuYang, T.; Shi, B.; Meng, H.; Mao, Z.-W.; Xia, W.
Abstract: Tumor hypersialylation drives immunosuppression and limits immunotherapy efficacy by shielding tumor cells and engaging inhibitory immune receptors. Here, we engineered Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN{Delta}pgi-SAS) as a metabolically confined "desialylation catalyst" to remodel the tumor microenvironment. This strain combines HER2-directed adhesion, hypoxia-inducible surface sialidase display for targeted glycan cleavage, and sialic acid catabolism to prevent glycolytic recycling. Critically, disrupting glucose metabolism ({Delta}pgi) restricts bacterial proliferation to sialic acid-rich tumor microenvironment, significantly enhancing biosafety. In mice, EcN{Delta}pgi-SAS colonized tumors and effectively desialylated tumor cells, synergizing with anti-PD-L1 to suppress growth of immunologically "cold" tumors. Mechanistically, desialylation reversed immunosuppression by broadly enhancing antitumor immunity. Orally administered EcN{Delta}pgi-SAS substantially inhibited colorectal carcinogenesis, repaired epithelial barrier integrity by restoring tight junctions, and prevented adenoma formation. This integrated strategy establishes a clinically translatable platform for reversing immunosuppression in solid tumors.

Title: PepRePs: Peptide-Retargeted Phosphatases Designed with Generative Language Models
Authors: Hong, L.; Ho, T.-C.; Tseng, Y.-S.; Vincoff, S.; Chen, T.; Donahue, T. C.; DeLisa, M. P.; Chen, P.-H.; Chatterjee, P.
Abstract: Phosphorylation is a fast, reversible layer of post-translational control that directly governs protein activity, signaling flux, and cell state. Kinases and phosphatases collectively establish these phosphorylation states, but their dysregulation drives cancer, neurodegenerative diseases, and developmental disorders. Selectively manipulating the phosphorylation of individual proteins in cells remains challenging, particularly for disordered substrates. Here, we introduce Peptide-Retargeted Phosphatases (PepRePs), a genetically encoded system that fuses a peptide binder to a serine/threonine phosphatase subunit to localize phosphatase activity to a target protein. We first establish the PepReP architecture using characterized tau-binding peptides, then apply protein language model-guided peptide design to target Rab8A, PTEN, and STAT3. Across endogenous and exogenous targets, PepRePs reduce phosphorylation, with downstream effects on tau aggregation, Rab8A-associated protein interactions, and cellular proliferation following PTEN and STAT3 targeting. Sequence-based peptide design enables targeting without structural inputs, supporting application to substrates with disordered regions that challenge conventional structure-based binder design. By coupling programmable peptide binders with modular phosphatase subunits, PepRePs enable targeted control of protein phosphorylation to probe cellular signaling and develop strategies for correcting disease-associated protein dysfunction.

Title: Diet-conditioned microbiota enhances fecal microbiota transplantation efficacy in alcoholic liver disease through caproic acid-PPARα signaling
Authors: Choudhary, N.; Mittal, A.; Kumar, S.; Yadav, K.; Kumari, A.; Maheshwari, D.; Rath, P. P.; Maras, J. S.; Mohmmed, A.; Kumar, A.; Sarin, S.; Sharma, S.
Abstract: Background and Aim: Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) in Alcohol-related liver disease (ALD) has shown therapeutic potential, with variable efficacy and unclear mechanism. Because dietary protein influences gut microbiota composition, we hypothesized that donor dietary preconditioning could enhance FMT efficacy. We therefore examined in a murine ALD model if high-protein donor diet improves FMT outcome. Methods: ALD was induced in C57BL/6N mice using a Lieber-DeCarli ethanol diet combined with thioacetamide administration for 12 weeks. FMT was performed using stool from diet-modulated donors, and recovery was assessed on day7 post-FMT. Multi-omics analysis using 16s rRNA and mass spectroscopy was performed for Gut microbiota composition, plasma- and stool-metabolome, and hepatic proteomes. Multi-omics outcomes were validated in ALD animal and Huh7 hepatocytes. Results: Both protein-based FMTs improved ALD recovery; Veg-FMT indicated superior efficacy, significantly reducing hepatic injury (AST 1.2FC, p=0.002; bilirubin 1.2FC, p=0.03; steatosis 1.7FC,p=0.01) and restoring gut barrier integrity (occludin 1.5FC,p=0.04; mucin 2 2.2FC, p=002; and plasma endotoxin 1.7FC, p=0.02). A significant 2FC increase was observed in Lachnospiraceae NK4A136, Coriobacteriaceae UCG-002, and short-chain fatty acids, particularly caproic acid. Functional validation confirmed that caproic acid promoted hepatic fatty acid {beta}-oxidation through PPAR-dependent mechanisms, reducing triglyceride accumulation and lipogenesis in both cellular and animal models. Conclusion: Donor preconditioning with a plant-protein enriched diet enhances FMT efficacy in ALD by gut microbiota modulation with increased metabolites like caproic acid. These findings highlight a microbiota-metabolite-host axis through which diet-modulated FMT improves hepatic lipid metabolism and injury, and identifies a pathway via which FMT imparts its effect.

Title: Metabolic commitment to human motor neurons is characterized by mitochondrial depletion and pyruvate rewiring
Authors: Torregrosa-Munumer, R.; Turkia, J.; Spirin, D.; Kvist, J.; Saarimaki-Vire, J.; Povea-Cabello, S.; Ermis, R.; Pennonen, J.; Kuuluvainen, E.; Otonkoski, T.; Hietakangas, V.; McWilliams, T. G.; Fernandez-Vizarra, E.; Katajisto, P.; Tyynismaa, H.
Abstract: Mitochondrial remodelling is a key feature of neurogenesis in cortical and hippocampal neuronal lineages, yet the temporal control of organellar homeostasis in developing human motor neurons remains poorly understood. Here, we generated a high-resolution temporal resource integrating proteomics, metabolomics, and mitochondrial characterization across human iPSC-to-motor neuron differentiation. This analysis revealed prolonged mitochondrial depletion during early neurogenesis, characterized by reduced mitochondrial content, mitochondrial fragmentation, and lysosome-dependent turnover. This state persisted throughout the neural progenitor stage and was followed by recovery of mitochondrial content during neuronal maturation. During this transition, pyruvate utilization shifted from pyruvate carboxylation towards pyruvate dehydrogenase-dependent oxidation. Pharmacological manipulation of pyruvate partitioning demonstrated that this metabolic switch is required for human neuronal differentiation. Our findings establish a temporal framework for the metabolic control of human motor neuron differentiation and reveal a progenitor-specific state linking mitochondrial depletion to pyruvate metabolism.

Title: Glutathione Protects Hematopoietic Stem Cells from Proteotoxic Stress
Authors: Paul, A.; Tom, H.; Merchant, S.; Phan, J.; Lemoff, A.; Mathews, T. P.; Karner, C. M.; Hoxaj, G.; Zhao, Z.; Morrison, S. J.
Abstract: Glutathione is a redox buffer, best known for preventing oxidative stress and ferroptosis, but rarely studied in stem cells. We studied glutathione function in hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) by deleting the glutamate-cysteine ligase catalytic subunit (GCLC), which synthesizes glutathione, or glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), which employs glutathione to prevent ferroptosis. GCLC deficiency eliminated glutathione from hematopoietic cells, severely impairing HSC function and hematopoiesis. In contrast, GPX4 deficiency did not affect HSC function and had little effect on hematopoiesis, even after vitamin E depletion, suggesting glutathione has ferroptosis-independent functions in HSCs. Consistent with this, GCLC deficiency increased reactive oxygen species levels in hematopoietic cells. But treatment with antioxidants or ferroptosis inhibitors gave little or no rescue of HSC function despite reducing ROS levels. Rather, GCLC-deficient, but not GPX4-deficient, HSCs exhibited unfolded protein accumulation, proteostatic stress, and cell death marked by elevated p53 levels and Annexin V staining. Deficiency for p53 prolonged the function of GCLC-deficient HSCs after transplantation. Glutathione is thus necessary in HSCs for proteostasis but may be dispensable for ferroptosis inhibition in vivo.

Title: A tonic PDGFA-dependent niche organizer maintains alveolar homeostasis
Authors: Frabotta, R. S.; Konkimalla, A.; Whitlow, T.; Tsuge, K.; Liu, S.; Forrester, M. T.; Tata, A.; Tata, P. R.
Abstract: Tissue homeostasis requires mechanisms that preserve quiescence while allowing rapid activation after injury, but how tissues actively restrain injury responses during homeostasis remains poorly understood. Here we identify alveolar type 1 (AT1) cells as organizers of the distal lung niche through tonic expression of PDGFA, which maintains alveolar fibroblast identity and restrains myofibroblast activation. Cell type-specific ablation revealed that loss of AT1s, but not other major alveolar cell populations, was sufficient to evoke spontaneous fibroblast activation and tissue-wide responses that recapitulate injury. In silico ligand-receptor analysis, ex vivo screening, and conditional genetic models identified AT1-derived PDGFA as a key homeostatic signal. Loss of AT1-derived PDGFA caused spontaneous myofibroblast induction and tissue remodeling, whereas increasing PDGFA promoted fibroblast proliferation while suppressing myofibroblast differentiation. Integrated phosphoproteomic, transcriptomic, and chromatin accessibility analyses showed that PDGFA engages SHP2-ERK signaling, suppresses MRTFA-associated SRF programs, and promotes E2F-associated cell-cycle programs, thereby opposing the pro-fibrotic effects of TGF{beta}-driven fibroblast activation. Restoring PDGFA signaling abrogates myofibroblast features from human idiopathic pulmonary fibrotic lungs and attenuated fibrotic remodeling in vivo. These findings define a tonic AT1-derived PDGFA signal that maintains alveolar homeostasis and offers a therapeutic target to prevent or revert lung fibrosis.

Title: Evolution and remodeling of acceptor specificity in the NodZ α-1,6-fucosyltransferase
Authors: Smith, N. T.; diCenzo, G. C.; Howe, G. W.
Abstract: Glycosyltransferases have broad diversity in their acceptor substrates, yet the molecular and evolutionary basis of this diversity remains poorly understood. NodZ is an -1,6-fucosyltransferase that fucosylates Nod factors, lipochitooligosaccharide molecules involved in the establishment of rhizobium-legume symbioses. While NodZ is the only known bacterial member of the GT23 family of -1,6-fucosyltransferases, the determinants of its acceptor selectivity and the evolutionary origins thereof are unclear. Here, a phylogenetic analysis of 332 NodZ-like proteins revealed a distinct rhizobial clade and significantly greater structural diversity in the N-terminus than in the C-terminus. Kinetic analysis of a Mesorhizobium japonicum NodZ demonstrated selectivity for longer chitooligosaccharide acceptors (comprised of four to five GlcNAc units), while alanine scanning revealed W139 as a primary determinant of this chain length preference. We propose that W139 forms an aromatic platform that engages distal GlcNAc units present only in longer acceptors, coupling productive binding to acceptor chain length. We then used the NodZ phylogeny to reconstruct ancestral NodZ homolog sequences, which indicated that W139 emerged at the base of the rhizobial clade, and thus may represent a key evolutionary step towards canonical NodZ function. Additionally, the most recent resurrected ancestor was capable of fucosylating chitooligosaccharides with lower efficiency than the extant NodZ, suggesting that efficiency towards chitooligosaccharides was improved during the evolution of this family. Results described here demonstrate that evolutionary diversification of the N-terminal region can remodel acceptor specificity while preserving the conserved catalytic architecture of GT23 fucosyltransferases, providing a framework for understanding and engineering fucosyltransferase specificity.

Title: Prime editing enables high-throughput identification and characterization of selective MutSβ inhibitors
Authors: Jing, Y.; Yan, J.; Yang, D.; Chen, Y.; Senoussi, I.; Woodward, J.; Williams, K.; Kim, H.; He, K.; Daub, H.; Dahiya, V.; Thomsen, M.; Ling, J.; Ravisankar, P.; Pritykin, Y.; Balmus, G.; Cejka, P.; Hussmann, J. A.; Liu, L.; Vogt, T. F.; Finley, M.; Adamson, B.
Abstract: DNA mismatch repair (MMR) maintains genome stability but paradoxically drives expansion of pathogenic repeats responsible for trinucleotide repeat disorders. Attenuating repeat instability through targeted inhibition of MMR is therefore a therapeutic strategy of interest; however, progress is constrained by a lack of robust methods for defining and isolating MMR subpathways. We exploited features of prime editing to profile the effects of core MMR genes on thousands of programmed DNA mispairs in cells and resolved distinct MMR processes, including a noncanonical, loop-directed mechanism. Guided by these results, we built a set of scalable reporters that detect loss of separable MMR processes and screened ~72,000 small molecules for activity against MutS{beta}-directed MMR. This effort identified a novel series of MutS{beta} inhibitors that reduced (CAG)n expansion in a cell model. Altogether, this study establishes several methods for systematically interrogating MMR, with demonstrated capacity to identify inhibitors of therapeutic value.

Title: Blood-brain barrier-traversing multivalent TGFβ trap for anti-cancer immunomodulation of gliomas
Authors: Lee, D.; Chung, S. W.; Kong, B.; Xie, Y.; Kang, B.; Yang, J.; Huang, B.; Rao, D.; Choi, J. S.; Ra, E. A.; Anastasiadis, P.; Lee, G.; Kim, D.-H.; Lim, M.; Suk, J. S.
Abstract: Clinical studies have revealed that glioblastoma (GBM) is refractory to immunotherapy, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), due to the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) primarily intensified by intratumoral upregulation of transforming growth factor-{beta} (TGF{beta}). Primary GBM tumor bulks are surgically removed in clinic, but invasive tumor cells infiltrated into surrounding normal brain tissue cannot be eradicated by systemic therapy due to the integral blood-brain barrier (BBB), leading to near-inevitable tumor recurrence. To address these translational challenges, we have engineered a TGF{beta}-inhibiting protein nanocage comprising human heavy-chain ferritin protein and TGF{beta} receptor II ectodomain that enables BBB penetration and multivalent TGF{beta} entrapment, respectively. We demonstrate that the nanocage platform, denoted T{beta}R2-HFt, following systemic administration, traverses the BBB, and extensively modulates immunosuppressive TME, both stromal and immune components, thereby potentiating the therapeutic efficacy of a clinically used ICI in multiple mouse glioma models. Notably, a majority of the glioma-bearing animals that received surgical tumor resection, followed by treatment with T{beta}R2-HFt and the ICI, survived the tumor and resisted tumor rechallenge, providing a potential means to control GBM in a durable manner.

Title: digestome: a licence-clean marker-gene panel for functional profiling of anaerobic digestion microbiomes
Authors: Päll, T.
Abstract: Functional profiling of anaerobic digestion microbiomes is routinely performed against KEGG or MetaCyc, whose paid commercial licences block fee-for-service analysis for biogas operators, the setting where the results have the most immediate operational value. We present digestome, a curated marker-gene panel for anaerobic digestion built exclusively on sources that are free for commercial use (NCBIfam, public domain; Pfam, CC0; Rhea, CC BY), together with a scorer that reports pathway completeness, branch capability and, for hydrolysis, whether the enzyme is built for export. Benchmarked against 1,401 metagenome-assembled genomes from 134 anaerobic digesters, the panel assigned no methanogenesis route to any of 1,361 non-methanogens, and every acetoclastic call fell within Methanosarcina or Methanothrix. The result held for 3,043 species representatives from the Genome Taxonomy Database, spanning 203 phyla, which are built differently from binned metagenomes: the only background genomes given a route were two archaea carrying mcrA, and none of the 90 anaerobic methane and alkane oxidisers was given one. Specificity against non-methanogens does not show that a methanogen gets the right route: with a family-level check, 59 of 156 acetoclastic calls in that sample fell on methylotrophic genera that do not use acetate, and a lineage policy removed them, with 14 more left unconfirmed in unnamed genera. Testing whether a catalytic domain shares a polypeptide with an export module reduced the genomes credited with cellulolytic capacity from 597 to 50. A causal graph of the measurement shows that a profile reports the community together with three measurement choices (sampling, DNA extraction and sequencing depth, and reference genomes), which fixes what one profile can attribute and what a prospective validation would have to record.

Title: PanRes: A database of latent and acquired antimicrobial resistance allowing 3D-based protein homology search
Authors: Vojtkova, M.; Baltusis, M.; Martiny, H.-M.; Baral, A.; Pyrounakis, N.; Beleon, A.; Freitag, R.; Pico-Tomas, A.; Kaas, R. S.; Petersen, T. N.; Munk, P.
Abstract: Antimicrobial resistance databases are central to genomic surveillance, but resistance determinants remain distributed across resources with different scopes, structures, and annotations. We developed PanRes, a curated resistance database of 11,717 genes integrating acquired and latent determinants of antibiotic, biocide, and metal resistance within a unified ontology. We predicted representative protein structures and clustered them by structural similarity, grouping proteins into 505 high-confidence structurally conserved clusters coherent despite sequence divergence. Their structure-guided alignments were used to build Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) for remote homology search. In seven wastewater metagenomes from five European cities, PanRes 3D-based HMMs expanded detection beyond what was possible with BLAST, with 35.3% of retained hits identified only by the HMMs and generally showing greater divergence from known proteins. For beta-lactamases, several proteins retained beta-lactamase-like folds and catalytic geometry despite weak sequence similarity. PanRes is available through an interactive web platform (https://panres.rambio.dk/), a structure-informed resource for exploring the whole resistome.

Title: Serval: A modular framework for decoding imaging based spatial transcriptomics data
Authors: Tsui, J.; Adam, N.; Choi, W.; Liu, L. Y.; Flores, C.; Ansari, S.; Kong, E.; Thapliyal, Y.; Lee, H.; Haider, S.; Von Riedemann, I.; O'Flanagan, C.; IMAXT Cancer Grand Challenges Consortium,  ; Aparicio, S.; Roth, A.
Abstract: Imaging-based spatial transcriptomics technologies have opened new avenues for studying cellular organization and gene expression within intact tissues. However, the accuracy of downstream analyses depends critically on the decoding step that reconstructs barcodes from fluorescence patterns and maps them to gene identities. Despite a growing number of decoding methods, systematic benchmarking has been limited. Here, we introduce Serval, a modular framework for developing and benchmarking decoding methods across diverse spatial transcriptomics platforms. Serval separates key decoding stages into independently configurable modules, enabling flexible integration of alternative algorithms. Using this framework, we develop the Cosine decoder, a novel method that improves transcript recovery by optimizing cosine similarity to known barcodes. We evaluate Cosine and baseline methods on synthetic and real MERFISH datasets, showing that Cosine achieves higher transcript recovery and superior correlation with expression references compared to existing methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Serval framework generalizes beyond MERFISH. By extending to the DART-FISH platform, we show that Cosine improves transcript recovery, clustering stability and supports more direct annotation of complex biological structures such as the human primary motor cortex. These results establish that modular decoding frameworks facilitate robust, platform-agnostic benchmarking, ultimately supporting more accurate spatial transcriptomics analysis across diverse biological samples.

Title: State-selective nanobodies to probe Guanylate-binding protein coat assembly and function
Authors: Pagani, L. L.; Kuhm, T. I.; Pinto, C.; Perton, E. G.; Arents, M.; Nguyen, P. N. M.; Steyaert, J.; Pardon, E.; Jakobi, A. J.
Abstract: Cell-autonomous immunity against gram-negative bacterial pathogens relies on Guanylate-binding proteins (GBPs). GBPs are interferon-inducible guanosine triphosphate hydrolases that coat cytosolic bacteria and promote non-canonical inflammasome activation. GBP coat assembly is initiated by GBP1, which binds bacterial lipopolysaccharide and recruits further paralogs in a hierarchical and nucleotide-dependent manner. Dissecting the contributions of individual GBPs has remained challenging because the seven human paralogs are structurally similar and undergo nucleotide-driven conformational changes that are difficult to resolve in cellular and biochemical experiments. Here, we developed a nanobody toolbox for the state-selective probing of human GBP coat assembly. We identify eight nanobodies with distinct paralog, domain, and conformational specificities and define their binding profiles and epitopes using complementary biophysical assays and cryogenic electron microscopy. We further demonstrate the utility of selected nanobodies by demonstrating their functionality in membrane reconstitution assays and in infected cells. A dimer-disrupting nanobody blocks progression of GBP-coat assembly from soluble GBP1 assemblies to LPS-associated coats, suggesting a stage-specific structural transition during coat formation. In contrast, a dimer selective nanobody binds assembled coats without measurably perturbing their organisation and is robustly recruited to GBP1-positive bacteria in infected cells, indicating that this dimer interface remains intact and accessible in coat-associated GBP1. Together, these nanobodies establish a set of state-selective reagents to distinguish, perturb, and probe GBP assemblies in structural and cellular studies.

Title: Host-to-symbiont transfer of fatty-acid-derived carbon in the Paramecium bursaria-Chlorella variabilis photosymbiosis
Authors: Chen, Y.-J.; Wei, C.-Y.; Hsu, C.-W.; Wang, P.-L.; Hsiao, S. S.-Y.; Lee, D.-C.; Yang, C.-L.; Ku, C.; Kamal, M. M.; Leu, J.-Y.
Abstract: Metabolic exchange stabilizes photosymbioses, but carbon transfer is usually framed as exporting photosynthate from algal symbionts to heterotrophic hosts. Previous work showed that Paramecium bursaria reorganizes its lipid droplets during symbiosis and that perturbing host lipid metabolism reduces endosymbiont abundance. Here, we investigated reciprocal organic-carbon exchange between P. bursaria and its intracellular Chlorella symbionts. Symbiosis was associated with extensive lipid remodeling in both partners and marked triacylglycerol accumulation in endosymbiotic algae. Following host supplementation with 13C-oleic acid, NanoSIMS and EA-IRMS detected 13C enrichment in intracellular algae. Isotopologue-resolved lipidomics further showed incorporation of host-acquired fatty acid carbon into algal storage and membrane lipids. These findings reveal an unexpected host-to-symbiont direction of organic-carbon transfer and expand the conventional model of metabolic exchange in photosymbiosis.

Title: Genomic SEM reveals shared genetic architecture and expands locus discovery for locomotor activity in heterogeneous stock rats
Authors: Chitre, A. S.; Sanches, T. M.; Ang, G.; Amissah, N. K.; Avila, R.; Bimschleger, H.; Campo, P.; Cannella, N.; Chen, D.; Cheng, R.; Cohen, K. A.; Crow, A. D.; Dereschewitz, E.; Doyle, M. R.; Eid, M.; George, A. M.; Horvath, A. P.; Ishiwari, K.; Johnson, B. B.; Keung, E.; King, C.; Martin, C. D.; Garcia Martinez, A.; Munro, D.; Netzley, A. H.; Nguyen, K.-M.; Peng, B.; Pullmann, D.; Rahman, S. R. M. U.; Roberts, A. T.; Sadegi, M.; Sevigny-Resetco, D.; Soverchia, L.; St. Pierre, C. L.; Suzuki, N.; Thompson, B. M.; Tyagi, S.; Ubaldi, M.; Vogel, R. M.; Wang, T.; Wang, Y.; Chen, H.; Ciccocioppo, R.; d
Abstract: Locomotor response to a novel environment is a heritable, addiction-relevant behavioral phenotype in rodents. We characterized its genetic basis in 9,341 male and female heterogeneous stock (HS) rats from eight studies. Locomotor activity was heritable across studies, while pairwise genetic correlations were positive but variable, indicating shared yet nonidentical genetic influences. Given nonuniform genetic architecture, we compared three complementary approaches to locus discovery that analyzed SNP effects 1) on a pooled locomotor phenotype (MEGA), 2) across studies under a fixed-effect model (METAL), or 3) on a shared genetic factor (Genomic SEM). To ensure comparability, all three locus-discovery approaches were applied to a common subset of seven studies. Together, these approaches identified 38 loci, with both convergence and method-specific discovery across analyses. Genomic SEM identified 31 loci, compared to 8 for MEGA and 13 for METAL. To interpret the loci, we integrated brain molecular QTLs, predicted coding and splice consequences, and open-field locomotor phenotypes from knockouts of orthologous mouse genes. Our results highlighted established neurobehavioral candidates spanning locomotor and reward-related biology (Negr1 and Lmo4), serotonergic signaling (Htr1b), and GABAergic signaling (Gabrg2), as well as relatively novel genes including Tcerg1l, Pcdh10, and Tmem132e. Our results illustrate how Genomic SEM can integrate genetically correlated yet heterogeneous behavioral measures and enable discovery of loci underlying their shared genetic architecture, highlighting its utility for complex-trait studies in rodents.

Title: Linkage disequilibrium moderates how evolving genetic background shapes variant-level architecture
Authors: Lee, H.; Terhorst, J.
Abstract: Evolutionary theory offers a unifying explanation for the genetics of complex traits and diseases by modeling how a trait and its genetic basis are maintained by evolutionary forces. A growing body of evidence suggests that linkage disequilibrium (LD) couples a variant's evolution to that of the genetic background it resides on. However, widely used single-variant theories omit this coupling between variants and the background, or hold the background fixed. We close this gap by developing a model of linkage LD evolution accounting for stabilizing selection, recombination, and genetic drift. The model deduces the genetic architecture of individual variants subject to the co-evolving genetic background. More efficient selection in larger populations is partially offset by slower decay of existing LD and increased generation of new LD. Conversely, noisier LD in smaller populations exposes the variants to episodes of stronger selection. We ask whether ancestry differences in the relationship between effect-size magnitude and minor allele frequency require different selection strengths or can arise from differences in demographic history alone. Stabilizing selection needs to be more than three times stronger in Africans than in Europeans under the constant-size demography, whereas an Out-of-Africa demography alone can explain most of the observed frequency-dependence gap. As this example indicates, selection strength is in general not identifiable from the frequency--effect-size relationship alone, because different combinations of selection and demographic history can produce the same pattern in data with further redundancy added by LD.

Title: Haplotype-phased, chromosome-level, annotated genome assembly of the soybean rust pathogen Phakopsora pachyrhizi
Authors: Greatens, N. F.; Elmore, M. G.; Ramachandran, S. R.; Wright, A.; Tallon, L. J.; Whitham, S. A.; Koch Bach, R. A.; Pedley, K. F.
Abstract: Phakopsora pachyrhizi, the causal agent of soybean rust, is among the most aggressive and economically impactful pathogens affecting soybean (Glycine max) production worldwide. As a dikaryotic rust fungus, P. pachyrhizi maintains its genetic information as two discrete haplotypes that are sequestered within separate nuclei for most of its life cycle as it reproduces asexually via the production of infectious urediniospores. Previous genomes of three P. pachyrhizi isolates collected in South America revealed a large genome with a high transposable element content, measuring up to 1.25 Gb and 93%, respectively. Although these efforts provided valuable foundational resources, the complexity of the genome resulted in highly fragmented assemblies. Here, we generated a highly contiguous, substantially improved, annotated genome resource from the P. pachyrhizi isolate LA04-1, collected during the initial outbreak of soybean rust in the continental United States in 2004. The assembly is haplotype-phased, with each haplotype assembled into 18 chromosomes totaling 572 Mb and 569 Mb in size. The isolate contains unique mating-type genes and does not share haplotype genomes with any available isolates with whole-genome sequencing datasets. This resource will be valuable to future investigations into the underlying mechanisms of virulence in this important plant pathogen.

Title: Intraindividual longitudinal changes of the proteome reveal dynamic markers of biological aging
Authors: Lermer, R.; Qian, X.; Pusch, S. T.; Schaefer, T.; Adam, J.; Li, L.; von Scheidt, M.; Linkohr, B.; Peters, A.; Mann, M.; Schunkert, H.; Heinig, M.
Abstract: Proteomic aging clocks have emerged as biomarkers of aging, but most rely on cross-sectional data. Here, we present a proteomic aging clock based on longitudinal measurements of liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry plasma proteomics at up to three time points in the population-based KORA cohort, comprising 9,105 samples from 4,100 individuals in the final dataset aged 25-88 years. The model predicts chronological age and yields a measure of proteomic age acceleration associated with lifestyle and clinical risk factors. Risk factor-stratified analyses reveal shared proteomic signatures among cardiometabolic exposures and distinct signatures for smoking and physical activity. Within individuals, dyslipidemia and impaired kidney function track transitions to increases in age acceleration, while higher age acceleration is associated with increased all-cause mortality. Mediation analysis suggests that risk factors are linked to mortality indirectly through age acceleration. Affected proteins and pathways highlight extracellular matrix remodeling, complement and coagulation pathways, and liver-derived plasma proteins as key contributors to aging. Mendelian randomization identifies proteins with evidence consistent with a causal role in aging-related traits. Together, these findings are consistent with biological aging being dynamically responsive to changes in modifiable risk factors.

Title: PREpiBind: Protein Representation-integrated Epitope-MHC Class II Binding Prediction
Authors: Jang, D. H.; Kim, D.; Hwang, U.; Park, B.; Choi, Y.; Lee, J.
Abstract: Motivation: Accurate peptide-MHC class II (pMHC-II) binding prediction is complicated by MHC polymorphism and context-dependent peptide recognition. Protein representations are usually evaluated in different pipelines, obscuring their contribution to predictive performance. Results: We present PREpiBind, a joint-attention framework comparing ten protein representations under a fixed architecture and identical data splits across qualitative binding, mass spectrometry, and thresholded IC50 datasets. PLMs generally achieved the strongest pooled performance; ESM3 Large reached a ROC-AUC of 0.927 +/- 0.002 on the qualitative dataset. PREpiBind PLM variants exceeded evaluated reference methods on qualitative and mass-spectrometry benchmarks, whereas NetMHCIIpan-4.3 was higher on thresholded IC50 using its binding-affinity head. PLM advantages narrowed in allele-wise and held-out MHC-molecule evaluations, and H2-out rankings depended on aggregation, indicating scenario-dependent representation performance. Availability and implementation: Source code and the training and evaluation datasets are available at https://github.com/daylight-00/PREpiBind and archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22934281; trained model checkpoints are available at https://huggingface.co/daylight-00/prepibind. Implemented in Python and released under the MIT License. Contact: nicole23@snu.ac.kr Supplementary information: Supplementary data are available online.

Title: RNA synthesis and degradation regulate biomolecular condensates through non-equilibrium feedback
Authors: Sanchez-Burgos, I.; Tejedor, A. R.; Ocana, A.; R. Espinosa, J.; Collepardo-Guevara, R.
Abstract: Transcriptional condensates operate far from equilibrium, where continuous RNA synthesis and degradation dynamically reshape condensate composition. To investigate how RNA synthesis regulates condensate properties at sub-molecular resolution, we introduce REACT-RNA, a chemically specific coarse-grained molecular dynamics framework that explicitly couples RNA polymerisation, degradation, and nucleotide fluxes to sequence-dependent protein-RNA phase behaviour, and apply it to FUS and MED1 condensates. We find that RNA polymerization occurs preferentially at condensate interfaces because interfaces promote a highly reactive microenvironment that combines nucleotide influx, enrichment of reactive RNA chain ends, and enhanced molecular dynamics. Interfacial RNA polymerisation generates a spatially organised RNA population, with newly synthesised short RNAs enriched near the interface and longer RNAs partitioning towards the condensate core, which decreases the interfacial free energy and promotes multivalent RNA-protein interactions. As RNA concentration and chain length evolve over time, condensate composition, density, and stability change dynamically in response. Sustained RNA polymerisation drives re-entrant condensate dissolution, even of aged gel-like condensates, whereas RNA degradation stabilises long-lived non-equilibrium condensates containing elevated RNA content. Our results suggest that RNA synthesis, degradation, and nucleotide fluxes drive transcriptional condensates out of thermodynamic equilibrium while condensates in turn promote reactive molecular configurations that favour RNA production, enabling transient accumulation of RNA-rich compositional imbalance during bursts of transcription.

Title: The pharmacokinetics, bio-distribution and therapeutic efficacy of a trimeric nanobody against SARS-CoV-2 in the golden Syrian hamster COVID-19 model
Authors: Sharma, P.; Mega, D.; Kirby, A.; Buckle, I.; Kipar, A.; Clark, J.; Bentley, E.; Eyssen, L.; Kijak, E.; Herriott, J.; Sharp, J.; Owen, A.; Carroll, M. W.; Owens, R.; Stewart, J. P.
Abstract: Nanobodies are promising medical countermeasures against respiratory viruses, but their local pharmacokinetics and therapeutic window remain incompletely defined. We evaluated the pharmacokinetics, biodistribution and efficacy of a SARS-CoV-2-neutralising trimeric nanobody (A8) in golden Syrian hamsters. Following intranasal administration, A8 concentrations were quantified in nasal wash, bronchoalveolar lavage, lung and serum, and tissue distribution was assessed immunohistologically. Therapeutic efficacy was examined after intranasal treatment before or following challenge with SARS-CoV-2 B.1.351. Intranasal administration of A8 produced sustained respiratory exposure with minimal systemic absorption, whereas intraperitoneal dosing generated transient serum exposure and limited pulmonary delivery. A8 was detected within airway lining material, respiratory epithelial cells, type II pneumocytes and alveolar macrophages. Prophylactic administration 2 h before infection prevented weight loss, while treatment 24 h post infection accelerated recovery and reduced viral subgenomic RNA in respiratory tissues. Doses as low as 0.1 mg/kg were effective when administered at 24 h post infection, with no clear dose response relationship. Treatment delayed until 48 h post infection was less effective. These findings demonstrate that intranasal A8 achieves favourable compartmentalised exposure and that therapeutic efficacy depends principally on early respiratory delivery rather than dose magnitude, supporting further development of inhaled nanobody therapeutics against SARS-CoV-2.

Title: Hairpin Architecture and Extended Sequence Context Shape APOBEC3 Mutagenesis in Monkeypox Virus at Different Genomic Scales
Authors: Madorskaya, A. V.; Kazanov, F. M.; Bogdanov, D. A.; Ponomarev, G. V.; Smolnikova, A. E.; Garshina, D. V.; Matveev, E. V.; Abasov, R. K.; Azgari, C.; Adebali, O. D.; Ivankov, D. N.; Gelfand, M. S.; Kazanov, M. D.
Abstract: The 2022 global mpox outbreak was characterized by an unusual accumulation of more than fifty APOBEC-signature substitutions in MPXV genomes. A previous study suggested that these substitutions preferentially occur within and near hairpins or cruciforms - stem-loop structures formed by inverted repeats. Here, we show that this conclusion resulted from an inappropriate statistical analysis and, using two substantially larger datasets, demonstrate that APOBEC-signature mutations are specifically enriched at TC motifs located at the 3' ends of hairpin loops, but not in other regions of hairpins/cruciforms or in their vicinity. We further identified a preference for stem-loop structures with longer stems and shorter loops, consistent with patterns previously reported for the APOBEC mutagenesis in cancer genomes. Our analysis also revealed a positive association between APOBEC-signature mutation propensity and hairpin stability in single-stranded DNA. Nevertheless, stem-loop structures with long stems and short loops are relatively rare in the MPXV genome, limiting their contribution to the genome-wide distribution of APOBEC-signature mutations to a predominantly local effect. In contrast, extended nucleotide context downstream of the TC motif showed strong genome-wide predictive value, with a marked preference for guanine-rich trinucleotide immediately downstream. Analysis of the upstream nucleotide context was consistent with the mutational specificity of APOBEC3A. Together, these results identify distinct structural and sequence determinants of the APOBEC-associated mutagenesis in MPXV and show that local hairpin/cruciform architecture and extended nucleotide context contribute at different genomic scales.

Title: HIV-1 Ribonucleoprotein Complex Organization Facilitates Assembly of the Mature HIV-1 Capsid
Authors: Waltmann, C.; Gupta, M.; Engelman, A. N.; Lyumkis, D.; Voth, G. A.
Abstract: The encapsulation of the viral RNA condensate inside the capsid is a crucial step in the late stages of the HIV-1 replication cycle. While it is agreed that RNA encapsulation depends on RNA-bound integrase (IN), that capsid-bound IN-RNA filaments are present within the capsid, and that the ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex takes up only a fraction of the capsid volume, the timing of filament formation and ribonucleoprotein (RNP) encapsulation are unclear. Here, we ran virion-scale, coarse grained molecular dynamics simulations to identify how the organization of the RNP and IN in particular affects mature capsid assembly and genome encapsulation. These virion-scale simulations allow for direct comparison between experimental capsid morphologies and those self-assembled in the simulations. It was found, when relatively few tetramers are on the RNP surface, that IN tetramers could facilitate RNA encapsulation without filling a significant fraction of the capsid volume, but do not form a capsid-templated filament. When octameric IN-RNA filaments are modeled, it was found that WT-like capsid morphologies form only when the IN is organized as a single long filament, in agreement with recent experimental suggestions. These capsids are more conical and elongated than the capsids assembled around the RNP with tetrameric IN. Thus, we suggest the IN-RNA filament assembles ahead of the capsid and directs it to its final conical morphology, consistent with the experimental observation of less elongated capsids when IN oligomerization is disrupted.

Title: Development of a NanoBRET assay platform to detect intracellular target engagement in living cells for the Glycine Transporter 1 (SLC6A9)
Authors: Jensen, M. H.; Avgeris, I. P.; Kocaturk, N. M.; Mikkelsen, A. N. L.; Frolund, B.; Farnaby, W.; Wellendorph, P.; Mortensen, J. S. H.; Bavo, F.
Abstract: Glycine transporter 1 (GlyT1) is a clinically investigated target whose conformational plasticity enables ligands to engage distinct extracellular and intracellular binding sites. However, methods to directly quantify intracellular binding remain limited and largely rely on radioligand-based approaches. Here, we report a NanoBRET-based binding assay to quantify intracellular GlyT1 target engagement in living cells using a fluorescent tracer derived from the GlyT1 inhibitor Cmpd1. With a structure-based approach followed by pharmacological characterization we identified a suitable meta-substituted exit vector for linker and fluorophore attachment while maintaining GlyT1 binding. A series of fluorescent probes was synthesized and evaluated, leading to the development of GlyT1-probe which displayed high-affinity binding and enabled robust NanoBRET measurements. Unlike the functional uptake assay, the NanoBRET assay distinguished intracellular from extracellular GlyT1 inhibitors and resolved structure-activity relationships at the intracellular binding site. This assay provides a quantitative approach to interrogate conformation-selective GlyT1 target engagement in living cells, facilitating the characterization of GlyT1 ligands targeting the intracellular site.

Title: TMEM209/NPP-28 partitions PLK-1 between the nuclear envelope and nuclear interior during mitosis
Authors: Puccini de Castro, V.; Barger, S. R.; Azamfirei, R.; Su, T. Y.; Green, R. A.; Biggs, R. J.; Moore, F. E. Q.; Lee, S.; Oegema, K.; Lara-Gonzalez, P.; Bahmanyar, S.
Abstract: The onset of mitosis in animal cells is marked by nuclear envelope breakdown (NEBD), which requires coordinated disassembly of nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) and the nuclear lamina. Polo-like kinase 1 (Plk1/PLK-1) initiates NEBD through phosphorylation of NPC components, but mechanisms that spatially regulate PLK-1 between NPCs and the nuclear interior are unclear. Here, we identify the Caenorhabditis elegans TMEM209 homolog NPP-28 as a transmembrane nucleoporin that concentrates PLK-1 at the nuclear envelope while limiting its nuclear accumulation to promote NEBD. We identify docking sites within NPP-28 that mediate PLK-1 nuclear envelope-association. NPP-28 is phosphorylated by PLK-1 in vitro, and mutational analysis suggests that NPP-28-mediated docking facilitates NEBD, whereas phosphorylation prevents premature NEBD. Simultaneous loss of npp-28 and the transmembrane nucleoporin npp-12/gp210 exacerbates mitotic NEBD defects in early embryos and causes severe defects in germline development. Together, our findings identify NPP-28 as a spatial regulator of PLK-1 during mitosis with functional relationships with other conserved transmembrane nucleoporins depending on context.

Title: The single-PDZ domain protein TXBP-3 regulates contractility in the C. elegans spermatheca
Authors: Khalid, M.; Cram, E. J.
Abstract: In the C. elegans reproductive system, oocyte transit through the spermatheca relies on parallel calcium and Rho-dependent signaling pathways to regulate actomyosin contractility. Here, we identify the conserved single-PDZ domain protein TXBP-3/TAX1BP3 as a dosage-dependent regulator of spermathecal contractility. TXBP-3 is expressed in contractile tissues, including the spermatheca and spermathecal-uterine (sp-ut) valve. Animals lacking txbp-3 do not display overt phenotypes or defects in ovulation. However, in nematodes expressing the genetically encoded calcium sensor GCaMP, deletion of txbp-3 results in more rapid transit of embryos through the spermatheca. Conversely, tissue-specific overexpression of TXBP-3 results in slower transit times due to hypercontraction of the spermathecal neck and sp-ut valve, causing oocyte severing and failures of embryos to exit the spermatheca. We find TXBP-3 promotes the active phosphorylated state of the calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) UNC-43. When TXBP-3 is overexpressed or unc-43 is depleted, ovulations in which the embryo fails to exit show disrupted calcium signaling. Additionally, TXBP-3 functions independently of the RhoGEF RHGF-1 and in parallel with the RhoGAP SPV-1 to maintain the alignment of actin fiber bundles and protect embryo structural integrity. Together, our results establish TXBP-3 as a regulator of contractility, kinase activation, and cytoskeletal architecture in contractile tissues.

Title: CorB and MgpB (YegH) alleviate excess-magnesium stress and contribute to egg white tolerance and virulence in Salmonella
Authors: Iwadate, Y.; Slauch, J. M.
Abstract: Maintaining proper cation homeostasis is essential for the survival of all living organisms. During infection, Salmonella must adapt to host-imposed magnesium (Mg2+) limitation. To compensate, Salmonella induces high-affinity Mg2+ transporters and synthesis of polyamines, organic cations that partially substitute for Mg2+. Once Mg2+ levels are restored and cells enter stationary phase, excess cations must be exported; failure to do so results in loss of viability. The CorC-domain protein PaeA exports excess polyamines, whereas MgpA and CorC reduce intracellular Mg2+ levels. Here, we identify two new CorC-domain proteins, MgpB (formerly YegH) and CorB, as mediators of Mg2+ homeostasis, showing that they also reduce intracellular Mg2+ accumulation and protect cells from endogenous excess-cation stress. Genetic analyses revealed the functional redundancy among these proteins in conferring resistance to exogenous high Mg2+, endogenous stress induced after Mg2+ starvation, and egg whites. Deletion of mgpB and/or corB conferred little to no phenotype. However, these mutations showed synergistic phenotypes in strains lacking MgpA. This synergistic relationship was also evident in mouse competition assays. Lack of MgpA, CorC, MgpB, and CorB leads to an increase in intracellular Mg2+ levels. Moreover, expression of mgpB and corB are increased in high Mg2+, all consistent with their role as putative Mg2+ exporters. Together, these findings identify MgpB and CorB as new mediators of Mg2+ homeostasis and reveal a multilayered system that enables Salmonella to finely balance intracellular cation levels during environmental and host-imposed stress.

Title: Non-redundant cardiolipin synthase family proteins shape lipid composition and stress resilience in Bacteroides fragilis
Authors: Schnizlein, M. K.; Hong, B.; Nguyen, J. N. T.; Jones, K.; Rodriguez, A. I.; Fiebig, A.; Campagna, S. R.; Balunas, M. J.; O'Halloran, T. V.; Crosson, S.
Abstract: Gut-resident bacteria must withstand membrane-disrupting stresses such as bile acids to persist in the intestinal environment. The Bacteroidota are a dominant phylum of the human gut microbiota. However, the genes responsible for synthesis of membrane lipids in this phylum remain relatively uncharacterized. Bacteroides fragilis is a prevalent member of this phylum and encodes two predicted cardiolipin synthase family proteins, ClsA and ClsB. We previously identified both cls genes as bile-acid fitness factors in B. fragilis P207, but the contributions of clsA and clsB to cell physiology remained unclear. Here we combine targeted gene deletion with high-resolution lipidomics, metabolomics, and elemental mass spectrometry to show that ClsA and ClsB have distinct and non-redundant functions in the cell. Each cls gene differs in its growth-phase expression pattern, and deletion of each gene produces distinct effects on cell morphology, fitness under membrane-perturbing stress, and the broader metabolome. clsA and clsB strongly influence the levels of different glycyl-seryl peptidolipids, a Bacteroides lipid family that includes immune-active lipids and whose loss impairs bile acid resistance and gut colonization. In contrast to the acute ion-gradient disruption caused by the secondary bile acid deoxycholate, deletion of clsA and clsB did not measurably alter steady-state intracellular ion levels under standard growth conditions. Together, these results define related, but non-redundant roles for two cardiolipin synthase family proteins in a common member of the human gut microbiota.

Title: Quantitative profiling of basal and stress-induced ribosome collisions
Authors: Marks, J.; Ayres-Galhardo, P. H.; Tamilselvam, B.; Roberson, A. B.; Pitts, R.; Guydosh, N. R.; Meydan, S.
Abstract: Background: Ribosomes stall when they encounter problematic codons or cellular stress that perturbs translation. Stalled ribosomes can lead to the formation of ribosome collisions, also known as disomes, that engage cellular surveillance and stress signaling pathways. How many disomes form during basal conditions and how disome levels change under stress remain poorly understood. Results: We used spike-in normalized Ribo-seq and Disome-seq to quantify transcriptome-wide disome levels. Applying this approach in yeast and human cells, we found that disomes generate approximately 2-10% of all footprints under basal conditions. A high-resolution Disome-seq experiment in human cells identified reproducible disome-forming sites that contribute to the basal level of disome formation in the cell. Exposure of yeast cells to methyl methanesulfonate and human cells to anisomycin increased disome abundance up to four-fold and redistributed collisions in a stress-specific and context-dependent manner. Conclusions: These data provide a quantitative, transcriptome-wide framework for measuring disome levels and reveal how translational stress reshapes the landscape of ribosome collisions in cells.

Title: Recent effective population size of the snowy owl (Bubo scandiacus) tracks historical climate variation
Authors: Enevoldsen, E. L. G.; Aguilar-Gomez, D.; Jacobsen, K.-O.; Solheim, R.; Oien, I. J.; Aarvak, T.; Hoff, S. N. K.; Kersten, O. S.; Wiebe, K. L.; Therrien, J.-F.; Menyushina, I.; Nielsen, R.; Boessenkool, S.; Baalsrud, H. T.
Abstract: Arctic ecosystems are undergoing rapid climate warming, providing an opportunity to examine molecular evolution under environmental stress. Here, we used whole-genome resequencing to assess population structure, genetic diversity, and recent demographic history in the snowy owl (Bubo scandiacus), a highly mobile Arctic apex predator classified as Vulnerable by the IUCN. We analysed genome-wide data from individuals sampled across the species' circumpolar range using a chromosome-level reference genome. Population genomic analyses revealed an absence of detectable population structure, indicating extensive gene flow and near-panmixia across continents. Genome-wide nucleotide diversity was low ({pi}= 2.47 x 10^(-4)), while runs of homozygosity were dominated by short tracts, indicating limited standing genetic variation despite little evidence for recent close inbreeding. Our demographic inference revealed a sustained decline in effective population size over the past ~1,600 years, a pronounced reduction coinciding with the Medieval Warm Period followed by a partial recovery during the subsequent cooler interval. This direct, measurable effect of past climate warming on effective population size raises concerns for the long-term survival of the snowy owl. Our results demonstrate that high connectivity and low levels of recent inbreeding have not necessarily buffered this species against climate-driven demographic erosion of genetic diversity. This study highlights the value of using whole-genome population genomics to inform genomic monitoring and conservation decision-making in rapidly changing environments.

Title: Identifying fundamental properties of neuromuscular disorder genes through genomic feature analysis
Authors: Martin, A.; Llanes-Cuesta, M. A.; Hartley, J. N.; Frosk, P.; Drogemoller, B. I.; Wright, G. E. B.
Abstract: Neuromuscular disorders (NMDs) encompass conditions that affect the peripheral nervous system. They are often caused by genetic alterations that impair skeletal muscle function. Molecular diagnosis remains challenging because some causal genes have not yet been identified. We therefore used feature-selection approaches to characterize genomic properties that distinguish NMD genes from other protein-coding genes. Curated genes implicated in NMDs (n = 639; GeneTable of NMDs) were merged with 134 genomic features for autosomal protein-coding genes spanning gene complexity, genetic variation, expression patterns, and other gene traits. Machine-learning-based feature selection using Boruta was combined with statistical analyses to compare NMD genes with other protein-coding genes. We also evaluated NMD genes against high-confidence non-NMD disease genes, examined variation across NMD subgroups, and assessed genes added to the NMD catalogue between 2020 and 2024. Compared with other protein-coding genes, NMD genes showed higher expression in disease-relevant tissues, including skeletal muscle and heart; greater transcript complexity and population genetic constraint, and stronger conservation across several evolutionary measures. Of 33 features that distinguished NMD genes from both high-confidence non-NMD disease genes and other autosomal genes, 28 were expression measures. Feature profiles varied across NMD subgroups, while genes added between 2020 and 2024 showed profiles similar to established NMD genes across all Boruta-confirmed features. This study identified genomic features that distinguish NMD genes from high-confidence disease genes and broader autosomal protein-coding genes. These findings provide insight into the gene architecture, expression, constraint, and evolutionary conservation of NMD genes and may inform candidate-gene prioritization in genetically unresolved NMDs.

Title: Mechanistic classification of the AAA superfamily with protein language models
Authors: Swan, J. A.; Hill, C. P.
Abstract: The ATPases Associated with various cellular Activites (AAA) are a class of proteins with diverse structure-function relationships whereby conserved 3-dimensional architecture is employed in varied mechanistic contexts. While cryo-electron microscopy has revealed extensive mechanistic data, predicting how specific sequence elements dictate unique biochemical mechanisms remains a challenge. Here, we present a machine learning framework to resolve these sequence-function relationships. We established a hierarchical classification scheme based on five distinct modes of coupling ATP hydrolysis to mechanical work. Using CatFunc, a lightweight protein language model (PLM)-based pipeline, we leveraged evolutionary context from millions of protein sequences for supervised classification of AAA domains based on mechanism. We observed excellent recall of our mechanistic annotations in masked validation studies, demonstrating that domain level context is sufficient to encapsulate the various observed mechanisms. Notably, systematic misclassifications revealed a shared evolutionary and mechanistic ancestry within the rotary motor class. Applying the model to out-of-distribution proteomic datasets, we established metrics to detect unrepresented functions. Our framework provides a scalable strategy for decoding molecular function from sequence data, offering a transferable approach for other biomedically important families such as membrane transporters, G protein-coupled receptors and kinases.

Title: The ModelSEED Biochemistry Database, 2026 update: grading multi-source thermodynamics
Authors: Freiburger, A.; Faria, J. P.; Zhu, R.; Edirisinghe, J. N.; Liu, F.; Taylor, C.; Setlur, V.; Giessmann, R. T.; Beber, M. E.; Noor, E.; Upadhyay, V.; Anand, M.; Maranas, C. D.; Huss, S.; Nikoloski, Z.; Arkin, A. P.; Cottingham, R. W.; Wood-Charlson, E. M.; Ramanathan, A.; Henry, C. S.; Seaver, S. M. D.
Abstract: The ModelSEED Biochemistry Database (https://modelseed.org/biochem) supplies foundational mass- and charge-balanced reaction networks for metabolic reconstructions. Here we present an update on the biochemistry where the database has been expanded to [~] 46,000 compounds, and [~] 56,000 reactions, featuring [~] 37,000 metabolic structures. We have expanded our approach for handling thermodynamic data, enabling multiple sources of data to be derived, integrated, and presented to the wider research community. We now publish predictions of pKa, reaction energy (and respective uncertainties), and estimates of reaction direction from multiple independent sources. Each reaction is graded gold, silver or bronze according to the strength of the evidence behind it, so that users can weigh its reliability directly. We also release reaction directions predicted by an ensemble of large language models. This multi-source approach exposes agreements and discrepancies between sources for [~] 33,000 reactions. Finally, to ensure data integrity, a new conflict-resolution pipeline reconciles structures across sources, documenting input from curators. Our work is publicly available at https://github.com/ModelSEED/ModelSEEDDatabase.

Title: Cross-Dataset Reanalysis of Mouse Alzheimer Disease Single-Cell RNA-Sequencing Data Reveals a Reproducible Innate Immune Activation Signature
Authors: Anand, A.; Natarajan, E.
Abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) studies of Alzheimer disease (AD) mouse models have proliferated across independent laboratories, brain regions, and platforms, yet the cross-study reproducibility of transcriptional signatures derived from such data remains underexplored. We reanalyzed six publicly available mouse brain scRNA-seq datasets (GSE140399, GSE140510, GSE143758, GSE208683, GSE214244, and GSE296027; 360,620 cells, 102 annotated clusters) using a standardized pipeline (Figure 1) comprising quality control, Leiden clustering, confidence-tiered marker-based cell-type annotation, sample-level pseudobulk differential expression, cross-dataset consistency analysis, and pathway enrichment. Pseudobulk differential expression, performed on 32 samples (16 AD, 16 Control) from five of the six datasets, identified 301 significant genes (FDR-adjusted p < 0.05) out of 20,629 tested, of which 290 (96.3%) were upregulated and 11 (3.7%) downregulated in AD. The upregulated set was dominated by innate immune and interferon-response genes (Ccl3, Ccl4, Ccl6, Itgax, Cst7, Tlr4, Trem2) and showed extremely strong enrichment for immune system and innate immune system pathways (Reactome, p {equiv} 1.9 x 10-43 and 2.1 x 10-29 respectively), phagosome and osteoclast differentiation (KEGG), and interferon alpha/beta signaling. Of the 301 significant genes, 235 (78%) showed the same direction of effect across all datasets in which they were tested. The sixth dataset, GSE296027, was excluded from differential expression analysis due to a gene-identifier corruption artifact introduced during pseudobulk aggregation (detailed in Methods and Limitations) but contributed valid cell-type composition and microglial subclustering data, independently recovering a disease-associated microglia-like state. These findings indicate that a reproducible, strongly immune/interferon-skewed transcriptional signature, rather than a balanced up/down transcriptional shift, characterizes the mouse AD models analyzed here.

Title: Enrich.AI: An Agentic AI Platform for Interactive GeneSet Enrichment Analysis and Biological Interpretation
Authors: Koumadorakis, D. E.; Exarchos, T. P.; Vlamos, P.; Vrahatis, A. G.
Abstract: Motivation: Enrichment analysis is widely used to extract biological meanings from gene lists. However, the large number of available tools and reference libraries often make the interpretation of results challenging. Inexperienced users lack clear guidance on which datasets and terms are most relevant to their data, whereas experienced researchers must navigate large result sets and consult multiple resources to identify biologically relevant findings. Integrating AI into this process can help to bridge these gaps. Results: We present Enrich.AI, a conversational biology assistant that integrates statistical enrichment analysis with automated biological interpretation. The agent operates on an LLM-based ReAct architecture and dynamically selects among the tools for enrichment (220+ gene set libraries), literature search (40+ million publications via Europe PMC), gene annotation, and database retrieval. Given a gene list and a short description of the biological context, Enrich.AI produces a written interpretation grounded in the retrieved literature and six interactive, configurable visualizations. A conversational interface enables human-in-the-loop refinement, letting researchers without programming experience explore results iteratively. The reliability of these interpretations was validated through a systematic evaluation on 50 gene sets, demonstrating high faithfulness to retrieved evidence and a low hallucination rate.

Title: MOSAIC: Learning Graph Node Embeddings from Spectrally Isolated Dominant Subspaces of Accumulated Diffusion Operators
Authors: Mohseni Ahooyi, T.; Stear, B.; Zhang, Y.; Lahiri, A.; Terry, J.; Zhang, S.; Simmons, J. A.; Corbett, R.; Sullivan, P.; Chinwalla, A.; Nemarich, C.; Rokita, J. L.; Diskin, S.; Silverstein, J. C.; Taylor, D. M.
Abstract: Graph embedding transforms complex networks into low-dimensional representations for analysis and downstream machine learning. Existing methods often rely on eigenvalue ordering, random-walk sampling, or neural optimization. We introduce MOSAIC, Multistep Operator Spectral Accumulation with Isolated Components, an unsupervised framework that constructs an accumulated diffusion operator from successive powers of a graph transition matrix. MOSAIC uses Krylov subspace analysis to identify dominant spectral components according to their convergence behavior. This approach emphasizes persistent and spectrally separated diffusion modes rather than selecting embedding coordinates solely by eigenvalue magnitude. We evaluated MOSAIC using a biomedical graph projection derived from the Data Distillery Knowledge Graph that contained 5,171 human genes and 10,147 phenotypes. Across embedding dimensions from 16 to 128, MOSAIC achieved node-type classification AUROCs from 0.9863 to 0.9926 and exceeded FastRP, Node2Vec, HashGNN, and GraphSAGE. For gene-phenotype link prediction, validation and test associations were withheld before embedding generation. Under progressive removal of all edges or specific edge classes, MOSAIC retained more node-label information than FastRP, including after extreme graph sparsification. In a focused DICER1 analysis, 106 of 137 documented phenotype associations received scores above 0.90, demonstrating concordance with known pleiotropic biology and prioritizing additional relationships for independent evaluation. These results support MOSAIC as a fully unsupervised framework for learning informative graph representations. Although demonstrated using a biomedical graph projection, MOSAIC is domain independent and can be applied to other complex networks

Title: Refining Protein Co-Membership in Reactome: A Weighted Scoring Approach Based on Hierarchy and Sequences of Patwhays
Authors: Beust, C.; Dameron, O.; Theret, N.; Becker, E.
Abstract: In network biology, analyzing pathways is critical to study mechanisms or sequences of biological events. The pathway co-membership approach aims to link proteins belonging to the same pathway inside a network that is a clique. Although this method is great for projecting pathway knowledge onto proteins, it remains unsuitable for some downstream applications relying on graph distances like random walks with restart. To address this limitation, we introduce a weighted pathway co-membership method that incorporates biological distances between proteins. We achieve this by developing an abstraction framework for Reactome pathways, which captures both their hierarchical organization and sequential relationships. By assigning weights to these abstractions, we define a scoring system for proteins within the pathway co-membership clique. We illustrate our approach using a Reactome pathway ("Signaling by TGF-beta receptor complex", R-HSA-170834), and explain how we generate the weighted co-membership cliques of the 29 Reactome top-level pathways. Next, we construct the entire weighted pathway co membership network of the Reactome knowledge base. Validation and evaluation of our method is performed using cancer hallmark gene sets and a random walk with restart experiment, comparing our approach to state-of-the-art methods. We show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods for gene prioritization on cancer hallmarks.

Title: Tractable and Thermodynamically Consistent pKa Prediction via First-Dissociation Aggregation
Authors: Liu, Z.; Zhu, Q.; Li, Q.; Zhu, Y.; Xu, Y.; Dai, B.; Li, Y.; Liu, Z.; Yang, S.
