Within SpatialOmicsLab, ST-Coscientist outperformed expert-led workflows and other scientific agents across six benchmark settings spanning spatial clustering, cell-type deconvolution and spatially variable gene detection. It constructed alignment-aware workflows for three-dimensional MERFISH data and addressed biological questions by selecting and analysing relevant reference datasets. Procedural memory increased the success rate of integrating and validating additional analytical tools from 48% to 95%. Together, SpatialOmicsLab and ST-Coscientist establish an extensible ecosystem for reproducible spatial transcriptomic research, enabling AI co-scientists to address evolving biological questions with an expanding analytical repertoire.

Title: drugMR: A multi-omics pipeline for genetically anchored drug-target discovery
Authors: Comesana Cimadevila, G.; Dib, M.-J.; Bracher-Smith, M.; Ducotterd, F.; Salih, D. A.; Bray, N. J.; Simmonds, E.; Escott-Price, V.
Abstract: Motivation: Genetically supported drug targets are an estimated 2.6 times more likely to succeed clinically, yet a disease association alone does not show which protein to target, in which direction, or what other effects may follow. This currently requires chaining separate tools. Results: drugMR is a Nextflow pipeline that, from GWAS and pQTL summary statistics, runs cis-Mendelian randomisation, colocalisation, SMR-HEIDI with bulk and/or single-cell QTLs, three-trait colocalisation and a phenome-wide screen for adverse effects and repurposing. Datasets are added through a manifest, every step runs in containers on a laptop, cluster or cloud, and results are explored in a dashboard. Applied to schizophrenia with brain pQTLs, drugMR tested 2,019 proteins in 4 h 19 min and prioritised 58 proteogenomic targets, 22 with multi-omic support; 4 had potential adverse effects. Availability and implementation: drugMR: https://github.com/guillermocomesanacimadevila/drugMR; documentation: https://guillermocomesanacimadevila.github.io/drugMR/. Demo data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22917384.

Title: Approximate local alignment via chained MEM divergence estimation for detecting horizontal gene transfer
Authors: Oualline, G.; Pandey, S.; Zhang, X. B.; Boucher, C. A.; Yu, Y. W.
Abstract: Local alignment tools struggle at querying against thousands of bacterial genomes, because the reference indexes are memory-intensive and base-level dynamic programming is slow. We present alamem (https://github.com/yunwilliamyu/alamem), an approximate local aligner that streams unprocessed reference databases and estimates average nucleotide identity (ANI) from Maximal-Exact-Match (MEM) chaining statistics. Alamem can query a bacterial genome against >85,000 prokaryotic genomes in under 30 seconds (with multithreading) using 4 GB of memory, making it over 16x faster and 21x more memory-efficient than existing local aligners using their default running modes. On top of alamem, we built alasight (https://github.com/graceoualline/alasight) for detecting signatures of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) by finding pairs of alamem hits to divergent genomes. Alasight achieves over an order of magnitude better sensitivity on data from real bovid microbiomes than existing mobile genetic element-detection software and provides depth and sparsity information supporting each putative HGT region.

Title: Evo2HiC: a multimodal foundation model for integrative analysis of genome sequence and architecture
Authors: Fang, T.; Li, Y.; Wang, X.; Xiao, Z.; Hang, S.; Murtaza, G.; Yang, J.; Xu, H.; Jha, A.; Noble, W. S.; Wang, S.
Abstract: Understanding how genome sequences shape three-dimensional (3D) genome architecture is fundamental to interpreting diverse biological processes. Although previous studies have shown that sequence information can predict 3D genome architecture, these models fall short in capturing cell type-specific structures because they are trained solely on sequence inputs. The widely available Hi-C data, which contains rich structural information across biosamples, can provide complementary features to sequence data for studying cell type-specific architectures. Recently, DNA foundation models have demonstrated encouraging performance in capturing long-range genomic dependencies, holding promise for modeling chromatin interactions. However, the extremely high computational cost of running these models limits their applicability to Hi-C analysis, which requires genome-wide sequence embeddings. Here, we present Evo2HiC, a multimodal foundation model that jointly models genome sequences and structures to study cell type-specific chromatin structure. The key idea of Evo2HiC is to distill a large-scale DNA foundation model, Evo 2 (7B), into a compact encoder, while guiding the distillation with Hi-C data to preserve genomic features critical for 3D genome analysis. The model supports two types of encoders, one that operates directly on DNA sequences, and a second that additionally takes as input corresponding Hi-C data. Using the DNA-only encoder and predicting raw Hi-C contact matrices, Evo2HiC improved distance-stratified Spearman correlation by 10.9% over Orca. Moreover, by jointly embedding Hi-C and sequence information Evo2HiC achieved the best overall Pearson correlation when predicting five representative epigenomic assays. Interpretation analysis of Evo2HiC revealed its ability to identify cell type-specific sequence motifs that explain changes in epigenomic signals. Finally, we demonstrated the cross-species generalizability of Evo2HiC on 177 species from the DNA Zoo dataset for Hi-C resolution enhancement. In summary, Evo2HiC is a foundation model that integrates genome sequences and 3D chromatin structure information, substantially reduces computational cost while maintaining state-of-the-art accuracy on predicting various epigenomic signals and genome architecture, enables the identification of cell type-specific motifs, and demonstrates robust generalizability across species.

Title: Cross-cohort Mamography]{Representation-dependent domain adaptation for cross-cohort generalization of mammography diagnostic models
Authors: Pandey, A. K.; Ahmad, S.
Abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) models for mammography can achieve high diagnostic performance when training and test data originate from similar populations and imaging environments, but performance often deteriorates under cross- cohort domain shift. Differences in acquisition systems, image characteristics, preprocessing, population composition, and disease prevalence can introduce distributional variation that is poorly captured by conventional within- dataset validation. Recent studies have further shown that Foundation Model representations can retain substantial dataset-specific information. However, it remains unclear how image representation influences diagnostic transfer to completely unseen cohorts and whether domain-adversarial learning provides comparable benefits across different representation types. Methods: We systematically evaluated cross-cohort mammography classification using seven independent datasets spanning diverse geographic, institutional, scanner, and imaging environments. Three image representations were compared: handcrafted radiomic features, EfficientNet-B0-derived features, and embeddings from the medical vision-language model MedSigLIP-448. Each was evaluated under three preprocessing conditions: unprocessed images, Otsu-based breast-region extraction, and Otsu extraction combined with Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE). Patient-level classification was performed using a mean-pooled multilayer perceptron (MLP) baseline and an attention-based Domain-Adversarial Neural Network (DANN). Generalization was evaluated using a multi-source Leave-One-Domain-Out (LODO) framework in which six datasets were used for model development and the seventh was completely withheld as an unseen test cohort, iteratively across all seven datasets. Performance was primarily assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC). Results: Cross-cohort performance depended strongly on image representation and model architecture. MedSigLIP consistently provided the highest performance on unseen cohorts. With MedSigLIP features, mean LODO AUC-ROC increased from 0.598 with MLP to 0.685 with DANN for unprocessed images, from 0.607 to 0.678 after Otsu preprocessing, and from 0.603 to 0.659 after CLAHE+Otsu preprocessing. When DANN-MLP differences were evaluated across held-out datasets and preprocessing conditions, a significant gain was observed for MedSigLIP after correction for multiple comparisons, whereas corresponding gains were not significant for Radiomics or EfficientNet-B0. A mixed-effects analysis similarly showed a positive MedSigLIP X DANN interaction, although this narrowly missed conventional statistical significance. Unprocessed images produced the highest numerical mean performance for MedSigLIP-DANN, but preprocessing itself had no significant overall effect. Notably, linear probing showed strong dataset discriminability in MedSigLIP and EfficientNet representations but little linearly recoverable dataset information in Radiomics, indicating that low dataset separability alone did not predict better diagnostic generalization. Conclusion: Cross-cohort mammography generalization depends strongly on the choice of image representation and its interaction with the classification strategy. MedSigLIP provided the most transferable representation in our multi-source unseen-domain evaluation, and the performance gain associated with DANN was concentrated in MedSigLIP rather than consistently observed across representation types. These findings suggest that the effectiveness of domain-adversarial learning is representation-dependent and that neither conventional preprocessing nor low dataset discriminability alone ensures robust transfer to unseen clinical cohorts.

Title: mCranberry: A rationally engineered monomeric red fluorescent protein with 85% quantum yield
Authors: Chaubey, S.; Mukherjee, S.; Adams, A.; Walker, A. R.; Furgason, M. L. M.; Babu, H. K. R. R.; Mathews, I. I.; Manna, P.
Abstract: Fluorescent proteins (FPs) are the workhorse of modern-day cellular imaging and biosensing. However, rationally predicting and engineering the photophysical properties of FPs remain challenging, as these are governed by complex three-dimensional microenvironments and post-translational modifications. Here, we present a novel surface-mutation-guided engineering strategy combined with iterative rounds of rational mutagenesis to improve key photophysical properties of red fluorescent proteins (RFPs). This approach generated two bright, monomeric RFP variants from the mFruits lineage, mCranberry and mCranberry2, with quantum yields of 85% and 80%, respectively. Strategic incorporation of charged amino acid residues on the protein surface enhanced fluorescence quantum yield without compromising photostability. Comprehensive photophysical characterization and live-cell microscopy demonstrate enhanced performance of these variants and establish their utility as robust probes for fluorescence imaging. However, the exact mechanism of such improvements is subject to further investigation. Collectively, this work introduces a strategy for optimizing fluorescence properties and provides a framework that may be broadly applicable to other pigment-protein systems such as genetically encoded metal-ion indicators and photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes.

Title: Angiotensin II Promotes Mitral Valve and Left Atrial Pathology in Fibrillin-1C1041G/+ Mice
Authors: Franklin, M. K.; Howatt, D. A.; Pettey, A. C.; Moorleghen, J. J.; Levitan, B. M.; Mullick, A. E.; Saffitz, J.; Lu, H. S.; Daugherty, A.
Abstract: Background: Activation of the renin-angiotensin system (RAS) contributes to aortic diseases caused by fibrillin-1 haploinsufficiency (Fbn1C1041G/+). However, whether RAS activation influences mitral valve disease associated with FBN1 variants remains undefined. This study determined whether inhibition or augmentation of the RAS affects mitral valve pathology in Fbn1C1041G/+ mice. Methods: Angiotensinogen (AGT) antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) were administered for 12 weeks to inhibit the RAS in male and female Fbn1C1041G/+ mice. To augment the RAS, mice were infused with angiotensin II (AngII; 1,000 ng/kg/min) for 28 days. Mitral valve and heart function were monitored by ultrasound. At termination, hearts were dissected free and tissue sectioned to assess mitral valve leaflet thickness and pathology. Results: Mitral valve leaflet thickness was significantly increased in Fbn1C1041G/+ mice compared to Fbn1+/+ littermates of both sexes. ASO-mediated AGT inhibition did not alter this phenotype despite markedly reduced plasma AGT concentrations. AngII infusion increased mitral valve leaflet thickness in Fbn1C1041G/+ mice with increased proteoglycan and collagen content, while exerting minimal effects in Fbn1+/+ mice. Twenty-five percent of AngII-infused Fbn1C1041G/+ mice died of non-vascular causes. Ultrasound showed mitral valve dysfunction in AngII-infused Fbn1C1041G/+ mice. Grossly expanded left atria were common in AngII-infused Fbn1C1041G/+ mice. These markedly enlarged left atria contained increased fibrosis, macrophage accumulation, and platelet-rich masses. Conclusions: Mitral valves of Fbn1C1041G/+ mice did not respond to AGT inhibition but were markedly more susceptible to AngII infusion, with greater increases in thickness and compositional changes than mitral valves of Fbn1+/+ mice. In addition, AngII promoted mitral valve dysfunction that were associated with pronounced left atrial pathology.

Title: Progressive Actomyosin Remodeling Defining a Structured Podocyte Injury Response in Nephrotic Syndrome
Authors: Langner, E.; Parra, K.; Jiang, S.; Jain, S.; Mahjoub, M. R.; Genin, G. M.; Miner, J. H.; Suleiman, H. Y.
Abstract: Nephrotic syndrome, the leading cause of chronic kidney disease worldwide, is associated with injury and eventual loss of podocytes, the specialized epithelial cells that form the final layer of the kidney's filtration apparatus. The progression from injury to loss is largely irreversible. However, some forms of nephrotic syndrome undergo remission, suggesting that injured podocytes may retain a capacity for repair, the structural basis of which remains unknown. Podocytes respond to injury by the stereotypical morphological change known as foot process effacement (FPE), which can be visualized using transmission electron microscopy. Using modified ultrastructure expansion microscopy (U-ExM) protocol combined with super-resolution microscopy, we discovered that injured podocytes exhibit a three-stage progression of FPE maturation, with kinetics determined by the degree of actomyosin contractility. Through longitudinal study of adriamycin-induced nephropathy in mice, we identified three sequential stages of actomyosin reorganization within the sarcomere-like structures (SLSs) that define the injury response: focal infiltration of myosin IIA into synaptopodin-rich foot processes (Stage 1), disordered intermingling of synaptopodin/myosin IIA (Stage 2), and the formation of highly organized periodic contractile arrays oriented perpendicular to the direction of capillary blood flow (Stage 3). Longitudinal quantification revealed predictable temporal dynamics, with mature Stage 3 predominating by day 7-9 post-injury. To determine whether this sequence is conserved in human disease, we analyzed kidney biopsies from patients with minimal change disease, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, membranous nephropathy, and diabetic nephropathy. The same three stages were present across all four diseases, and their distribution tracked disease course: acute podocytopathies exhibited heterogeneous early-stage patterns, whereas chronic injuries converged on uniform, mature SLS organization. These findings demonstrate that podocyte injury is a graded, potentially reversible process rather than a binary switch. They identify structured actomyosin remodeling as a conserved wound response across mechanistically distinct kidney diseases and suggest that therapeutic strategies targeting specific stages of this progression could alter the trajectory of diverse glomerular diseases.

Title: Compressive stress couples calcium signalling to translational control and proteostasis
Authors: Fragale, G.; Hershey, B. J.; Li, Y.; Parodi, G.; Beznoussenko, G. V.; Allievi, E.; Ajazi, A.; Berti, N.; Zheng, W.; Lavagnino, Z.; Matafora, V.; Pisati, F.; Manfrini, N.; Biffo, S.; Martinez, L.; Karakatsani, A.; Guadagno, M.; Moor, A. E.; Parazzoli, D.; Cosentino-Lagomarsino, M.; Mazza, D.; Bachi, A.; Maiuri, P.; Havas, K. M.
Abstract: Compressive stress is a pervasive feature of solid tumour growth, and mechanical loading is known to activate calcium signalling through the mechanosensitive channel Piezo1. How this signal is converted into changes in cellular biosynthetic capacity, however, remains unclear. Here we show that compressive stress engages a Piezo1-dependent calcium checkpoint that reduces translational output with increasing mechanical load, independently of mTORC1 and the integrated stress response. Compression triggers Piezo1-dependent release of endoplasmic reticulum Ca2, activating eEF2 kinase to slow translational elongation. This same Ca2 signal drives mitochondrial remodelling and reactive oxygen species production, which reinforce translational repression through redox-dependent oxidation of the translation initiation factor eIF2{beta}. In parallel, Ca2-dependent AMPK activation triggers autophagic ribosome degradation, alleviating compression-induced macromolecular crowding and restoring cytoplasmic rheology despite sustained mechanical load. These mechanisms act at distinct levels of translational control: initiation, elongation and ribosome abundance; yet converge to limit biosynthetic output under compression. Consistent with a role for this pathway in tumour adaptation to mechanical constraint, eEF2K expression correlates with poor overall survival in a public PDAC patient dataset. Together, these findings define a mechano-metabolic checkpoint through which cells actively tune biosynthetic capacity to their physical environment.

Title: Chronic ER Stress Disrupts Mitochondrial-Associated ER Membrane Integrity in Corneal Endothelial Cells.
Authors: Lee, S.; Kim, S. Y.; Akram, O.; Qureshi, S.; Kashi, A.; Steidl, W.; Ritzer, L.; Price, M.; Price, F. W.; Schon, E.; Kumar, V.
Abstract: Purpose: Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy (FECD) is an age-related degenerative disease of the corneal endothelium cells (CEnCs), affecting 4% of the US population over 40. While Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and mitochondrial stress have been independently associated with FECD pathogenesis, few studies have examined ER-mitochondrial interactions/ER-mitochondrial contact sites/mitochondria-associated ER membrane (MAM), or MAM proteins, and their contribution to ER and mitochondrial stress in FECD. This study aims to characterize alterations in MAMs and identify key MAM proteins associated with ER and mitochondrial stress in FECD. Methods: Human corneal endothelial cell line (HCEnC-21T) and Fuchs corneal endothelial cell line (F35T) were cultured and subjected to ER stressor tunicamycin for 6 and 24 hours. MAM proteins were isolated by subcellular fractionation, and key ER and mitochondrial-damage-sensor proteins, such as PERK and Parkin, respectively, were identified by immunoblotting. ER-mitochondrial contact sites were quantified using the MAM plasmid and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) in normal and Fuchs cell lines, as well as in human tissues under chronic ER stress. Results: ER-mitochondrial contact distance significantly increased in Fuchs tissues compared with normal tissues, and a similar increase was observed in 21T cell line after tunicamycin treatment. There was a significant increase in the intensity of the MAM plasmid upon tunicamycin treatment at 6 hours in the 21T cell line compared to the non-treated control. However, MAM plasmid intensity significantly decreased at 24 hours compared to 6 hours post-tunicamycin treatment in 21T cell line. Analysis of MAM function by quantifying phosphatidylserine synthase 1 (PSS1 [gene PTDSS1]) expression in 21T cells showed a reduction in PTDSS1 expression after 24 hours of tunicamycin treatment. ER stress protein PERK and mitochondria damage sensor protein (Parkin) significantly increased in the MAM fraction after tunicamycin at 24 hours in 21T cell. Conclusions: Fuchs cell lines and tissues demonstrate decreased ER-mitochondrial interactions/MAMs, which are also seen in 21T cell line after chronic ER stress. Under chronic ER stress, ER and mitochondrial stress mediator proteins are translocated to MAM. This study highlights the importance of MAMs as a potential mediator of ER-mitochondria crosstalk in degenerating corneal endothelial cells for FECD.

Title: Exploring the substrate specificity and catalytic mechanism in a PAPS independent ASST from Salmonella typhimurium
Authors: Nimbona, N. M.; Obeid, H.; Balci, D.; Joublin-Delavat, A.; Gladis, A.; Cladiere, L.; D. Davari, M.; Grandjean, C.; Daligault, F.; Czjzek, M.
Abstract: Sulfation plays an important role in many metabolic processes such as substrate detoxification, solubilization or activation. The enzymes responsible for these reactions, sulfotransferases, occur in all domains of life and can be classified in two major, evolutionary independent groups, PAPS dependent and PAPS independent or arysulfate sulfotransferases (ASST) enzymes. Besides the fact that they play key roles in biological functions, sulfotransferases can be interesting enzymatic tools to selectively sulfate specific positions of various metabolites. To this end we need to understand the relation between sequence, structure and function. Actually, eukaryotic PAPS dependent sulfotransferases have extensively been studied, while we largely lack knowledge about the diversity of bacterial PAPS-independent ASSTs. We have conducted a multidisciplinary study of a bacterial sulfotransferase from Salmonella typhimurium, revealing the importance of active site residues for activity and guiding substrate specificity. Based on the crystal structure in complex with substrate, we used molecular docking combined with Quantum Mechanics/Molecular Mechanics (QM/MM) free energy calculations to investigate the reaction catalytic mechanism with a focus on the role of specific active site residues in substrate specificity. Our results show that the catalytic mechanism involving three conserved histidines is common with previously determined ASSTs, and highlight a specific pair of aromatic residues, Phe174 and Tyr557, that play an important role in defining the substrate specificity in ASST clade 5. These findings enhance our general understanding of how substrate specificity is attained and has the potential to guide further enzyme engineering to expand the acceptor scope of ASSTs.

Title: Photobiocatalytic Diastereo- and Enantioselective Synthesis of Non-Canonical Amino Acids Bearing Challenging Stereochemical Dyads and Triads
Authors: Bo, Z.; Cheng, L.; Zhang, X.; Singh, A.; Liu, P.; Yang, Y.
Abstract: Catalyst-controlled stereodivergent synthesis of acyclic molecules bearing multiple stereogenic centers remains a longstanding challenge in asymmetric catalysis, particularly through intermolecular radical C-C coupling. Here, we report the directed evolution of pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP)-dependent biocatalysts for the stereodivergent synthesis of non canonical amino acids bearing either skipped , {gamma}-stereochemical dyads or contiguous , {beta}, {gamma}-stereochemical triads. Starting from a thermophilic tryptophan synthase {beta}-subunit, protein engineering generated complementary enzyme variants that selectively construct three of the four possible , {gamma}-stereoisomers through biocatalyst-controlled reversal of both remote {gamma}-stereochemistry and proximal -stereochemistry. These engineered enzymes catalyzed intermolecular radical C-C bond formation with a broad range of secondary alkyltrifluoroborates, affording , {gamma}-disubstituted amino acids in excellent yields and stereoselectivities. Furthermore, directed evolution enabled efficient {beta}-dehydroxylative radical coupling of the non-native threonine-derived aminoacrylate intermediate, providing amino acids bearing contiguous , {beta}, {gamma}-stereochemical triads with up to 96:4:<0.1:<0.1 d.r. and >99:1 e.r.. To further demonstrate the synthetic utility of this platform, the stereochemically enriched amino acids were transformed into valuable {gamma}-chiral amines through engineered PLP dependent tryptophan decarboxylases, establishing a dual PLP enzyme based biocatalytic cascade for the enantiodivergent synthesis of privileged amine scaffolds. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that enzyme controlled {gamma}-stereoselectivity originates from active-site remodeling that modulates {pi}-{pi} interactions and steric contacts governing the facial selectivity of the radical addition step. This work expands the synthetic capabilities of radical biocatalysis by enabling catalyst-controlled stereodivergent assembly of complex acyclic stereochemical arrays and establishes engineered PLP enzymes as versatile catalysts for the synthesis of stereochemically complex amino acids and chiral amines.

Title: Repurposing dopamine D3 receptor fluorescent ligands for D2 receptor
Authors: Ots, K.; Laasfeld, T.; Hollo, K.; Ilisson, M.; Ortigueira Noya, S.; Grassl, F.; Tousi, D.; Allas, H.-R.; Majellaro, M.; Enkvist, E.; Heinrich, M. R.; Sotelo, E.; Allikalt, A.
Abstract: The dopamine D2 receptor is a principal target of antipsychotic and antiparkinsonian drugs, yet well-characterized fluorescent ligands for the D2 receptor remain scarce compared with its relative, the D3 receptor. Here we show that fluorescent ligands developed for the D3 subtype can be repurposed as tools for studying the D2 receptor pharmacology. Using a machine-learning-assisted, live-cell fluorescence microscopy assay, we screened twelve fluorescent probes and identified eight ligands that bound specifically to the D2 receptor at 10 nM. Four ligands exhibited classical saturable binding, yielding Kd in the nanomolar range, whereas the remaining probes displayed unsaturated, time-dependent binding profiles. Kinetic analyses revealed substantial differences in association and dissociation behavior, highlighting the importance of time-resolved measurements. Competition binding with dopamine and haloperidol yielded affinity estimates consistent with literature values. These results expand the toolkit of validated D2 receptor fluorescent probes and support cross-receptor repurposing as a strategy for fluorescent ligand development.

Title: Unsupervised 3D classification and characterisation of osteocyte and chondrocyte lacunae in the murine osteochondral unit
Authors: Banerjee, A.; Durongbhan, P.; Uniyal, P.; Gaillard, V.; Schadow, J. E.; Boersma, E. C.; Stok, K. S.; Ruffoni, D.; Lenthe, G. H. v.
Abstract: In the murine osteochondral unit, morphology of chondrocyte lacunae (CCL) within calcified articular cartilage and osteocyte lacunae (OCL) within the underlying subchondral bone reflects local biomechanical conditions that are altered in disease, making reliable discrimination of both lacunar populations important for studying osteochondral physiology and pathology. Histology is generally considered the gold standard for identifying CCL and OCL. However, it is inherently limited to two-dimensional assessment and a relatively small tissue section, restricting comprehensive characterisation of three-dimensional lacunar structure. Synchrotron-radiation micro-computed tomography (SR-microCT) enables volumetric quantification of lacunae; where classification is typically based on the position of each lacuna relative to the cement line separating calcified cartilage from bone, requiring manual delineation of this convoluted interface. Such approaches are labour-intensive, operator-dependent, and rely on access to specialised synchrotron infrastructure that is not widely available. To address these limitations, we present a fully automated, annotation-free pipeline for classifying OCL and CCL in the mouse osteochondral unit based on desktop micro-computed tomography (microCT), independent of cement line identification. The proposed unsupervised workflow requires neither tissue separation nor labelled training data, enabling objective and scalable discrimination of lacunar populations directly from volumetric image data. Seven morphometric and positional features per lacuna were extracted from SR-microCT and desktop microCT datasets and analysed using Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP). Validation of the pipeline outcome on SR-microCT against manual classification across specimens yielded very-high agreement, with Gwet's AC1, the Matthews correlation coefficient, and balanced accuracy each approaching 0.99, in both healthy and post-traumatic osteoarthritis specimens. Such a workflow can be readily adapted for the investigation of osteochondral interface in various other species.

Title: Position-wise Fold-Switch Prediction in Metamorphic Proteins: A Comparison of Handcrafted and Language Model Features
Authors: Machingal, P.; Hemachandra, N.; Balaji, P. V.
Abstract: In this work, we focus on predicting fold-switching phenomena observed in certain protein structures. Proteins that undergo fold-switching are called metamorphic proteins. We model fold-switch prediction in proteins as a position/residue-wise classification task. We use various features extracted from a protein's sequence as well as structure to train the classifiers. We propose a novel class of handcrafted parametrised features that encode the structural context of a residue. We also use embeddings from existing protein language models (PLMs) to train the classifiers. We train binary and 3-class classifiers, with the 3-class classifiers providing granular information on the type of fold-switch. In our computations, higher classification performance is achieved for binary prediction as compared to 3-class granular prediction. The handcrafted features perform comparably with the PLM embeddings on our standard test set. A rigorous error analysis by us during the review period revealed a critical data-leakage vulnerability in the metamorphic protein test data. This analysis also revealed that the PLM-based classifier suffers sequence-memorisation bias and fails to generalise to novel fold-switching sequences. On the other hand, one of our domain-informed handcrafted feature based classifier detects fold-switching without relying on sequence memory.

Title: Synthesis-aware generative design in trillion-scale chemical spaces for automated drug discovery
Authors: Seo, S.; Sung, Y.; Hwang, S.-Y.; Kang, M.; Lee, J.; Bordi, S.; Raguz, L.; Choi, J.; Melnichenko, D.; Namkung, W.; Lee, S.; Lim, J.; Wanner, B. M.; Han, J. M.; Kim, W. Y.
Abstract: Autonomous drug discovery via generative molecular design is critically bottlenecked by the production of chemically intractable structures. Multi-trillion-scale make-on-demand libraries guarantee synthetic feasibility, but conventional virtual screening cannot efficiently navigate these vast spaces or address multi-parameter optimization. We introduce Hyper Screening X, a generative AI framework integrating structure-based design with automated synthesis hardware. By encoding deterministic reaction logic in a generative flow network, the framework evaluates only 10 million candidates to navigate an 11-trillion-compound space, jointly optimizing physicochemical properties while ensuring compatibility with automated synthesis. Prospective validation against an SLC1A5 variant with a cryptic interface yielded a 96% synthesis success rate and a 50% functional hit rate, identifying two first-in-class lead compounds. This synthesis-aware strategy advances autonomous, closed-loop drug discovery.

Title: KRAKEN: A provenance-tracked knowledge graph for multiomic and wellness research
Authors: Glen, A. K.; Witherington, D.; Leslie, T.; Baumgartner, A.; Fernando, A.; Vemuri, B.; Nahman, O.; Glusman, G.; Hood, L.; Pflieger, L.; Rappaport, N.
Abstract: Existing general-purpose biomedical knowledge graphs tend to focus on disease mechanisms and drug repurposing, leaving multiomic and wellness-relevant content underrepresented. KRAKEN (Knowledge Research & Analysis Kit for Evidence Networks) addresses this gap by integrating existing graphs (including Translator KG Open, RTX-KG2, and ROBOKOP) with specialized sources such as RefMet, LIPID MAPS, NIH Common Data Elements, Polygenic Score Catalog, and derived wellness measures including biological age and biological BMI. The resulting graph spans ~26M nodes and ~121M edges across 62 entity types. KRAKEN adopts the Biolink Model as its semantic layer, ensuring compatibility with standardized resources emerging from the NIH NCATS Biomedical Data Translator program. A lightweight, modular build system rebuilds the full graph (including entity resolution), with peak memory consumption under 48 GB, and supports flexible inclusion or exclusion of sources, allowing the user to scope the graph to a domain of interest. Built-in analytical tools include multi-hop reasoning, subgraph extraction, text, vector and hybrid entity search, and enrichment analyses, all accessible through an interactive web interface, a REST API, and a Model Context Protocol server, the last enabling direct consumption by agentic and LLM-based systems. KRAKEN is freely available at https://app.krakenkg.com.

Title: A permeable G310 constriction limits K+ flux in the activated KCNQ2 pore and is disrupted by the encephalopathy variant G310S
Authors: Qoshimboyev, S.; Marimuthu, P.; Makhkamov, M.; Razzokov, J.
Abstract: KCNQ2 (Kv7.2) subunits contribute to the channels that carry the neuronal M-current, and variants in KCNQ2 cause epilepsies that range from self-limited neonatal seizures to developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE). Structures of KCNQ2 bound to PIP2 and cannabidiol show a widened activation gate, yet it has remained unclear which point of the activated pore limits K+ flux and how DEE variants at that point act. We simulated the KCNQ2 pore domain (PDB 8J01) in a POPC bilayer under an applied field of about 565 mV, restraining only the terminal residues of S5 and S6 so that G310 and S314 were free. The activated pore conducted K+ at 4.3 pS (95% CI 2.5-6.9; 17 net filter crossings in 1120 ns over four replicas), while the closed-state pore (PDB 7CR3) conducted none in 560 ns. Conduction proceeded by knock-on through a filter that was doubly occupied in 84-92% of frames. Along S6 the narrowest position of the activated pore was not the canonical gate residue S314 but the glycine of the Pro-Ala-Gly motif, G310: activation widens S314 by 0.37 nm but G310 by only 0.07 nm, and restraining G310 to its closed-state width in one replica abolished gate crossings. The DEE variant G310S reduced conduction about six-fold (G310S/wild-type ratio 0.16, 95% CI 0.02-0.66; p = 0.003). Its serine hydroxyls project into the constriction and halve the water column in the G310 plane (8.7 to 4.7 waters), an effect reproduced in CHARMM36m (9.9 to 4.3). The first coordination shell of a K+ ion at the constriction was, however, conserved (6.3 vs 6.5 oxygens), because the serine hydroxyls replace the waters they displace. The hydroxyls did not retain the ion: contacts lasted tens of picoseconds, and ions were instead turned back at the serine ring, fewer reaching the gate plane (45 vs 79 excursions per microsecond) and fewer of those crossing it (5% vs 23%). In mixed tetramers carrying one or two variant subunits the effect on the water column was additive, each subunit removing about a quarter of it (f = 0.22 and 0.58 of the full effect). These results identify G310 as the flux-limiting constriction of the activated KCNQ2 pore in our simulations and point to a permeation defect as one component of G310S loss of function.

Title: Adaptive motility and feeding strategies of deep-branching predatory protists
Authors: Bouvard, J.; Girard, A.; Bentley, S. A.; Auradou, H.; Wan, K. Y.
Abstract: Heterotrophic flagellates play a major role in nutrient recycling and shaping aquatic microbial communities. Many motile species have evolved diverse predatory strategies to exploit microbial prey, from bacteria to small eukaryotes. Excavates, deep-branching eukaryotic lineages with distinctive biflagellate morphology and conserved cytoskeletal features, exhibit varied feeding behaviours, including grazing, raptorial feeding, and filter-feeding. However, the temporal dynamics of their motility, feeding, and spatial distribution in relation to bacterial population density remain under-explored. Here, we quantify the behavioural ecology of excavates using high-resolution, single-cell tracking and quantitative analysis. Focussing on two Discoba species - the marine Jakoba libera and freshwater Reclinomonas americana - we identify different behavioural patterns: J. libera swims, forages and feeds, while R. americana swims and feeds. Prey availability differentially affects motility: J. libera increases the number of swimming cells when food is scarce, while R. americana shows the opposite trend. Spatial statistics reveal fundamental differences in their feeding and redistribution strategies. J. libera acts as an active forager, whereas R. americana behaves as a strict filter feeder. A third species, the anaerobic Kipferlia bialata (from a different clade), adopts a foraging strategy similar to J. libera. Together, these results elucidate the adaptive relationship between prey availability, feeding modes, and motility in bacteriovorous excavate flagellates, offering new insights into the ecological and evolutionary dynamics of microbial predators.

Title: Direct visualization of lysosome-mediated intracellular transport and membrane anchoring of TNF-α in human T cells
Authors: Burgess, A.; Gunasekara, H.; Xie, J.; Hu, Y. S.
Abstract: Tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-) represents a major pro-inflammatory cytokine associated with chronic inflammation. Enhanced understanding of intracellular trafficking of TNF- enables the identification of drug targets that modulate TNF- secretion at the cellular source. However, conventional cytokine assays provide only bulk measurements of secreted TNF- or static measurements in fixed cells and therefore cannot provide mechanistic information. Here, we report a fluorescence imaging platform to visualize and quantify intracellular TNF- trafficking in human T cells. Using a Jurkat T cell line stably expressing TNF- fused to mStayGold as a model system, we revealed through single-particle tracking (SPT) that T cell activation increased the motility of TNF- vesicles and that microtubule perturbation disrupted this increased motility. 3D structured illumination microscopy uncovered spatial associations between TNF- vesicles and lysosomes, and SPT further demonstrated their coordinated transport. Using total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy, we captured the sub-second splitting of single TNF- vesicles into multiple puncta that subsequently separated, suggesting delivery of TNF- from the vesicle to the plasma membrane. Confocal-based super-resolution microscopy further resolved TNF- vesicles fusing with the plasma membrane and transmembrane TNF-. Together, these imaging capabilities for tracking and super-resolving the intracellular transport and membrane delivery of TNF- in live T cells enable mechanistic studies of TNF- trafficking and release.

Title: Membrane Filtration Removes Lipids and Compromises the Acoustic Stability of Nanobubbles
Authors: Yaali, M.; Berndl, E.; Khan, A.; Strohm, E.; Kosmides, T.; Exner, A. A.; Kolios, M. C.
Abstract: Nanobubbles (NBs) have been widely investigated as ultrasound contrast and therapeutic agents, yet whether submicron gas bubbles can directly generate measurable ultrasound signals remains controversial. Because acoustic scattering scales with bubble size, several studies have recently attributed nanobubble echogenicity primarily to larger bubbles. A recent Science Advances publication, attributed the loss of ultrasound signal after filtration to the removal of residual larger bubbles [1]. This interpretation assumes that filtration acts solely as a size-selection process. Here, we show that filtration also alters the shell properties and stability of lipid-coated NBs, independent of size. Filtered NBs (F-NBs) show significant lipid loss and accumulation on the filters themselves, resulting in decreased bubble stability and greater susceptibility to destruction under acoustic excitation. To decouple size from processing effects, we generated NB populations size-matched to filtered samples using increased centrifugation (IC-NBs), a comparatively gentler separation method. Despite comparable size distributions, IC-NBs retained sustained ultrasound scattering, whereas filtered NBs showed significantly reduced acoustic persistence. Filtration through 5 m pores, ~5-fold larger than the largest bubbles, preserved acoustic persistence but still reduced bubble concentration by ~30%, suggesting that membrane contact may contribute to bubble loss beyond size exclusion. Complementary lipid and gas-content assays provided further evidence of filtration-induced changes. The 0.45 m filtration removed substantially more total lipid than could be attributed to free-lipid removal alone, while the lipid associated with the larger bubbles removed during filtration accounted for only ~5% of the additional lipid loss. Encapsulated gas content remained comparable to that of size-matched centrifuged controls, suggesting that the reduced acoustic stability of filtered NBs is more closely associated with changes in lipid content than with loss of the gas core. These results indicate that membrane filtration is not a purely size-selective process: it removes substantially more lipid than size exclusion predicts and yields bubbles that are less stable under ultrasound, most likely through changes in shell lipid content or in the surrounding lipid reservoir, underscoring the importance of processing-induced effects in interpreting nanobubble echogenicity.

Title: Anneal-MaxCal: kinetic ensembles from a Markov model learned along a solute-tempering ladder
Authors: Brotzakis, Z. F.; Rekatsinas, N.
Abstract: A full characterisation of a molecular system requires its metastable states, their populations and their interconversion rates. Molecular Dynamics can in principle provide this characterisation but is limited by sampling and by force-field inaccuracies. Enhanced sampling addresses the first problem, but typically requires prior knowledge of reaction coordinates or metastable states and often sacrifices the kinetics, while maximum-caliber reweighting by Brotzakis, Vendruscolo and Bolhuis [Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A., 118(2):e2012423118, 2021] has been implemented to that matter on reweighting continuous pathways by imposing rate constants as kinetic constraints in two-state protein folding. Here, we introduce Anneal-MaxCal, which tackles both problems by imposing rate constants or time-resolved data on a Markov model learned along an annealed solute-tempering ladder spanning softer to physical interactions. MBAR assigns physical free energies to all 160 cells of a slow TICA subspace, against 79 visited at the physical coupling. The square-root approximation (SqRA), a discretised diffusion on this free-energy landscape, converts these populations into a detailed-balance rate matrix. Its prefactors, which act as a position-dependent diffusivity across each cell face, are learned from transitions at the softer couplings and extrapolated log-linearly to the physical coupling. This yields rates and a committor across the TICA space, although the physical rung contains a single barrier crossing. For alanine dipeptide, 665 ns of simulation give a relaxation time of 5430 {+/-} 996 ps against 4413 {+/-} 446 ps from 15.4 s of unbiased dynamics, whereas a constant prefactor is 2.5 times too slow. Maximum caliber then minimally perturbs this prior, with the posterior populations following from a generalised Doob transform. A synthetic time-resolved density with a tenfold slower back-transition lowers {Delta}F from 5.191 to 2.885 kBT , raises the product-basin population from 0.0055 to 0.0529 and slows relaxation 9.47-fold, leaving the reactant basin unchanged. Forward and backward rates accelerated 3 and 20-fold raise {Delta}F by 1.892 kBT and shorten relaxation from 4818 to 289 ps.

Title: Blockiness as Determinant of Liquid Phase Formation by Polypeptide-Like Polymers in Stickers-Spacers Paradigm
Authors: Vasilenko, E. O.; Belous, D. S.; Ivankov, D. N.
Abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) driven by intrinsically disordered protein regions underlies the formation of membraneless organelles. The role of these structures in cell biology is an active area of research, yet their physical understanding remains less developed than that of protein assemblies with well-defined, rigid tertiary structures. The amino acid composition of disordered regions, particularly the abundance of charged residues, is known to modulate phase behavior. These factors govern accessible conformations, the assembly of compact sticker clusters, and the porosity of the resulting polymer networks. In contrast, the spatial distribution of side-chain volumes remains a comparatively understudied sequence determinant. Here, we employ a model that captures the patterning of side-chain volumes and interaction strengths without specifying chemical identity to show how sequence blockiness modulates the phase-nucleation propensity, connectivity, and compactness of polypeptide-like polymer assemblies. Using a library of polymers with identical composition but permuted residue arrangements, we show that clustering of bulky residues generates cooperative sticker domains and identify the threshold blockiness required to stabilize polymer networks. Coarse-grained simulations and mean-field theory reveal that this effect arises from an interplay among steric repulsion, solvent entropy, and higher-valency interactions, whereby blocky patterns promote the formation of multi-node percolated networks. Segregation of stickers and spacers is therefore one of the sequence parameters governing LLPS which may be useful for interpreting the evolution of disordered protein sequences, high-throughput proteome screening, and engineering of stimuli-responsive biomaterials. These rules may be exploited to predetermine condensate stability, viscoelasticity, and molecular exchange rates without altering chemical functionality.

Title: VesiScope: A stand-alone tool for the automatic detection, quantification and size analysis of GUVs from phase contrast microscopy images
Authors: Cecchi, D.; Lasala, A.; Poli, F.; De Remigis, E.; Moccia, S.; Palagi, S.
Abstract: Fluorescence microscopy is routinely used in the quantitative analysis of Giant Unilamellar Vesicles (GUVs) because it makes GUVs visible and easy to detect. Nonetheless, it requires fluorescence-equipped microscopes and, especially, the addition of tagged molecules that may introduce undesired and unaccounted variations compared to the pristine formulation. Alternatively, phase-contrast microscopy can be used to observe GUVs without labelling, yet the automatic detection of GUVs in phase-contrast images by standard image processing techniques is difficult. To overcome this limitation, we developed a framework for the automated detection and size characterization of label-free GUVs based on YOLOv11 model, a state-of-art lightweight Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for object detection. Trained on 164 phase-contrast microscope images containing 4666 manually annotated vesicles, the model enables robust detection under low contrast-to-noise ratio and heterogeneous illumination. The trained model is implemented in a stand-alone desktop application supporting multiple analysis in a single run, pixel-to-micrometer calibration, and automated size distribution analysis. This approach achieves high detection accuracy and competitive cross-microscope generalization using YOLOv11 nano on greyscale image. Retraining scripts compatible with standard hardware are also provided to enhance adaptability. This tool enables fast and reliable analysis of GUVs without altering their composition, supporting experimental reproducibility.

Title: Directed evolution of a thermostable family-A DNA polymerase into a reverse transcriptase for 2'-modified RNA
Authors: Vincent, E.; Lopez, C.; Sieskind, R.; Commenge, I.; Navaza, R.; Haouz, A.; Delarue, M.
Abstract: RNA-based therapeutics increasingly rely on nuclease-resistant xeno-nucleic acids (XNAs), but engineering polymerases capable of reading and amplifying these non-canonical substrates remains a major challenge. Natural DNA polymerases cannot process C2' sugar modifications, and the complete structural determinants governing this limitation remain poorly understood, limiting rational design strategies. In this study, we apply directed evolution methods to Thermus thermophilus DNA polymerase using a microfluidic implementation of the Compartmentalized Self-Replication (CSR). We identify an engineered variant, termed E5, capable of reverse transcribing C2'-modified RNA, a previously inaccessible activity for this enzyme. Next-generation sequencing allow us to track evolutionary trajectories across nine rounds of evolution. Through an integrated analysis combining statistical methods, protein language models, and crystallographic data, we reveal unknown epistatic networks controlling polymerase function. This large-scale experimental dataset (>196,000 thermostable enzyme variants) provides a robust basis for predicting sequence-to-function relationships, accelerating development of enzymes for aptamer discovery and synthetic biology applications.

Title: Sense-and-response to intracellular signaling via nucleocytoplasmic localization control of a synthetic transcription factor platform
Authors: Garcia-Diaz, P.; Bhatt, B.; Morgado, M. T.; Kim, K.; Okoye, A.; Foight, G. W.
Abstract: Many therapeutically relevant signaling pathways are sensed inside the cell, yet a modular synthetic biology platform for responding to intracellular signaling at the post-translational level is lacking. Signaling pathways control the nuclear localization and activity of native transcription factors via phosphorylation of nuclear localization/export or cytoplasmic anchor sequences. Here, we apply this concept to develop a platform of nucleocytoplasmic localization tags (NCtags) that control the nuclear translocation of a synthetic transcription factor (synTF) for transgene induction in engineered cells. We identify human-based synTF components that are basally cytoplasmic and induce transgenes under the control of NCtags with minimal background. We demonstrate the modular nature of this platform through transcriptional reporter induction in response to a calcium-inducible NFAT-derived NCtag, and development of novel NCtags responsive to hyperosmolarity, cAMP, or logical combinations of cAMP and calcium. Multiple factors in the tumor microenvironment elevate cAMP in T cells, leading to reduced function. We demonstrate that NCtag-synTF fusions expressed in T cells can respond to endogenous sources of cAMP or calcium in breast cancer spheroids to induce transgene expression. Our use of human components and an all-in-one lentiviral vector encoding the NCtag-synTF-transgene system establishes this as a novel platform for sense-and-response inside therapeutic cells.

Title: High-throughput in vivo DNA data encoding by multiplexed conjugationand orthogonal base editing
Authors: Funke, L. F. H.; Lin, Z.; Liao, W.; Ji, Y.; Poh, C. L.
Abstract: Bacterial conjugation and CRISPR base editing offer complementary routes for programmable DNA transfer and heritable genomic writing, but their combined potential for information encoding in living cells remains unexplored. Here, we introduce CONCORD, a bacterial encoding platform that couples multiplexed bacterial conjugation to genomic base editing for synthesis-free in vivo DNA data writing. A recipient Writer strain expresses the base-editing machinery and is equipped with a writing template, whereas reusable donor Guide strains deliver the encoding sgRNA signals by conjugation. Using this setup, we encode binary information into genomic DNA in a high-throughput manner. Moreover, we systematically evaluated multiple orthogonal base editors for an expanded encoding repertoire and improved data recovery through redundancy encoding. We deploy the system to encode 45,689 bits into DNA including two culturally and historically significant artifacts: a greeting from NASA's Voyager Golden Record and a photograph of Navajo petroglyphs and recovered these datasets with 100% and 99.5% accuracy, respectively, without computational error correction. Connecting and engineering the unique mating and immune system of microbial cells we have established a framework for programmable information writing in bacterial populations, with applications for biological event recording and sustainable DNA data storage.

Title: Archetype analysis of multiplexed antibody imaging reveals interpretable morphological programs in optical pooled screens
Authors: Coelho, P. P.; Leote, A. C.; Yao, H.; Wu, P.; Kudo, T.; Wang, H.; Ermakov, V.; Saboowala, A.; Makino, T.; Littman, R.; Lopez, R.; Kim, J.; Hafner, T.; Rozenblatt-Rosen, O.; Richmond, D.; Garraway, L.; Singh, A.; Marioni, J.; Regev, A.
Abstract: High-content imaging-based screens with small molecule or genetic perturbations rely on rich optical phenotypes, yet how distinct subcellular markers contribute complementary biological information remains unclear. Here, we introduce CellMAPP, a multiplexed organelle imaging platform that uses optical pooled screens with iterative antibody staining to map cellular architecture under perturbation. Using 17 markers across 524 genetic perturbations in MCF-7 cells, we systematically examined how individual, and combinations of, markers capture diverse morphological responses. We find that markers provide complementary views of perturbation effects, with increased multiplexing improving signal and the breadth of hit recovery, although some phenotypes are better recovered from a subset of features rather than a full profile. Because non-molecular image-based profiles can be challenging to link with interpretable biology, we developed CHART (available at https://github.com/Genentech/CHART), an archetype analysis framework that identifies distinct reference morphological states for each marker and uses multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to automatically annotate them, connecting cellular images to recognizable organelle phenotypes. Integrating archetypes across multiple markers revealed modular morphological programs that describe coordinated organelle reorganization in response to perturbation. This framework identified regulators of defined organelle states such as micronuclei, nominated novel gene functions and revealed complex patterns of multi-organelle reposition. Together, optical profiling with MAPP and CHART provides an interpretable, scalable framework for image-based screens that sheds light on rules governing cellular structural reprogramming.

Title: Higher-Order Organization Links Circulating Metabolites to Glucocorticoid Action in Human Adipose Tissue
Authors: Bennett, K.; Chantzichristos, D.; Garner, T.; Jansson, P.-A.; Meyer, A.; Doman, E.; McQueen, J.; Svensson, P.-A.; Ragnarsson, O.; Johannsson, G.; Stevens, A.
Abstract: Glucocorticoids (GCs) are regulators of metabolism, yet how physiological GC exposure remodels adipose metabolism and its relationship with circulating biomarkers remains poorly understood. In a randomised cross-over study of individuals with primary adrenal insufficiency, near-physiological GC exposure was compared to withdrawal using integrated serum metabolomics, abdominal subcutaneous microdialysis metabolomics, and adipose tissue transcriptomics. GC exposure induced coordinated changes in adipose lipid and amino-acid metabolism. Pathway-level entropy analysis revealed GC-state-dependent transcriptional reorganisation, with concentrated organisation during exposure and diffuse organisation during withdrawal. Integrative hypergraph and topological analyses revealed GC-state-dependent reorganisation of circulating metabolite-adipose tissue relationships, with greater higher-order coordination during exposure. The circulating phenylalanine/kynurenine ratio discriminated GC state, showed the strongest shared connectivity to GC-regulated adipose networks, persisted at midnight and in an independent dose-response study, and exhibited circadian rhythmicity. These findings reveal dynamic GC regulation of adipose metabolism and identify a circulating biomarker with potential to guide personalised GC therapy.

Title: Multi-domain analysis of the fecal microbiome of dairy heifers, beef heifers, bred beef heifers, and adult beef cows in the central United States using paired 16S rRNA and 18S rRNA metabarcoding
Authors: Palmer, D.; Adkins, P. R. F.; Isensee, P.; Dorfmeyer, R. A.; Su, E.; Turner, G.; Davis, D. J.; Bivens, N. J.; McAdams, Z. L.; Ericsson, A. C.
Abstract: The growth and performance of cattle is dependent on efficient feed conversion, facilitated by the gut microbiome, including both prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms. Extrinsic factors such as management practices and intrinsic factors like age and genetics can shape these communities. To characterize the relative effects of such factors on the prokaryotic and eukaryotic microbiomes, fresh fecal samples from dairy heifers (n = 8), beef heifers (n = 8), bred beef heifers (n = 8), and adult beef cows (n = 8) were subjected to paired 16S rRNA (V4) and a novel 18S rRNA (V4-V5) metabarcoding assay, and 18S rRNA amplicons were annotated using two databases in parallel. Taxonomic resolution of 18S rRNA amplicons was excellent, with SILVA and EUKARYOME databases each providing better resolution of different groups of organisms. While no differences in eukaryotic richness or alpha diversity were detected, beta diversity differed in all pairwise comparisons except between beef heifers and bred beef heifers. Prokaryotic richness was lower in adult beef cows than the other groups, and beta diversity differed in all pairwise comparisons. Adult beef cows were the most distinct, characterized by replacement of fungal organisms with protozoa and loss of thermophilic bacteria in the eukaryotic and prokaryotic compartments, respectively. Among numerous differentially abundant features, dairy heifers harbored greater abundance of Cooperia oncophora while beef heifers contained greater abundance of Buxtonella sulcata and Mucor. Correlation network analysis revealed multiple significant positive and negative associations between bacterial, fungal, and protozoal features during maturation of the fecal microbiome. Collectively, these data highlight the richness and diversity of both the prokaryotic and eukaryotic compartments of the bovine fecal microbiome, and the influence of management practices and age on both communities. From a technical standpoint, these data demonstrate the ability to resolve fungal, protozoal, and metazoan organisms, including potential parasites and pathogens, with a single metabarcoding assay. They also highlight the nuanced differences between databases and the value of parallel analyses using more than one database.

Title: Fatty acid metabolism and dietary lipid composition shape B-cell responses
Authors: Ngwenyama, B. B.; Bourguignon, L.; Gianneli, E. B.; Benazzouk, Y.; Laflamme, M.; Giacomini, I.; Nguyen, T. K.; Viau, C.; Collin, A. L.; Zani, F.; Blagih, J.
Abstract: B-cell activation requires extensive metabolic reprogramming, yet how B cells acquire and utilize extracellular fatty acids and adapt to changes in lipid availability remains poorly understood. Here, we show that B-cell activation and the extracellular lipid environment dynamically regulate B cells. B-cell receptor (BCR) and Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) stimulation induced distinct mitochondrial and lipid-handling programs, differentially regulating fatty-acid uptake, cholesterol acquisition, lipid storage and mitochondrial respiration. Disrupting long-chain fatty-acid uptake, acyl-CoA activation, or mitochondrial utilisation impaired B-cell proliferation, demonstrating that multiple steps of fatty-acid metabolism are required for B-cell expansion. However, increasing extracellular fatty-acid availability alone did not enhance proliferation, indicating that fatty-acid acquisition and metabolic utilisation are functionally distinct. B cells also acquired fatty acids directly from adipocytes, identifying the local microenvironment as a potential source of metabolic substrates. In vivo, dietary fatty-acid chain length differentially shaped the germinal-centre response. A long-chain fatty-acid-rich diet increased germinal-centre B cells and T follicular helper cells and induced mitochondrial and transcriptional changes that partially converged with those observed following obesogenic feeding. Circulating lipidomics further revealed shared remodelling of lipid species between long-chain fatty-acid-rich and obesogenic diets, including altered partitioning of stearate-containing lipids. Exogenous fatty acids also modified membrane order in activated B cells, suggesting that lipid availability can influence both metabolic and biophysical properties. Together, these findings establish fatty-acid uptake, activation, and utilization as integral components of B-cell metabolic adaptation and demonstrate that dietary fatty-acid composition can remodel the lipid environment and germinal-centre response.

Title: MDS-causing mutations of ZRSR2 impair minor intron splicing by reducing its interaction with SF3B complex
Authors: Chiba, T.; Natsumoto, E.; Obayashi, E.; Masaki, S.; Tanaka, S.; Kataoka, N.
Abstract: Minor introns are rare but evolutionarily conserved introns in the human genome. Defects in minor spliceosome components have been reported to cause several human diseases. Mutations in ZRSR2 are frequently observed in myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) patients. However, the precise molecular mechanism by which these mutations cause a loss of ZRSR2 function in minor intron splicing remain elusive. In this study, we characterized the impact of MDS-causing missense mutations in ZRSR2. Most of the mutant ZRSR2 proteins we tested showed different subnuclear localization pattern from that of wild-type ZRSR2 protein. Co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) analysis revealed that UHM missense mutations disrupted the interaction between ZRSR2 and SF3B complex. We also demonstrated that ZRSR2 preferentially immunoprecipitated minor spliceosome components over major spliceosome components and it directly interacts with SF3B1. Furthermore, co-IP analysis utilizing a variety of ZRSR2 mutants revealed that mutations in the UHM and Zn2 domains significantly attenuated the interaction with SF3B complex. Finally, UHM and Zn2 mutations markedly disrupted the supporting activity of ZRSR2 for minor intron splicing. Our results indicate that disruption of the physical interaction with SF3B complex is one of the hallmarks of MDS-causing mutations of ZRSR2, which results in aberrant splicing of minor introns.

Title: Cell-specific FUS loss enhances ageing-associated transcriptional elongation in lung fibrosis
Authors: Rogel-Ayala, D. G.; Cordero, J.; Aguirre-Alarcon, H. A.; Rubio, K.; Swaminathan, G.; Charif, N.; de Isla, N.; Szymanski, W.; Kolluru Venkataswamy Reddy, G.; Braubach, P.; Mahmood, S.; Guenther, S.; Rivera, M. N.; Graumann, J.; Braun, T.; Wygrecka, M.; Dobreva, G.; Barreto, G.
Abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is an age-related, lethal lung disease affecting over 3 million people worldwide. During aging, impairment of diverse molecular processes compromises cellular homeostasis. Eukaryotic cells adapt to this ageing-associated stress by large-scale transcriptome changes affecting the expression of genes involved in signaling, protein homeostasis, cell plasticity and immune response. The molecular mechanisms regulating extensive transcriptome rearrangements leading to senescence in specific cell types of IPF lungs remain sparsely investigated. Here we uncover fundamental molecular mechanisms underlying cellular senescence by integrative analysis of multi-omics studies and functional experiments monitoring fibrotic and senescence hallmarks in primary lung fibroblasts from control and IPF patients. Loss-of-function of the DNA/RNA binding protein fused in sarcoma (FUS) in control fibroblasts enhanced fibrotic and senescence hallmarks resembling IPF fibroblasts. Dissecting the molecular mechanisms, reduced FUS levels in IPF fibroblasts abolished R-loop formation at transcription start sites (TSS), leading to increased RNA polymerase II (Pol II) recruitment and its phosphorylation at serine 2, resulting in enhanced translocation speed of elongating Pol II and increased expression of fibrosis- and senescence-related genes. Summarizing, FUS maintains low Pol II processivity in control fibroblasts by stabilizing R-loops at TSS, acting as a gatekeeper of fibrotic and age-associated transcriptional programs.

Title: Calpain-mediated regulation of WAVE tyrosine dephosphorylation by PTP61F promotes lamellipodia formation
Authors: Milani, W.; Husmann, A.; Bogdan, S.
Abstract: WAVE is a major driver of lamellipodial protrusions. Previous studies suggested that Abelson (Abl)-dependent tyrosine phosphorylation of WAVE promotes actin polymerization and lamellipodia formation. Here, we provide evidence that Abl tyrosine kinase rather restricts lamellipodial localization of WAVE and inhibits lamellipodial cell spreading. Additionally, overexpression of a cytoplasmic PTP61F phosphatase increases WAVE localization at lamellipodia tips. PTP61F overexpression or pharmacological inhibition of Abl/Src kinases even protects cells from lamellipodia disruption induced by pervanadate, a potent protein tyrosine phosphatase inhibitor. By contrast, overexpression of a phosphatase-deficient PTP61F trapping mutant phenocopies loss of wave function. We identify the tyrosine Y234 as a prominent phosphorylation site in WAVE. Rescue experiments using CRISPR/Cas9-based KO wave mutant cells confirmed an important role of PTP61F-mediated WAVE dephosphorylation in lamellipodia formation. Our data suggest a model in which calpain-mediated proteolytic release of ER-bound PTP61F antagonizes Abl/Src-dependent WAVE phosphorylation and acts as a mechanism promoting re-localization of WAVE to lamellipodial tips.

Title: Organelle Volume Facilitates Spindle Positioning During C. elegans Female Meiosis
Authors: Lazureanu, D. G.; Krueger, E.; Qiu, W.; Kopley-Smith, A. A.; Smith, C. S.; Voloshchuk, N.; Cortes, D. B.; Park, M.; Uryu, K.; Silva, M.; Trautman, E.; Innerberger, M.; Preibisch, S.; Vaxenburg, R.; Stark, A. K.; Bleck, C. K. E.; Reilly, M.; Wang, M. C.; Shroff, H.; McNally, F. J.
Abstract: Cortical positioning of oocyte meiotic spindles is required for reducing chromosome number by segregating chromosomes into polar bodies. In C. elegans, kinesin-1 transports membrane-bound organelles inward into a central ball that is hypothesized to push the meiotic spindle outward. Using focused ion beam scanning electron microscopy, we found that the percent volume occupied by membrane-bound organelles was 28% in a mature oocyte that has completed endocytosis of the yolk precursor, vitellogenin, compared to 17% in a less mature oocyte that has not yet endocytosed vitellogenin. We therefore hypothesized that blocking endocytosis of vitellogenin would reduce the size of the central ball of organelles packed inward by kinesin-1 and limit outward movement of the spindle. Depletion of vitellogenin or proteins required for endocytosis resulted in a smaller central volume of kinesin-coated organelles and defective spindle positioning. A computer simulation of a simple exclusion model faithfully recapitulated wildtype and mutant spindle position phenotypes. These results support a volume exclusion model for positioning acentriolar meiotic spindles.

Title: Mouse oocytes organize mRNA-protein assemblies and ER-associated translation hubs to drive meiosis
Authors: Sanada, T.; Takada, Y.; Wang, J.; Takei, N.; Kotani, T.
Abstract: Oocyte meiosis in animals is essential for producing fertilizable eggs. As transcription becomes largely quiescent, meiotic progression depends on temporally regulated translation of accumulated maternal mRNAs. However, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we identified diverse and highly organized mRNA-protein assemblies in mouse oocytes that coordinate cytoplasmic mRNA regulation and enable spatiotemporal translation to drive oocyte meiosis. Twelve RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), including DDX4/VASA, HDLBP/Vigilin, and TDRD3, were assembled into widely distributed aggregates in germinal vesicle (GV)-stage oocytes. We depleted DDX4 and HDLBP using Trim-Away and found that these RBPs regulate the precise assembly of RNA granules and protein aggregates through distinct mechanisms, promoting temporal protein synthesis at cortical translation factories with the endoplasmic reticulum, termed CORTE. All 12 RBPs formed distinct mRNA-protein assemblies, whose size and distribution changed upon meiotic initiation. These findings reveal the molecular basis of spatiotemporal mRNA-protein-organelle networks underlying animal reproduction and development.

Title: A gut-on-chip model reveals architecture-dependent epithelial responses to microbial challenge
Authors: Nandimandalam, M.; Pandey, P.; Mock, M.; Holzberger, M.; Lochner, M.; Buettner, M.; Bleich, A.
Abstract: Advanced in vitro models that better recapitulate human intestinal physiology are needed to improve translational relevance and reduce reliance on animal experimentation. Microfluidic gut-on-chip systems provide controlled architectural and mechanical microenvironments that more closely resemble native tissue than conventional static cultures. However, how these features influence epithelial responses to microbial stimuli remains incompletely understood. In this study, we compared conventional two-dimensional (2D) Caco-2 monolayers with a perfused three-dimensional (3D) gut-on-chip model exhibiting crypt-like epithelial organization. Microbial challenge was employed as a biologically relevant perturbation to investigate barrier-associated responses under distinct culture conditions. Following exposure to the probiotic Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN), epithelial morphology, barrier-associated gene expression, inflammatory signaling, and temporal response patterns were assessed over time. In a complementary approach, susceptibility to bacterial stress was examined using increasing doses of Citrobacter rodentium (C. rodentium). Both culture systems responded dynamically to microbial exposure; however, differences in response patterns were observed between static and perfused cultures. EcN induced transient alterations in epithelial organization followed by recovery-associated responses, while C. rodentium caused dose-dependent structural and transcriptional changes. Notably, epithelial damage became apparent at lower bacterial loads in conventional 2D cultures, whereas the chip-based model maintained tissue integrity under comparable conditions. Together, these findings indicate that epithelial architecture and the surrounding culture environment influence barrier-associated responses to microbial challenge. The study highlights the utility of gut-on-chip systems for investigating host-microbe interactions and provides a framework for functional comparison of advanced intestinal in vitro models.

Title: Niche-dependent epistasis within the cancer genome shapes metastatic fitness
Authors: Liu, X.; He, L.; Zhao, M.; Golomb, S. M.; Ma, W.; Yang, X.; Aleksandrovic, E.; Borges, H. M.; Dean, K. M.; Wang, L.; Hon, G. C.; Gan, D.; Zhu, H.; Li, J.; Xu, L.; Zhang, S.
Abstract: Epistasis, the genetic interaction between loci, directs non-additive genotype-to-phenotype outcomes. Within a multicellular organism, how the tissue niche (E) shapes gene-by-gene epistasis (GxG) and its phenotypic consequences remains poorly studied. Using tumor lung metastasis as an experimental model, we mapped GxGxE through combinatorial CRISPR perturbation coupled with depletion of defined host myeloid populations in mice. The metastatic niche first selects disseminated tumor cells on GxG epistatic fitness, then drives transcriptome convergence regardless of genotype. Removing anatomically distinct myeloid populations reshaped the metastatic epistasis landscape despite identical tumor genotypes. Gene-by-gene-by-environment epistasis therefore operates at the organismal level, with interaction magnitude and sign set by niche cells. Beyond metastasis, our data suggest that the tissue niche conditions how genetic interactions translate into divergent phenotypes.

Title: Ethanol stress induces siRNA-mediated epimutations and phenotypic variability in fission yeast
Authors: Villalba de la Pena, M.; Sarkies, P.
Abstract: Epigenetic information is required for the maintenance of gene expression states through cell division. Some epigenetic information can also persist through generations, raising the possibility that epigenetic differences may arise in populations and contribute to evolutionary processes such as drift and natural selection. Evaluating this requires characterising the properties of such epimutations, so that their rate, stability and genome-wide distribution can be assessed. Recent experiments in many organisms have demonstrated that epimutations occur, but have limited stability relative to DNA sequence mutations. However, the extent to which epimutations contribute to evolution is still unclear, in part because it is not clear whether epimutations respond dynamically to environmental conditions. Here, we use the fission yeast S. pombe, in which evolutionarily relevant epimutations have been observed, but not yet systematically characterised, to test whether a physiologically relevant stress, ethanol exposure, leads to changes in the properties of epimutations. Using laboratory evolution experiments with repeated population bottlenecks to minimise selection, we show that epimutations associated with changes in small interfering (si)RNAs occur at a greater rate in ethanol. Ethanol-induced epimutations are enriched at transposable element loci and correlate with changes in transposon expression. Ethanol exposure also increases gene expression noise genome-wide and variability in growth rate; importantly, both these increases are suppressed in mutants lacking siRNAs. Together, these results demonstrate that stress can alter the generation of heritable epigenetic information, and suggest that siRNAs may have a role in promoting phenotypic variability in response to environmental stress.

Title: STEER-seq: a recombinase based platform for pooled multimodal single-cell perturbation screening
Authors: Migliori, V.; Suo, C.; Dufva, O.; Gyulev, I.; Polanski, K.; Symeonidou, V.; Rodschinka, G.; Sarropoulos, I.; Iwama, S.; Steemers, A. S.; Gontarczyk, A. M.; Powell, H.; Cujba, A.-M.; Park, J.-E. S.; Garnett, M.; Vassiliou, G. S.; Teichmann, S. A.; Bassett, A. R.
Abstract: Pooled gain-of-function screening is a powerful method for screening for transcription factors whose overexpression leads to changes in cellular identity. However, variable transgene copy number, integration site and genomic context from random viral integration can confound quantitative comparisons between perturbations. We present STEER-seq (Single-cell Transgene Expression via Exchange Recombination sequencing), a virus-free platform for pooled ORF gain-of-function screening in human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs). STEER-seq combines irreversible Bxb1-mediated integration at a defined genomic safe-harbour locus with promoterless donor libraries and barcode-enabled perturbation tracking, enabling single-copy expression from a common promoter and genomic context and direct recovery of perturbation identity by single-cell sequencing. In a focused haematopoietic screen, SPI1 expression alone was sufficient to drive differentiation towards HSC/MPP-like progenitors in the absence of exogenous cytokines, with transient induction generating progenitors that retained multilineage haematopoietic differentiation potential. Joint RNA-chromatin accessibility profiling linked transcription factor-induced transcriptional responses to chromatin remodelling and enabled reconstruction of perturbation-induced gene regulatory networks, including a RUNX2-driven osteoblast programme. Scaling STEER-seq to around 2,000 human coding sequences enabled systematic discovery of transcription factors capable of inducing distinct cell-state programmes, including neural progenitor-, melanocyte- and vascular smooth muscle-like states, as well as maintenance of pluripotency. STEER-seq provides a scalable, quantitative framework for single-cell and multimodal gain-of-function screening, enabling functional discovery and engineering of human cell identity.

Title: CLN6 is a glycerophosphoglycerol epimerase in bis(monoacylglycero)phosphate biosynthesis
Authors: Sheokand, P. K.; James, A. M.; Posern, C.; Singh Sahrawat, A.; Breithofer, J.; Ganellin, J.; Proulx, M. K.; Leese, S. K.; Turner, K.; Lacabanne, D.; Bulfon, D.; Jenkins, B.; van der Kleij, J.; Johnston, H. E.; Lord, S. O.; Basran, M. K.; Yu, C. S.; Booth, C. D.; Weimer, J. M.; Koulman, A.; Jäättelä, M.; Kunji, E. R. S.; Palmer, D. N.; Mitchell, N. L.; Prudent, J.; Zimmermann, R.; Gruber, K.; Schulz, A.; Murphy, M. P.; Petkevicius, K.
Abstract: Lysosomal catabolism depends on bis(monoacylglycero)phosphate (BMP), a phospholipid with atypical S,S stereochemistry of unknown biosynthetic origin. CLN8 and CLN5 catalyze sequential acylation steps in BMP synthesis, and their loss of function causes Batten disease, a group of inherited neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorders. Here we identify CLN6, a biochemically uncharacterized endoplasmic reticulum protein whose loss also causes Batten disease, as the calcium-dependent glycerophosphoglycerol epimerase that establishes BMP stereochemistry upstream of CLN8. CLN6 deficiency depletes BMP in cells, mice, and patient lysosomes, and reduces lysosomal hydrolase levels. BMP-precursor supplementation bypasses CLN6, restores BMP and increases hydrolase abundance in CLN6-deficient cells and mice. These findings place three Batten disease proteins in a single biosynthetic pathway and reveal BMP deficiency as a reversible cause of disrupted lysosomal hydrolase homeostasis.

Title: A modular mechanism determines the proton-pumping stoichiometry of respiratory complex I
Authors: Waddell, R. A.; Messent, H. L.; Costa-Lima, M. M.; Wright, J. J.; Salisbury, J. H.; Hirst, J.
