Abstract: Respiratory complex I, a crucial metabolic enzyme, uses the reducing potential of NADH to pump protons across energy-transducing membranes, but its mechanism of catalysis remains unknown. Here, guided by detailed structural information, we combine targeted mutagenesis and biophysical analyses to define the proton-pumping pathways in the three antiporter-like (proton-pumping) subunits of complex I from Paracoccus denitrificans and Escherichia coli. In Pd-CI, a four-proton pump, one of the three proton-uptake pathways is inactive, reconciling the four-proton/three-subunit mismatch. In Ec-CI two pathways are inactive - and Ec-CI pumps only two protons. We define the structural determinants for redox-coupled proton uptake, establish a mechanistic framework for proton pumping, and reveal how the proton-pumping stoichiometry has been adapted to deliver efficient energy conservation in diverse bioenergetic environments.

Title: Probing Genomic Foundation Models with Splice-Variant Perturbations
Authors: Alavi, M. V.
Abstract: As benchmarks saturate, traditional validation methods fail to capture the probabilistic representations of genomic foundation models. This study probes self-supervised generalists (NTv3 650M, Evo2 40B, Genos 10B) alongside task-specific specialists (SpliceAI, AlphaGenome, Borzoi) using a mechanistically focused paradigm centered on expert-curated single-nucleotide substitutions within the splicing regions of the exon-rich OPA1 gene. Extending this analysis across the broader corpus of OPA1 mutations, variants of uncertain significance (VUS), and an independent 65-gene dataset of spliceogenic mutations demonstrates that generalists can match task-specific networks. Training data scale, genetic diversity, and evolutionary context are key for capturing RNA splicing syntax, whereas sparse routing may constrain performance. Mechanistically, foundation models exhibit a compute-asymmetry: the Evo2 40B model frontloads compute into massive parameter scale to resolve single-nucleotide variants within a narrow 425-bp context window, whereas the bidirectional NTv3 650M model and the Genos 10B mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture backload compute to inference, requiring spatial logit aggregation and expansive context windows of up to 94 kb. Furthermore, classification accuracy across these foundation models benefitted from locus-specific thresholding rather than mutation-class calibration, exposing representation boundaries of the models.

Title: Frustration Quenching and Network Topology of the Energy Landscape as Primary Determinants of Protein-Ligand Binding Pose Prediction by Deep Learning Models
Authors: Turano, L.; Foley, B.; Dennis, R.; Gatlin, W.; Verkhivker, G.
Abstract: Deep learning co-folding and docking models accurately predict ligand binding poses at orthosteric sites yet systematically underperform at allosteric pockets. Here, we demonstrate that this accuracy gap reflects a fundamental biophysical property of local energy landscape topology specifically, the magnitude of frustration quenching upon ligand binding rather than an intrinsic algorithmic defect. By evaluating leading co-folding and docking paradigms across curated benchmarks and large-scale uncurated datasets, we show that AI prediction success strongly tracks frustration quenching which the degree to which ligand binding relieves local energetic strain to form a steep energy funnel. Topologically, frustration-weighted residue interaction networks reveal that orthosteric pockets act as high-betweenness communication hubs embedded within contiguous, minimally frustrated pathways. In contrast, allosteric sites reside in low-betweenness peripheral regions with fragmented frustration profiles, presenting flatter, entropy-dominated landscapes that challenge structure prediction algorithms. Comparing generative diffusion with single-shot regression demonstrates that multi-pose sampling capacity is required to cross energy barriers and discover the frustration funnel, whereas joint receptor-ligand coordinate co-adaptation governs local optimization within the funnel. Collectively, this study reframes the allosteric "blind spot" as a quantitative property of energy landscape architecture rather than a defect of any specific predictive framework. We demonstrate that frustration quenching magnitude and structural network centrality serve as physical descriptors that define the intrinsic limits of AI performance, reframing AI accuracy from a benchmark metric into a physics-grounded quantitative reporter of macromolecular binding landscape architecture.

Title: Evolutionary stabilisation of stressful metabolism via integrated biocomputing and essential-gene metabolic locking circuits
Authors: Lu, Z.; Barry, C.; Tominaga, M.; Phan, A.; Jahanian, A.; Collier, T. R.; Wendrick, N. A.; Evans, S.; McDonnell, L.; Netzel, G.; McCubbin, T.; Jacob, S.; da Roza, P. A.; Xu, X.; Wang, C.; Ishii, J.; Behrendorff, J.; Beliaev, A. S.; Vickers, C. E.; Peng, B.
Abstract: Synthetic genetic circuits enable microbial differentiation from growth to production, yet metabolic burden, imbalance and toxicity frequently drive strain degeneration. Here, we use omics analyses and single-cell biosensors to investigate genetic responses in Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains engineered with stressful terpene biosynthetic pathways. Under metabolic stress, despite divergent stress responses, cells commonly and progressively lose induction of synthetic genetic circuits. In the prenyl pyrophosphate-accumulating strain, this loss is coupled with activation of amino acid biosynthesis and ribosome biogenesis. Accordingly, the essential glutamine synthetase gene GLN1 was coupled to induction of heterologous terpene synthesis through integrated two- and three-input biocomputing circuits that enable stringent, patterned ON/OFF switching. The integrated biocomputing and metabolic locking systems not only alleviate production degeneration but also enable non-degenerative adaptation of toxic terpene synthesis, allowing interrogation of evolutionary shifts for further metabolic optimisation.

Title: KAS-CUT&Tag for direct mapping of transcription bubbles
Authors: Wu, W.; Greene, J. E.; Ahmad, K.; Henikoff, S.
Abstract: Transcription by RNA Polymerase II (Pol II) generates dynamic transcription bubbles as it moves forward, but existing methods map transcriptional activity indirectly. Here, we introduce KAS-CUT&Tag, a method that combines N3-kethoxal labeling of exposed single-stranded DNA with CUT&Tag to directly map transcription bubbles. Bubble density correlates with nascent transcription levels and varies across Pol II-bound genes at promoters, gene bodies, and termination regions. Transcription bubbles are enriched at genes marked by active histone modifications H3K27ac, H3K4me3, and H3K36me3 and by chromatin-bound splicing factor U2AF2, but enrichment is highest at replication-coupled histone genes in K562 and GM12878 cells. KAS-CUT&Tag also detects co-occupancy of the histone gene transcription factor NPAT with Pol II at the Histone Locus Body, suggesting that in these cells NPAT is juxtaposed to transcription bubbles via interaction with Pol II. Together, KAS-CUT&Tag enables direct mapping of Pol II and regulatory interactions at transcription bubbles, providing a powerful tool for precise analysis of transcriptional activity.

Title: 'broadSeq', a benchmarking tool to contrast differential gene expression methods and identify when genomic neighbourhood matters
Authors: Das Roy, R.; Hallikas, O.; Kuure, S.; Jernvall, J.
Abstract: Several tools are available to detect differential gene expression. The predominant approach of different statistical methods is to consider changes in gene expression independent from their genomic context. Previously, DELocal was introduced that takes into consideration gene expression dynamics in the genomic neighbourhood. Whereas DELocal was shown to identify developmentally regulated genes in developing mouse tooth, its performance in other biological conditions remains undetermined. To benchmark DElocal together with other methods, we develop another tool 'broadSeq'. It provides easy to use interface for methods like DELocal , deseq2, limma, edger, EBSeq and many more. Here we report benchmarking results on different data sets that comprise wild type developing mouse organs from different embryonic time points, and also human cancer data. The examined datasets are from the heart, kidney, liver, brain, forebrain, and hindbrain. We found that most methods produce relatively comparable lists of differentially expressed genes. Nevertheless, DELocal identifies partially distinct sets of genes compared to the other methods. Evaluating the identified genes using gene and disease ontology terms show that the uniquely detected genes by DELocal are biologically relevant and also highly expressed compared to the genes identified by the other methods. Because consistently highly expressed genes show relatively subtle fold changes, the neighbourhood concept of DELocal appears to correct for the difficulty in detecting these differential expression of highly expressed genes. Finally, we provide the tools as combined bioconductor packages, allowing researchers to explore and decide the best methods for their data and questions.

Title: DECONVersation: Single Cell Foundation Model-Derived Embeddings for Robust Cell Type Deconvolution of Bulk RNA-seq
Authors: Oku, A.; Geiger, H.; Robine, N.; Fu, R.
Abstract: AI and deep learning have transformed single-cell transcriptomics, empowering unsupervised annotation, trajectory inference, and cross-dataset integration at scale. Here, we propose bulk RNA-seq deconvolution as a novel task for single-cell foundation models. Deconvolution estimates cell type proportions from bulk RNA-seq using single-cell reference data, with applications spanning tumor microenvironment profiling to the detection of disease-associated shifts in tissue composition. However, existing methods remain vulnerable to batch effects, subject-level variation, and marker gene selection sensitivity. We introduce DECONVersation, which leverages embeddings from pretrained and fine-tuned single-cell foundation models, coupled with a non-negative least squares solver, to estimate cell type proportions. Foundation model embeddings are robust to batch effects and implicitly encode complex gene relationships, sidestepping explicit marker gene selection. Benchmarked against MuSiC, DWLS, and BayesPrism, DECONVersation achieved comparable or superior performance across diverse tissues. Performance further improved with tissue-specific fine-tuning.

Title: A moonlighting serpin of Tannerella forsythia compromises the bactericidal activity of neutrophils
Authors: Morris, S. C.; Veillard, F.; Mizgalska, D.; Madej, M.; Benedyk-Machaczka, M.; Folkert, J.; Potempa, B. A.; Fuchs, A.; Potempa, J.; Bagaitkar, J.
Abstract: Serine protease inhibitors (serpins) are extremely rare in prokaryotes, and their role in immune evasion remains unclear. We identified a bifunctional TLR2-binding serpin (miropin) produced by Tannerella forsythia that broadly suppresses neutrophil antimicrobial capacity. Miropin binding to TLR2 primed neutrophils, enhancing phagocytic capacity yet, counterintuitively, promoting bacterial persistence. Mechanistically, like other serpins, miropin acted as an irreversible suicide inhibitor of neutrophil serine proteases (NSPs), blocking their activity upon granule mobilization and NETosis. Unexpectedly, miropin, independent of its protease-inhibitory activity, bound and inhibited myeloperoxidase (MPO), thereby blocking the oxidative burst. This simultaneous suppression of oxidative and non-oxidative bactericidal mechanisms promoted bacterial survival in vivo without significantly altering the tissue inflammatory response. Thus, we identified novel moonlighting roles (TLR2 signaling and MPO inhibition) for an unorthodox prokaryotic serpin and provided context for how T. forsythia and other oral pathogens survive within the subgingival niche, an environment highly enriched in activated neutrophils.

Title: Predicting viral host range for reverse zoonosis surveillance
Authors: Irvine, E. B.; Bikias, T.; Schifferli, T.; Plath, L.; Han, J.; Chen, N.; Stamkopoulos, E.; Sahin, B.; Frei, L.; Taft, J. M.; Reddy, S. T.
Abstract: Zoonotic transmission of viruses has triggered major outbreaks throughout history. However, human-to-animal transmission, or reverse zoonotic transmission, also represents an underappreciated public health threat. Reverse zoonoses can establish novel animal reservoirs that fuel viral evolution and enable eventual spillback into humans, underscoring the importance of defining viral host range. Current approaches for host range prediction are limited. Experimental methods are retrospective and rely on brute-force testing in a small number of models, whereas computational approaches often lack experimental grounding. Here, we present a platform that integrates high-throughput experimental screening with deep learning to predict viral host range from sequence. We screened a yeast-displayed SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain library against 15 ACE2 orthologs from diverse species, and deep sequenced the ACE2-binding and non-binding populations to generate an atlas of 8.8 million unique RBD:ACE2 interaction measurements. These data were used to train a transformer-based deep learning model that predicts RBD:ACE2 compatibility across animal species from sequence alone, and generalizes in a zero-shot manner to ACE2 orthologs not observed during training. Critically, the model pairs each prediction with a distance-based uncertainty estimate, allowing hundreds of candidate species to be triaged by both predicted host compatibility and confidence. This framework enables the rapid prioritization of animal species for SARS-CoV-2 surveillance and provides a general strategy for anticipating viral host range.

Title: Genotypic Responses of Rice to Ammonium and Nitrate under Contrasting Water Regimes: Agronomic, Biochemical, and Gene-Expression Analyses
Authors: Baby Thomas, H.; Agarwal, T.; Verulkar, S.
Abstract: Considering the increasing water and labor constraints in rice production, direct-seeded rice is becoming increasingly important. However, direct-seeded rice is vulnerable to water stress and inefficient nutrient use. Nitrogen use efficiency in rice is generally low, and improving nitrogen acquisition and assimilation is important for sustainable productivity. In this study, 48 recombinant inbred lines were evaluated under ammonium and nitrate nutrition in irrigated and rainfed environments across two cropping seasons. Agronomic, physiological, biochemical and molecular responses were assessed. Significant effects of genotype, nitrogen form, environments and their interactions were observed for several traits. Rainfed conditions reduced grain and biological yield compared with irrigated conditions. Ammonium produced a higher mean grain yield than nitrate by approximately 26.2 g m-2 under irrigated conditions and 154.2 g m-2 under rainfed conditions, although the responses varied among genotypes. Biological yield and SPAD values were generally higher with ammonium, whereas total chlorophyll showed season and environment-dependent responses. Glutamine synthetase activity was highest under ammonium treatment, while glutamate synthase activity was higher under nitrate treatment. Grain yield showed strong positive correlations with biological yield, but correlations between grain yield and GS or GOGAT activity were not significant. Expression of OsGln1.2, OsGln2 and OsGlt1 varied according to genotype, tissue and nitrogen treatment. Overall, the results demonstrate that responses to nitrogen forms are genotype- and environment-dependent, and that ammonium may provide a yield advantage under rainfed conditions. Integrating field performance with biochemical and molecular traits may help identify rice genotypes suited to water-limited systems.

Title: Structured biological evidence enables general-purpose language models to predict bacteriophage-host interactions
Authors: Zhang, Y.-z.; Xu, L.; Imoto, S.
Abstract: Biological interaction inference often requires integrating heterogeneous evidence that differs in biological meaning, provenance, specificity, and reliability. Existing computational approaches typically compress such evidence into numerical features, aggregate scores, or latent representations before prediction, obscuring the contribution of individual evidence records and limiting interpretation when evidence is conflicting or incomplete. Phage-host interaction prediction provides a demanding test case for this problem, requiring the integration of genomic, functional, and reference-derived evidence with differing coverage, specificity, and reliability. Here we introduce a structured-evidence inference paradigm that retains heterogeneous biological observations as modular, named, and experimentally perturbable records rather than compressing them before prediction. We implement this paradigm in PHI-Reason, which constructs structured textual profiles from genomic annotations, receptor-binding protein homology, nucleotide-neighbour relationships, alignment-free genomic similarity, and available CRISPR spacer information. A general-purpose large language model (LLM) performs inference directly over these structured profiles without task-specific training or manually engineered evidence-fusion rules. Across phage-host benchmarks, PHI-Reason achieved species-level top-1 accuracies of 67.4% and 57.2% on RefSeq-634 and VHDB-3150, respectively, and a multi-host accuracy of 0.673 on the Hi-C cohort, outperforming established numerical methods. On 207 experimentally supported associations from 2025-2026 excluded from the reference corpus, it achieved 52.2% species-level and 90.8% genus-level top-1 accuracy. Evidence perturbations identified nucleotide-neighbour context as the dominant signal and quantified complementary or misleading evidence contributions. Target-conditioned local Jacobian and output-grounding analyses further characterized evidence-dependent inference and departures of generated rationales from the supplied evidence. Extending the framework to eukaryotic virus-host prediction preserved high predictive accuracy (67.0%), supporting cross-domain portability. Moreover, replacing the reasoning LLM with Jev, a typed-decision model, maintained broadly comparable performance across phage-host benchmarks while reducing mean per-query inference time by 11- to 40-fold, supporting the separation of evidence representation from downstream inference. These results establish structured biological evidence as a portable interface between heterogeneous biological observations and downstream inference. By separating evidence representation from the inference engine, this paradigm supports both language-model predictions with inspectable rationales and faster typed decisions for high-throughput prediction, while making the contribution and limits of evidential support directly testable.

Title: Cell cycle exit is required for differentiation and cell fate diversification but not neoblast specialisation in planarians
Authors: Peron, S.; Balta, O.-M.; Noronha, A.; Smillie, T.; Mason, V.; Perez-Posada, A.; Solana, J.
Abstract: In planarians, adult stem cells constantly proliferate and differentiate into dozens of different cell types to maintain tissue homeostasis. However, how cell fate acquisition is coordinated with cell cycle progression remains poorly understood. To address this, we generated single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets from cells enriched for 2C or 4C DNA content and from animals subjected to RNAi against the cell cycle regulators cdh1 and h2b. We found that progenitor populations from multiple lineages contain actively cycling cells enriched in the 4C state. Cell fate acquisition to most cell types is acquired progressively during neoblast differentiation. Comparative analysis of cell cycle regulators confirmed a simplified regulatory repertoire in Schmidtea, supporting a central role for cdh1 in controlling cell cycle exit. RNAi-mediated knockdown of cdh1 caused homeostasis defects, impaired regeneration, accumulation of neoblasts and depletion of progenitors. Together, our findings demonstrate that cell cycle exit is required for terminal differentiation but not for neoblast specialisation. Instead, lineage commitment is initiated in actively cycling neoblasts, whereas terminal differentiation depends on cdh1-mediated cell cycle exit.

Title: BLIMP1 shapes germinal center B cell clonal diversity by gating chromatin accessibility during light-to-dark zone transition
Authors: Vijay, G. M.; Ramaswami, B.; Gierlack, S.; Pease, N. A.; Rothstein, D.; Singh, H.
Abstract: Germinal center (GC) B cell responses are defined by many positive regulators of affinity maturation, but few components that restrain clonal dominance, notably Nr4a1, are known. We reveal an unsuspected role for Blimp1 (Prdm1), a plasma cell determinant, as a feedback regulator of affinity maturation. Single cell RNA-seq and B cell receptor (BCR) seq showed that B cell specific Prdm1 loss drives an exaggerated GC reaction with larger clones, increased somatic hypermutation, and greater clonal dominance, independent of Nr4a1. Single cell chromatin profiling with base-resolution modeling indicated that Blimp1 represses expression of BCR-signaling genes, gating chromatin accessibility at ISRE, EICE, NFKB, and Oct motifs. In the absence of Blimp1, enhanced BCR signaling augments activities of transcription factors that promote G1/S transition during light-zone (LZ) selection and fuel dark-zone (DZ) expansion. Thus, Blimp1 attenuates BCR signaling and constrains the LZ to DZ transition, fine-tuning clonal competition thereby maintaining repertoire diversity.

Title: Human Th17 state classification reveals a selective vulnerability in acylcarnitine metabolism in type 2 diabetes
Authors: Ujagar, N. S.; Poudel, S.; Saraswat, S.; Sureshchandra, S.; Kim, J.; Le, U.-V.; Jones, A. R.; Hopkins, N.; Sriram, T.; Matson, M.; Pilier, E. H.; Mejia, M.; Bailin, S. S.; Wanjalla, C. N.; Sy, M. Y.; Newcomb, D. C.; Walsh, C.; Wagar, L. E.; Nikolajczyk, B. S.; Zhang, X. D.; Green, D. R.; Nicholas, D. A.
Abstract: Th17 cells are categorized as non-pathogenic (Th17np) and pathogenic (Th17p), states defined primarily in murine autoimmune models. In contrast, studying these states in humans remains difficult because these subsets lack validated identifiers. We developed a nanovial-based single-cell ELISA to isolate cytokine-secreting human Th17 cells and define Th17np vs Th17p cell transcriptional states. These signatures enabled predictive classification and flow-cytometric identification across tissues and diseases. Application of these strategies with single-cell metabolic modeling and functional profiling revealed that Th17np cells predominate in type 2 diabetes yet exhibit impaired fatty acid oxidation capacity despite elevated carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A (CPT1A). CRISPR perturbation and pharmacologic inhibition identified acylcarnitine metabolism as a regulator of Th17 state balance and exposed a selective metabolic vulnerability in type 2 diabetes. This framework links human Th17 cell pathogenicity to lipid metabolism.

Title: Brain-Resident CD8+ T Cells Regulate Neuronal Activity and Behavior via Interferon-Gamma
Authors: park, k.; jang, j.; jeon, s.; hwang, s.; choi, k.; cox, t.; Ngiow, S.; flores, j.; harrison, c.; liu, s.; Bennett, F. C.; silverman, m.; Wherry, E. J.; thaiss, c.; fuccillo, m.; Yim, Y. S.
Abstract: Maintaining brain homeostasis is crucial for proper function of the central nervous system and has traditionally been attributed to neuronal and glial interactions. However, recent research highlights the essential role of brain-resident immune cells in this process. Our study characterizes brain-specific CD8+ T cells and elucidates their significant contribution to brain homeostasis and behavior. We identified a distinct population of CD8+ T cells that infiltrates the brain during early development, undergoes clonal expansion, and acquires effector memory-like characteristics through interactions with microglia. Notably, the absence of these cells results in hyperactivation of neuronal activity and abnormal behaviors, due to loss of regulation of interferon-gamma (IFN-{gamma}) secreted by CD8+ T cells. Our findings demonstrate that IFN-{gamma} secreting brain-specific CD8+ T cells are crucial for maintaining the physiological level of neuronal excitability and normal behavioral patterns. This study provides novel insights into neuroimmune interactions, emphasizing the critical role of CD8+ T cells in sustaining brain function and behavior.

Title: The transition to postpartum lactation establishes a state of maternal antiviral resilience
Authors: Campbell, A. D.; Miller-Ensminger, T.; Arreguin, M. C.; Kennedy, E. A.; Hewins, P.; Stickler, C.; Esterowitz, N.; Assaad, M. R.; Kready, K.; Silver, P. A.; Hensley, S. E.; Jurado, K.
Abstract: Influenza A virus (IAV) causes severe disease during late pregnancy, yet how maternal adaptations in host defense shape susceptibility following childbirth remains unknown. Here, we show that the postpartum period represents a state of enhanced maternal antiviral immunity. Across postpartum stages, dams infected before weaning exhibited increased survival and reduced disease following lethal IAV challenge compared with nonpregnant females. Postpartum protection was associated with enhanced viral clearance and increased pulmonary antigen-specific CD8+ T cells and IL-17A-producing gamma-delta T cells. We identify the transition into lactation as a critical determinant of this protection. Protection extended to highly pathogenic avian influenza. Together, these findings reveal that maternal antiviral immunity remains actively shaped after childbirth, establishing the postpartum lactational period as a distinct state of maternal antiviral resilience.

Title: A mast cell receptor is associated with fibrosis and itch in systemic sclerosis
Authors: Kothari, R.; Capuzzi, D.; Kilgore, C.; Oh, H. J.; Patel, S.; Srikumar, A.; Leatherman, G.; Shah, A. A.; Kang, J.; Dong, X. P.
Abstract: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is an autoimmune connective tissue disease characterized by symmetric fibrosis of the skin and multiple internal organs. The mechanisms that trigger early fibrotic changes remain unclear. Mast cells are known to infiltrate human SSc lesional skin in early disease stages, yet the role of mast cells in initiating fibrosis and pruritus in SSc remains debated, in part due to unclear pathways of mast cell activation. Here, we show that mast cells, via the receptor Mrgprb2, contribute to fibrosis in the bleomycin (BLM)-induced skin fibrosis mouse model. Mast cells accumulate in the skin of BLM-treated wild-type (WT) but not Mrgprb2-knockout (Mrgprb2-/-) mice. Mrgprb2-/- mice show attenuated disease severity, with reduced collagen deposition and lower expression of matrix metalloproteinases and inflammatory markers associated with fibrosis. BLM treatment also increases pruritus in WT mice in the early stages of the model; an effect reduced in Mrgprb2-/- mice. This is the first report of itch in this model of skin fibrosis, further linking it to clinical SSc, where pruritus is an early and prevalent symptom affecting nearly half of patients. In a parallel human cohort, lesional SSc skin harbors significantly more mast cells than paired non-lesional skin from the same patients, demonstrating that mast cell accumulation is specific to affected tissue. Lesional mast cell counts also track with skin disease severity, correlating with modified Rodnan skin score and patient-reported skin tightness. Together, these findings implicate Mrgprb2-mediated mast cell activity in both fibrosis and pruritus in SSc, highlighting mast cells as a candidate therapeutic target in this understudied disease process.

Title: Restoration of deficient IL-15 signaling enhances innate lymphoid cell immunity in brain metastasis
Authors: McMullen, T. P.; Naef, P.; Zagni, E.; Tian, L.; Zhao, E.; Wechter, N.; Longworth, A. J.; Adam, I.; Insua-Rodriguez, J.; Savage, H.; Hur, I.; Garcia, S. A.; Ma, D.; Liew, M. H.; Mallya, S.; Kessenbrock, K.; O'Sullivan, T. E.; Mohyeldin, A.; Yu, J.; Lawson, D. A.
Abstract: Natural killer (NK) cells and type 1 innate lymphoid cells (ILC1s), collectively known as group 1 innate lymphoid cells (ILCs), are critical mediators of anti-tumor immunity, yet their role in brain metastasis remains poorly defined. Using single-cell RNA sequencing and functional depletion models, we show that group 1 ILCs fail to provide adequate tumor control in breast cancer brain metastasis (BCBM). In contrast to the liver, where diverse, functionally competent group 1 ILC populations facilitate excellent metastatic control, group 1 ILCs in BCBM show limited diversity and profound tissue-specific dysfunction such that their depletion had no effect on tumor burden despite modest parenchymal infiltration. We attribute this group 1 ILC dysfunction to severely restricted IL-15 availability, with IL-15R protein detected at 500-fold lower concentration in the brain than in the liver. Local IL-15 complex administration restored group 1 ILC accumulation, cytotoxicity, and tissue residency, significantly reducing brain metastatic burden independent of T cells. Intracranial delivery of IL-15-secreting induced pluripotent stem-cell-derived (iPSC)-NK cells, already in clinical testing for non-small cell lung cancer, significantly reduced tumor burden. Collectively, these findings reveal how tissue-specific differences in cytokine availability shape group 1 ILC population diversity and disease response, establishing localized IL-15 signaling as a compelling strategy to unlock innate immunity against intracranial malignancies.

Title: A semi-automated tool for improving Assessments and Lab Tests data annotation in ImmPort
Authors: Tursi, A. R.; Fortriede, J. D.; Burns, K.; Saba, N.; Pirani, P.; Strub, M. D.; Dunn, P.; Schaefer, H.; Andorf, S.
Abstract: Public data sharing in immunological and clinical research is essential for transparency, reproducibility, and secondary analysis. However, many datasets in repositories such as ImmPort lack sufficient structured data to enable reuse. ImmPort's Assessments and Lab Tests templates -- which capture critical clinical information -- are often incomplete or omitted due to their complexity and the manual effort required. To address this challenge, an application with a graphical user interface requiring no programming was developed to facilitate population of these templates. The tool streamlines the submission process by reducing time and complexity for data contributors while ensuring template formatting. It integrates ImmPort files, study-specific data files, and a curated data dictionary to automate the mapping of study variables to the required fields within each template. The tool was evaluated on seven ImmPort studies with diverse designs. It successfully generated submission-ready templates that passed ImmPort's internal validation and will be incorporated into the repository. By improving the feasibility and completeness of templates, this approach enhances the quality, findability, and reusability of data within ImmPort.

Title: Discoidins are cytosolic lectins that recognize methylated L-rhamnose epitopes on mycobacterial glycolipids and glycopeptidolipids upon vacuole damage
Authors: D'Amico, D.; Goudge, G.; Foulon, M.; Macale, L. S.; Lico, L. S.; Chen, C.-K.; Prados, J.; Zheng, R. B.; Franklin, A.; Hevia Hernandez, G.; von Gunten, S.; Lowary, T. L.; Moynihan, P.; Soldati, T.
Abstract: Mycobacteria are surrounded by a dynamic, glycolipid-rich envelope that governs virulence and immune recognition, yet how cytosolic lectins sense its organization during intracellular infection remains unclear. Here, we show that Dictyostelium discoideum discoidins act as cytosolic sensors of mycobacterial envelope exposure. During infection, Mycobacterium marinum damages the limiting vacuolar membrane, triggering recruitment of all canonical isoforms (DscA, DscC, DscD, and DscE) to distinct foci around bacilli. Discoidins are not recruited after sterile endolysosomal damage, indicating that, unlike galectins, they recognize non-self surface-associated bacterial glycans rather than exposed host glycans. DscA and DscE display distinct glycan specificities. Combining transposon mutagenesis, synthetic glycan arrays, biochemical fractionation, and envelope mutants, we identify a restricted set of lipid-associated determinants enriched in methylated L-rhamnose motifs within LOS-, PGL-, and GPL-related structures. Recognition requires the conserved beta-galactoside-binding pocket of the H-type lectin domain, and isoform-specific synthetic disaccharides inhibit binding to intact bacteria. Analyses exclude AG-PG, AM/LAM, alpha-glucan, and TDM as major ligands and identify LOS and GPL-like glycolipids as dominant targets. PDIM/PGL or LOS disruption reduces discoidin binding to intact bacteria, although some ligands remain detectable in envelope extracts, underscoring the importance of accessibility. LOS deficiency also reduces DscA recruitment to intracellular bacilli. Therefore, binding of discoidins to glycan epitopes depends on ligand presence and accessibility, as well as on envelope perturbations and unmasking of specific glycolipids and glycopeptidolipids. These findings reveal pathogen envelope glycans as direct targets of cytosolic lectin surveillance and establish discoidins as probes of mycobacterial envelope remodeling during infection.

Title: Type 6 secretion systems of adherent-invasive Escherichia coli isolated from Crohn's disease patients shape intestinal microbiota.
Authors: Botchorichvili, H.; Massier, S.; Chassaing, B.; Birer, A.; Chevarin, C.; Sevrin, G.; Rodrigues, M.; Denis, S.; Wawrzyniak, I.; Peyretaillade, E.; Bonnet, R.; Pereira, B.; Allez, M.; Seksik, P.; Denizot, J.; The Remind Group,  ; Buisson, A.; Journet, L.; Barnich, N.; BILLARD, E.
Abstract: Adherent Invasive Escherichia coli (AIEC) colonize the ileal mucosa of Crohn's disease patients. Among bacterial virulence factors potentially implicated, type 6 secretion systems (T6SS) are molecular machineries sending effectors in prokaryotic or eukaryotic target cells. Two T6SS have been reported in AIEC LF82 reference strain. Here, we show that T6SS genes are more prevalent in Crohn's disease patients' microbiota compared to healthy controls, and that T6SS are more frequent in AIEC pathovar compared to E. coli in general and associated with FimH pathoadaptive polymorphism. The use of an in vitro gastrointestinal system coupled with T6SS promoter reporter assay highlighted expression of LF82 T6SS under gastrointestinal conditions, with a major role for bile salts. In mice infected with AIEC LF82 versus T6SS-deleted mutants, T6SS showed a functional impact in modulating the composition of mucosa-associated gut microbiota. Thus, AIEC may use their T6SS to compete with endogenous microbiota to colonize host mucosa.

Title: Gfa, a new integron-borne fosfomycin resistance protein family
Authors: Kieffer, N.; Prieto, A.; Ortiz-Miravalles, L.; Hipolito, A.; Vergara, E.; Borrero del Pino, J.; Carvalho, A.; Escudero, J. A.
Abstract: Fosfomycin is increasingly used to treat multidrug-resistant Gram-negative infections, yet resistance surveillance largely relies on homology-based detection of known fos genes. Here, we identify Gfa, a previously unrecognized integron-borne fosfomycin resistance determinant uncovered through functional screening of 129 integron gene cassettes. Gfa confers high-level fosfomycin resistance across Enterobacterales and Pseudomonas aeruginosa and is resistant to phosphonoformate inhibition. Structural modelling and mutagenesis reveal a conserved cysteine-rich, zinc-organized architecture essential for activity and distinct from canonical Fos enzymes. Crude-extract assays confirm glutathione-dependent fosfomycin inactivation under metal-chelating conditions. Distant Gfa homologs also conferred resistance, although activity was restricted to a subset of proteins tested. Together, these findings establish Gfa as a previously unrecognized fosfomycin resistance family and highlight the limitations of homology-based mining for discovering novel resistance determinants and predicting which family members are functional.

Title: HIV remodels germinal centers through T follicular helper cell loss
Authors: Jacobs, D.; Abdool, F.; Pohlenz, L.; Curtis, D.; Gill, R.; Bush, J. P.; Martin, M.; Toman, J.; Kuhn, W.; Maistry, S.; Levy, A.; Veazey, R. S.; Watkins, M.; Rappaport, J.; Porterfield, J.
Abstract: T follicular helper cells (Tfh) within germinal centers are among the most permissive cells for HIV infection and serve as a critical part of the viral reservoir. Given the key role of Tfh in affinity maturation and the production of plasma cells and memory B cells, an understanding of this critical viral reservoir is fundamental not only for cure strategies but also for understanding immunodeficiency in people living with HIV (PLWH). Using rare clinical specimens from PLWH, we demonstrate that HIV causes both a change in the cellular composition of germinal centers and changes in their overall architecture in ways that are consistent with the immunodeficiency seen in PLWH, independent of their CD4 count. We note a significant decrease in the number of GC Tfh cells and an increase in the number of follicular CD8 T cells in lymphoid tissues obtained from PLWH. Our data further show that GC size is decreased both by HIV and with increased age. Single-cell RNA sequencing data demonstrate that HIV acutely decreases the expression of Tfh B-cell support pathways and disrupts Tfh expression of cell trafficking receptors. Additionally, in a lymphoid organoid model of acute infection that forms GC-like structures, these findings are recapitulated, suggesting that New Approach Methodologies could be germane to understanding the impact of HIV on the reservoir and immunodeficiency. This study describes previously undocumented remodeling of the germinal center niche in PLWH, providing insight into the immune microenvironment of a key HIV reservoir that may help inform future cure strategies.

Title: Metagenomic insights into dose-dependent alterations in the tobacco rhizosphere microbiome by pyrroloquinoline quinone
Authors: Liu, L.; Liang, Y.; Cai, J.; Cheng, Y.; an, c.; Shi, C.; Ke, C.; Qin, Y.; Lai, C.
Abstract: Pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ) is known to promote plant growth, yet how the rhizosphere microbiome varies with PQQ concentration remains poorly understood. We applied metagenomic sequencing to characterize the taxonomic composition and functional potential of the tobacco rhizosphere microbiome across PQQ treatments at 0.5, 1 and 2 mol/L plus an untreated control. The rhizosphere microbiome was dominated by Pseudomonadota and Actinomycetota and differed among treatments in a concentration-associated, non-monotonic manner. The most pronounced differences were observed at 1 mol/L, where alpha diversity showed dimension-specific variation and beta-diversity analysis resolved the most distinct community profile. Taxonomic and functional profiles varied concurrently, with Streptomyces, Sphingomonas, Rhodanobacter and Lysobacter, together with functions related to biosynthesis, energy metabolism, colonization and environmental sensing, showing higher relative abundance at this concentration. No broad-spectrum antimicrobial effect was detected at the community level, and antibiotic resistance gene abundance showed no significant differences among treatments after correction for multiple testing. These findings provide a basis for further evaluation of PQQ in modulating the rhizosphere microbiome in continuous cropping systems.

Title: Label-free identification of bacterial species using adapted vision transformers
Authors: Hallström, E.; Kandavalli, V.; Marino Miguelez, M. H.; Elf, J.; Wählby, C.
Abstract: Antibiotic resistance is an increasingly serious problem worldwide. Identifying the bacterial species can help guide antibiotic selection and improve patient outcomes. In sepsis, where every minute counts, rapid identification is particularly important, and new approaches are needed. In this study, deep learning models were trained to identify bacterial species from phase-contrast time-lapse images of cells growing in microfluidic traps, without fluorescent labels. We demonstrated this approach in two previous studies using laboratory strains. Here, the previous work is extended to clinical bacterial isolates, evaluating performance on isolates not seen during training. Furthermore, it was tested whether autofluorescence could aid species identification. Two validation sets were acquired in separate experiments from the training data, the first containing clinical-isolate traps with five species (Escherichia coli, Enterococcus faecalis, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus and Enterobacter cloacae), imaged every two minutes, and the second containing clinical isolates of two species (E. coli and K. pneumoniae) recovered from spiked donor blood, imaged every minute. Training with the best previous CNN method achieved unsatisfactory results. Therefore, vision transformers were explored, and a self-supervised adaptation procedure was developed for pretrained DINOv3 using a frozen teacher, followed by supervised classification using time-lapse montages. Mean macro-F1 was 93.6 {+/-} 1.3% for isolates precultured in Mueller-Hinton medium using 60 frames (118 minutes) and 87.2 {+/-} 2.7% for isolates precultured in blood using 55 frames (54 minutes) (mean {+/-} sample standard deviation across training seeds). Performance was evaluated over time by increasing the number of frames available to the model during testing, and Fourier-domain filtering approximated reduced numerical aperture. The results are promising and suggest that the aperture can be decreased while retaining good results. However, further evaluation on independent isolates, experiments and patient samples is needed to establish generalization. Together with previous findings, these results bring us closer to rapid image-based diagnostics that could transform the initial treatment of acute bacterial infections by enabling better-informed antibiotic selection.

Title: A niche-specific role for ArlRS enables Staphylococcus aureus growth within Kupffer cells
Authors: Hommes, J. W.; Orthner, L. M.; van der Wal, F.; Flannagan, R. S. W.; Shim, R.; Samaniego Barron, L.; Dao, M.; Lasa, I.; Horswill, A. R.; Surewaard, B. G. J.
Abstract: Staphylococcus aureus bloodstream infections cause severe morbidity and mortality despite antibiotic therapy. We previously identified Kupffer cells (KCs) as the primary hepatic macrophages that rapidly clear circulating S. aureus, yet a subset of bacteria survives intracellularly and seeds systemic infection. Here, using spinning-disk intravital and super-resolution microscopy, we show that bacterial two-component system (TCS) signaling is required for intracellular replication within KCs in vivo. A global mutant lacking all non-essential TCSs failed to form intracellular microcolonies, and targeted analysis identified the ArlRS system as specifically required for KC replication. {Delta}arlRS bacteria remained as single non-replicating organisms within KCs, exhibited reduced dissemination and kidney abscess formation, and showed attenuated virulence with improved host survival. Complementation with arlRS restored the wildtype phenotype. Notably, the intracellular replication defect was not observed in primary or cultured macrophages, indicating that ArlRS-dependent replication is highly niche-specific and not reproduced by conventional in vitro models. Furthermore, restricting the KC reservoir with vancomycin treatment after infection further reduced renal infection by {Delta}arlRS bacteria. These findings identify ArlRS as a critical regulator of intracellular replication within KCs and establish the KC intracellular reservoir as a key driver of S. aureus pathogenesis and a potential therapeutic target during bloodstream infection.

Title: A domesticated prophage enzyme links bacterial metabolism, episymbiosis and phage fitness
Authors: Nahar, N.; Kumar, A.; Grossman, A. S.; McLean, J.; Bor, B.; Dong, P.-T.; He, X.
Abstract: Prophages are increasingly recognized as drivers of bacterial adaptation, yet how domesticated prophage genes shape microbial symbiosis remains poorly understood. Here, we identify GDPDXhp1, a glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase encoded by prophage Xhp1 of Schaalia odontolytica XH001, as a metabolic regulator linking bacterial physiology, episymbiosis and phage fitness. Association with the epibiotic bacterium Nanosynbacter lyticus TM7x strongly induced gdpdXhp1 expression and triggered GDPDXhp1-dependent lipid droplet accumulation in XH001. GDPDXhp1 orchestrated glycerophospholipid remodeling, membrane biophysical properties, respiration and cell-surface glycan composition in XH001, thereby promoting TM7x episymbiosis. Remarkably, GDPDXhp1 was also required for productive Xhp1 infection by remodeling susceptible bacterial host envelope structures to facilitate phage-host interactions. Together, our findings reveal a domesticated prophage enzyme that contributes to bacterial metabolism, interspecies symbiosis and viral reproduction, highlighting prophage as an overlooked source of metabolic innovation in microbial symbiosis.

Title: Rational Design of 5' UTRs for Optimized mRNA Expression and Cost-Effective, Rapid Analysis of Capped mRNA
Authors: Fang, Y.; Liu, T.; Liang, Y.; Wang, X.; Shao, M.; Wang, C.; Yu, J.; Sun, Y.; Zhang, P.; Qian, Q.
Abstract: In vitro-transcribed (IVT) messenger RNA (mRNA) therapeutics require rigorous quality control of 5' capping efficiency and 3' poly(A) tail length, both of which constitute critical quality attributes (CQAs). Current analytical workflows for these CQAs rely on hybridization with nucleic acid probes and biotin-based affinity purification, which constrain throughput and increase per-assay cost. Here, we report a rationally designed 5' untranslated region (5' UTR) that sustains high translational efficiency while enabling probe-free, one-step purification for rapid quantification of capping efficiency and poly(A) tail length distribution. This approach exploits a strategically engineered 5' UTR incorporating a purine-only RNase A-resistant fragment terminating at a single pyrimidine cleavage site, together with a translation-enhancing element comprising an N6-methyladenosine (m6A) deposition motif and an 18S rRNA complementarity sequence. This dual-function design accommodates GA-rich sequence segments without compromising mRNA translational output. Compared with conventional probe- and biotin-dependent workflows, the present method substantially reduces cost and processing time and is compatible with simultaneous detection of segmented AmGn poly(A) tail variants. This integrated platform provides a simplified, probe-free and construct-universal for high-throughput in-process control (IPC) of mRNA therapeutics.

Title: Ab initio CryoEM maps minimizing preferred orientation problems in heterogeneous mixtures: ReconSIREN
Authors: Herreros, D.; Sorzano, C. O. S.; Carazo, J. M.
Abstract: Cryo-Electron Microscopy (CryoEM) Single Particle Analysis (SPA) is pivotal for elucidating protein structures and their conformational dynamics. Several critical steps are required to obtain accurate maps. First, the \textit{ab initio} relative orientations and shifts between images must be determined. Second, the common issue of specimens presenting a preferred orientation should be adequately addressed. Third, all of the above must account for particle flexibility and sample heterogeneity. Additionally, these steps are interrelated, making the search for all these parameters a real challenge when considering convergence robustness. In this context, we present ReconSIREN, a novel deep learning framework that addresses the key steps outlined before in an \textit{ab initio} manner while greatly minimizing one of the most important practical burdens in SPA, namely the errors introduced in the CryoEM maps by the existence of preferred orientations; the latter is achieved by a change of the optimization approach that avoids the so-called ``attraction problem'', and by the introduction of a new type of geometrical priors. It does so fully \textit{ab initio}, using deep learning training/inference steps without resorting to more traditional optimization approaches, and generating highly accurate initial reconstructions. We present maps as both homogeneous (consensus) maps and a full conformational landscape for analyzing flexibility and heterogeneity. Thanks to its Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, ReconSIREN distributes the estimation workload across independent experts, improving optimization efficiency and simplifying the process.

Title: De Novo Design of Flavoproteins with Controlled Excited State Dynamics
Authors: Anderson, R.; Bungay, E.; Underhill, J.; Liu, M.; Stuart, A.; Back, C.; Berrones-Reyes, J.; Dubiel, P.; Birrell, J.; G. Rao, A.; Williams, C.; Barringer, R.; Hinchliffe, P.; Lichtenstein, B.; Curchod, B.; Butt, J.; Oliver, T.; Mulholland, A. J.
Abstract: Designing photochemical properties in proteins is a frontier challenge in biomolecular design, which, when realised, will open new avenues in catalysis and biomolecular electronics. Here we demonstrate an integrated computational design framework, supported by ultrafast spectroscopy, combining protein design, quantum mechanical/molecular mechanics molecular dynamics (QM/MM MD) and electronic structure calculations, to control flavin excited states in de novo proteins. Iterative design yields FC-4D2, a flavocytochrome with covalently bound flavin and non-covalently bound heme B and Fl-4D2, where the heme-binding site is removed. Both proteins are highly thermostable, and access all physiologically relevant flavin redox and protonation states, while high-resolution X-ray crystallography confirms the near-[A]ngstrom-level accuracy in design. Incorporating QM/MM MD and linear-response time-dependent density functional theory (LR-TDDFT) into the design workflow enables engineering of a flavin-tryptophan charge-transfer variant, Fl-4D2CT, that modifies the flavin absorption spectrum, substantially alters its redox properties and suppresses fluorescence. Ultrafast studies reveal how protein design reshapes the excited state relaxation timescale and mechanism. Our study establishes a modular strategy for programming flavin photochemistry in designed proteins.

Title: Autofocusing molecular simulations for integrative structural biology of broad conformational ensembles
Authors: Antila, H. S.; Miettinen, M. S.
Abstract: Integrative structural biology seeks molecular descriptions consistent with complementary experimental measurements. A particular challenge arises for molecules whose broad conformational ensembles resist description by a few representative structures, such as natively unfolded proteins and fluid-phase biomembrane lipids. Although molecular simulations can generate such ensembles, their simultaneous agreement with a large number of experimental constraints is commonly prevented by model inaccuracies. Here we introduce autofocusing as an approach that integrates experimental information by automated finetuning of the physical model generating the ensemble. We demonstrate it for a fluid bilayer of the phospholipid POPC, for which no existing force field has simultaneously reproduced the complete set of 82 NMR C-H bond order parameters. Autofocusing brings all the 82 within experimental uncertainty while preserving agreement with independent small-angle X-ray scattering measurements and retaining or improving agreement with untargeted NMR relaxation rates and effective correlation times, thus supporting its description of membrane structure and dynamics beyond the calibration targets. The resulting simulations challenge a long-standing two-state interpretation of phosphatidylcholine headgroup structure, instead supporting a broad conformational ensemble poorly represented by crystal-derived conformers. These results establish autofocusing as a practical approach to constructing experimentally grounded conformational ensembles while retaining the computational tractability of classical molecular dynamics.

Title: Chain-Length-Dependent Interactions of Polyethylene Nanoplastics with Human Catalase reveals Size based Nanoplastic Toxicity
Authors: Tanaya, S.; Rath, S. L.
Abstract: Nanoplastic contamination is increasingly recognized as a biochemical stressor, yet the molecular determinants governing how polymer fragment size dictates protein-level interactions remain poorly understood. Here, we combine molecular docking and all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to characterize the interaction of polyethylene (PE) oligomers of increasing length (n = 3, 5, 7, and 14 repeat units) with human catalase, a tetrameric heme enzyme central to cellular antioxidant defense. Single-chain simulations reveal that short PE fragments (3-, 5-, and 7-mer) migrate from an initial domain-connector pose toward a heme-proximal, previously characterized inhibitor-binding site, whereas the 14-mer remains kinetically confined to a peripheral surface site, implicating short-chain PE as a potential catalase inhibitor. In multichain corona systems, backbone dynamics show a non-monotonic, chain-length-dependent destabilization, with the 3- and 5-mer inducing the greatest structural perturbation and the 14-mer best preserving native-like dynamics despite forming an extensive, percolating surface network across all four subunits. MM-PBSA free energy decomposition identifies van der Waals interactions as the dominant thermodynamic driver of binding, while electrostatic surface mapping indicates that cationic surface patches instead govern long-range spatial targeting of PE chains. These findings establish a framework linking nanoplastic fragment size to protein-level toxicity, with direct implications for assessing the biochemical risk of environmentally weathered polyethylene.

Title: Archaeal cell envelopes selectively activate innate immunity through TLR2 in contrasts with multi-receptor bacterial sensing
Authors: Martin-Gallausiaux, C.; Grosjean, C.; Baker, B.; Werts, C.; Borrel, G.; Gribaldo, S.
Abstract: The cell envelope of bacteria and fungi is a major source of microbial-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs), which are recognised by multiple host pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) such as TLRs and NODs. The key role of this recognition in protecting against infection and regulating diverse physiological processes has been studied for decades. In contrast, although the archaea are growingly recognised as an important component of the animal and human microbiome, their interaction with the innate immune system has been largely understudied. Here, we asked whether the archaeal cell envelope acts as MAMP. We selected 15 archaeal species from different environments, including the human microbiome, and harbouring diverse envelope characteristics, and we tested their ability to activate innate immune responses in human and murine immune cells. We first show that archaeal cells activate the innate immune transcription factor NF-kB and induce IL-6 secretion. Using whole archaeal cells, supernatants, and purified envelope components, we then find that none of the main PRR receptors which recognise the bacterial envelope (TLR4, TLR5, NOD1 and NOD2) are involved in this activation. We only detected activation of TLR2, regardless of the environmental origins of the archaea tested, although with overall lower activity compared to bacteria. We further demonstrate that different TLR2 heterodimers are involved, depending on the species, although the archaeal agonist remains unknown. Altogether, our results highlight a surprising paucity of interaction of archaeal cell envelope components with host PPRs, in contrast to bacteria, and open new avenues of research toward further investigation of archaea/host interplay.

Title: Chronic stress remodels gut bacterial ecology and polysaccharide metabolism with neuroendocrine consequences despite unchanged behavior
Authors: Slusser, A. C.; Relangi, T. R.; Hudson, L. A.; Le, D. T.; Hernandez, M. M.; Earp, T. J.; Wright, A. T.
Abstract: The gut-microbiome-brain axis (GMBA) links the gut and brain through metabolic, immunological, and neuroendocrine pathways, and can become dysregulated during psychological stress (PS). While previous studies primarily infer microbial function and use physical stressors that incompletely model human PS, here, functional multi-omics was applied to a chronic social-isolation mouse model. Although isolation caused no measurable behavioral changes, brain proteomics revealed stress-associated molecular responses. Taxonomic and short-chain fatty acid analyses suggested limited microbiome changes; however, metaproteomics uncovered sex-specific restructuring of bacterial ecology and carbohydrate-active enzymes. In females, isolation increased Petralouisia muris proteins involved in bacterial microcompartment metabolism and {beta}-glucuronidases across Lachnospiraceae taxa. Enriched {beta}-glucuronidase abundance coincided with reduced circulating glucuronides and altered brain estrogen-receptor activity, suggesting a microbial deconjugation-host estrogen-signaling interaction. These findings demonstrate that functional GMBA alterations may precede or occur independently of overt behavioral phenotypes and highlight the value of direct functional profiling in PS.

Title: MnSOD Diversifies, while FeSOD Dominates Superoxide Defense in Cyanobacteria
Authors: Khan, M. A.; Durand, A.; Steunou, A.-S.; Leleux, S.; Cassier-Chauvat, C.; Chauvat, F.; Ouchane, S.
Abstract: Cyanobacteria are unique among prokaryotes in possessing photosynthetic thylakoid membranes enclosing an internal lumen, where superoxide production is expected to be substantial. Thylakoid-associated superoxide dismutases (SODs) would seem the obvious first line of defense, yet many cyanobacteria rely instead on a single soluble cytoplasmic enzyme, raising the question of what role thylakoid-associated SOD isoforms actually play. Using Cyanothece sp. PCC 7425, which encodes both a cytoplasmic FeSOD and a thylakoid-associated MnSOD, we combined sequence analysis, structural, genetics, and biochemical approaches to characterise FeSOD and MnSOD cellular localisation and assess each enzyme's contribution to superoxide defense. Cyanobacterial MnSODs display diverse N-terminal architectures, consistent with soluble, transmembrane, or lipid-anchored forms, yet contribute only modestly to superoxide defense in Cyanothece PCC 7425 and, very likely, across cyanobacteria broadly. Soluble FeSOD instead provides the major line of defense, showing that thylakoid association does not guarantee physiological importance. This predominance of a cytoplasmic enzyme highlights the central role of cytoplasmic superoxide detoxification, consistent with superoxide being generated mainly at the PSI acceptor side, and extends to the chloroplast stroma of plants. Our findings support a model in which SOD distribution reflects metal availability, enzyme properties, and subcellular organisation : FeSOD protects the compartment harbouring the main targets of PSI-associated superoxide, whereas MnSOD is retained where thylakoid association offers additional local protection, but becomes dispensable when the local ROS burden is limited. Spatial matching between superoxide production, antioxidant localisation, and target vulnerability may thus shape the diversification and maintenance of antioxidant systems across cyanobacteria and chloroplasts.

Title: Shedding light on the virome of Caliothrips phaseoli, an emergent pest in peanut
Authors: bejerman, n.; de Breuil, S.; Dottori, C.; Debat, H.
Abstract: The bean thrips, Caliothrips phaseoli, is an emergent pest affecting peanut production. Thus, gaining a deeper understanding of the naturally occurring viral populations associated with this insect is of major importance, as such knowledge could support the design of novel pest management strategies that are both ecologically responsible and sustainable over the long term. In this study, we performed the first RNA high-throughput sequencing (HTS) analysis of C. phaseoli to unravel its virome, discovering a wide number of novel RNA viruses. Our HTS analysis revealed the presence of 31 viral segments, corresponding to 18 viruses, including double-stranded RNA viruses as well as positive- and negative-sense single-stranded RNA viruses. All these are novel viruses and cover multiple viral lineages belonging to diverse families. Overall, these results indicates that C. phaseoli hides a complex virome. The findings presented here provide an important framework for subsequent studies aimed at understanding the ecological significance, evolutionary patterns, and possible use of these viruses as components of biologically based management programs for this emerging peanut pest.

Title: Spatiotemporal Heterogeneity of HPV Integration Architectures Drive Oncogenic Features of Oropharyngeal Cancer
Authors: Gu, W.; Bhangale, A. D.; Du, X.; Deng, X.; Gensterblum-Miller, E. U.; Currie, J.; Brummel, C. V.; Nyabashi, V.; Buchakjian, M.; Casper, K. A.; Chinn, S. E.; Forner, D.; Malloy, K. M.; Mierzwa, M. L.; Prince, M. E.; Shah, J. L.; Shuman, A. G.; Stucken, C. L.; Swiecicki, P. L.; Worden, F. P.; Yalamanchi, P.; McHugh, J. B.; Kuhs, K. A.; Boyle, A. P.; Jiang, H.; Neal, M. E.; Spector, M. E.; Mills, R. E.; Brenner, C. J.
Abstract: Viral integration is common in human papillomavirus-positive oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (HPV+ OPSCC), but its structural and clinical significance remains unclear. We integrated targeted capture sequencing of 197 HPV+ OPSCCs with long-read nanopore sequencing of 17 tumors and models to characterize HPV-host rearrangements. We developed a novel quantitative informatics framework that classifies integration structures as Type1 (simple, single/low-copy) or Type2 (clustered, high-copy, rearranged). HPV integration occurred in 83% of tumors, with recurrent hotspots including TP63, MYC, CD274, TRAF2, and KMT2C. Type2 events were enriched for HPV E2 disruption, focal human amplifications, preferential transcription, and noncanonical HPV-host RNA fusion isoforms. Type2 tumors showed increased HPV oncogene expression and activation of MYC, NF-{kappa}B/TNF, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, Hippo/YAP-TAZ, and epithelial stemness programs. Multi-region and longitudinal analyses revealed intratumoral heterogeneity and clonal selection of Type2 architectures during progression, supporting integration structure as a potential marker of aggressive behavior and risk stratification.

Title: Buried Ion-Pairs Reshape Folding Pathways of Artificial Proteins
Authors: Liebau, J.; Kemp, G.; Auman, D.; Hoja, N.; Jussupow, A.; Baumgart, M.; von Heijne, G.; Kaila, V. R. I.
Abstract: Ion-pairs are central charged motifs that control the biological function of several proteins. Yet, the physical principles linked to the formation of ion-pairs during protein folding remain poorly understood. Here, we show that buried ion-pairs of de novo-designed helical bundle proteins reshape the folding pathways by introducing kinetic barriers that are overcome by a hydrophobic collapse linked to packing of the protein core. By combining protein design with co-translational folding studies, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, and molecular dynamics simulations, we show that introduction of a buried ion-pair leads to a shifted folding transition that balances desolvation and electrostatic interactions within the protein and the bulk solvent. Moreover, we find that the folding pathway is sensitive to modifications in non-polar interactions and motifs that electrostatically shield the ion-pair from its surroundings. Our combined findings provide a blueprint for understanding how functional motifs affect protein folding and how mutation of charged networks alter the stability of proteins.

Title: Bovine serum albumin interaction modulates the cellular potency of the BUB1 inhibitor BAY-1816032: fluorescence, molecular docking, and mesothelioma cell evidence
Authors: Gorjipour, F.; Cakiroglu, E.; Senturk, S.
Abstract: Albumin binding can substantially alter the unbound concentration and apparent cellular potency of small-molecule anticancer agents. BAY-1816032 is a selective BUB1 kinase inhibitor with activity in malignant pleural mesothelioma, but its interaction with serum albumin has not been defined. This study combined intrinsic bovine serum albumin (BSA) fluorescence measurements, molecular docking, and cell-viability assays to examine whether albumin association influences BAY-1816032 activity. BAY-1816032 produced pronounced quenching of BSA fluorescence at low drug-to-protein molar ratios, and the quenching response was greater at mildly acidic pH than at mildly basic pH. Docking to BSA (PDB 4F5S) placed the top-ranked pose in Sudlow site I (subdomain IIA), with a Vina score of -7.8 kcal/mol and predicted hydrogen-bond contacts with Tyr149, Arg256, and Asp450. In NCI-H28, NCI-H2052, NCI-H2452, and AB12 mesothelioma cells, supplementation of 10% fetal bovine serum medium with 2% (w/v; 20 mg/mL) BSA shifted BAY-1816032 concentration-response curves to the right. Relative to 10% serum alone, IC50 values increased from 2.4 to 11.1 uM in H28, 3.6 to 22.0 uM in H2052, 2.0 to 4.9 uM in H2452, and 2.4 to 11.1 uM in AB12. These data support an albumin-dependent reduction in the freely available drug fraction and identify site I as the leading computational binding-site hypothesis. Because fluorescence-intensity and docking data do not independently establish a dissociation constant or quenching mechanism, direct unbound-fraction measurements and competitive displacement experiments are required for quantitative confirmation.

Title: The Mitochondria-Modulating Small Molecule TEM1657 Suppresses NFKBIZ Pathway and Resolves Th17-Driven Psoriatic Inflammation
Authors: GAUTAM, P.; SALWINSKI, A.; Abdelwahab, A. B.; JALCE, G.; BOULANGE, L.; BETTINGER, J.; BROUARD, J. J. S.; ETLICHER, A.; PEROUF, R.; HALPER, J.; MILLARD, M.; DE ISLA, N.; HANNEWALD, P.; GINGLINGER, J.-F.; RUBIO, M.-T.; JOUZEAU, J.-Y.; BOURGAUD, F.; MOULIN, D.
Abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic skin disease characterized by red, scaly plaques mainly driven by dysregulated T cells that induce keratinocytes (KCs) proliferation and inflammation. Despite significant advancements in disease management through biologics and topical therapies, these treatments offer only temporary relief and fail to prevent disease recurrence. Considering the current therapeutic needs, we described herein a novel small molecule TEM1657, derived from 3,5-dicaffeoylquinic acid with anti-inflammatory potency in imiquimod-induced psoriasis mouse model as well as in Th17-stimulated KCs. Mechanistically, its action is mediated through modulation of mitochondrial dynamics, specifically via OPA1, an inner mitochondrial membrane protein that alters mitochondrial calcium influx, and further impacts cellular bioenergetics. Moreover, TEM1657 rapidly suppresses transcription of NFKBIZ and various other psoriasis-associated genes. These observations highlighted a pathway that represents an innovative target in psoriasis and other NFKBIZ-related disorders.

Title: A tetracycline-inducible promoter for gene expression in Gram-negative bacteria including Acinetobacter baumannii
Authors: Stella, N. A.; Ginde, R. K.; Ginde, R. K.; Calvario, R. C.; Doi, Y.; Shanks, R. M. Q.
Abstract: Carbohydrate inducible promoters on expression plasmids are widely used for biotechnology and basic science research. However, using carbohydrates for inducers has drawbacks including influencing bacterial metabolism, the inducer being used as a carbon source by the bacteria, high background expression, and only a subset of cells experiencing promoter activation. Furthermore, some bacteria including the pathogen Acinetobacter baumannii currently lack good carbohydrate-inducible promoters. To address this issue, a tetracycline-inducible promoter, PtetB, isolated from A. baumannii was cloned and evaluated in a number of important bacteria: Acinetobacter baumannii, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Pseudomonas fluorescens, and Serratia marcescens. A highly sensitive luxCDABE reporter was used to evaluate promoter activity. S. marcescens strains with elevated and reduced cyclic-AMP levels were used to evaluate the impact of cAMP on PtetB function. The PtetB promoter was induced over 800-fold in A. baumannii and 10-750-fold inducible in the other tested species. Background expression was lower from PtetB in the pseudomonads than previously described carbohydrate inducible promoters. Data indicated that the PtetB promoter system may be a useful tool for future basic science research with the tested bacteria.

Title: Scalable methylome-transcriptome profiling resolves clonal organization in human hematopoiesis
Authors: Shao, J.; Chen, M.; Liu, Y.; Sun, J.; Zhang, G.; Yan, Z.-Y.; Lin, H.; Ren, M.; Pei, S.; Peng, J.; Gong, Y.; WANG, S.
Abstract: Understanding human tissue maintenance and remodeling requires linking clonal ancestry to molecular state, yet scalable joint measurement remains challenging. Here, we introduce Droplet-MT and an integrated computational workflow for joint transcriptome and methylome profiling at ~10,000 cells per library. Methylation epimutations enable mutation-independent clonal reconstruction from high-coverage methylomes, while reference-based label transfer assigns cells to established clones at ~0.2% CpG coverage, reducing sequencing cost. Clone-aggregated somatic variants provide genetic annotation without additional single-cell genotyping. Across ~21,000 paired profiles from healthy blood and longitudinal acute myeloid leukemia, we resolved small and expanded clones with heterogeneous lineage output. In leukemia, the framework distinguished changes in malignant clonal abundance, state remodeling within persistent clones, and recovery of healthy polyclonal hematopoiesis. Malignant monocytes remained transcriptionally and epigenetically distinct from healthy and recovery-associated cells despite treatment-associated remodeling. Droplet-MT enables scalable analysis of human tissues by linking clonal organization with molecular state and retrospective genetic annotation.

Title: An iPSC-based experimental framework for investigating phenotypic variation associated with Jomon ancestry in the present-day Japanese population
Authors: Nakamura, Y.; Watanabe, Y.; Tanabe, H.; Hirai, A.; Higashi, K.; Kurokawa, K.; Toyoda, A.; Kato, T.; Tsukahara, M.; Koganebuchi, K.; Hamazaki, Y.; Takebe, T.; Imamura, M.; Ishida, T.; Ohashi, J.; Oota, H.
Abstract: Ancestry-related genomic variation may contribute to phenotypic diversity. However, its cellular consequences remain difficult to evaluate. To address this, we developed a human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-based framework for investigating such phenotypes. We used the Japanese population as a model of Jomon-related and continental East Asian ancestry admixture. Jomon ancestry, estimated using the Jomon allele score (JAS), was associated with clinical measures, including renal-related traits and serum triglycerides in 34,152 Tohoku Medical Megabank participants. Peripheral blood mononuclear cell transcriptomics of donors from the upper and lower extremes of the JAS distribution (n = 10) suggested group-level differences in immune-related gene expression. To test whether the serum triglyceride association coincided with hepatic cellular phenotypes, we differentiated hiPSCs from these donors into hepatocyte-like cells. Neither intracellular triglycerides nor lipid-related gene expression differed between groups. These findings highlight the value of a genetically characterized hiPSC-based framework for investigating ancestry-associated phenotypes across cellular contexts.

Title: Cromosomal genomes assemblies of twelve sheep breeds
Authors: ECHE, C.; Birdes, C.; Marcuzzo, C.; Sarry, J.; Suin, A.; Vernette, C.; Kuchly, C.; Gaspin, C.; Milan, D.; Donnadieu, C.; Iampietro, C.; Tosser-Klopp, G.; Klopp, C.
Abstract: The sheep research community benefits from a genome assembly that has been refined over the last 15 years. However, the rich diversity of sheep breeds suggests that a single individual genome is not enough to represent the species full genomic content. Third-generation sequencing technologies have recently made it possible to generate high quality assemblies that should enable to elucidate unique and/or complex phenotype determinisms depending on genetic structural variations. In the SeqOccin project, twelve breeds were selected to represent (mostly French) sheep genetic diversity: Basco-Bearnaise, Black Belly, Blanche du Massif Central, Corse, Ile de France, Lacaune, Manech Tete Noire, Noire du Velay, Ouessant, Rambouillet, Vendeen, Soay. High-molecular-weight DNA was extracted from blood samples and subjected to long read whole-genome sequencing. The reads were used to generate de novo assemblies and were aligned onto the public reference to call structural variants. PacBio HiFi and parental Illumina reads were used to assemble phased haplotypes of the Lacaune breed. For the other breeds, PacBio raw (CLR) or ONT reads were generated. Our work demonstrates the feasibility of assembling genomes with a reasonable amount of data and appropriate software packages, delivering one high-quality assembly and 11 standard sheep assemblies that pave the way for pangenome construction and structural variant functional studies.

Title: The Genetic Landscape of Structural Variants in Aspergillus flavus using ONT and PacBio Sequencing
Authors: Woods, A.; Lohmar, J. M.; Malik, A.; Lustig, A. J.
Abstract: Genetic rearrangement in the absence of selection is poorly understood. Long-read, high-depth sequencing has enabled analysis of the genetic landscape of spontaneous structural variants. We have applied PacBio Revio sequencing to identify the major classes of genetic alterations during long-term vegetative growth in Aspergillus flavus. These classes include a) precise deletions frequently associated with the flanking region of homology, b) clusters of short deletions that are heavily enriched within centromeric and subtelomeric regions that are typically 94% A+T, and c) deletions and expansions within a subset of homopolymer tracts. We find 70 homopolymer tracts longer than 44 bp, dispersed throughout the genome in noncoding regions and unassociated with transposable elements. A broader analysis of third-generation sequenced datasets from fungi found within the Phylum Ascomycota showed a high but variable prevalence of homopolymeric tracts across species. The adventitious identification of a putative flbA mutation, responsible for an altered conidial phenotype, by the Deep Variant AI system also demonstrates the power of this approach. These studies show that high-depth, long-read sequencing can probe SNPs, indels, homopolymeric tracts, and large-scale rearrangements in an unbiased fashion, and demonstrate that short deletions and homopolymer tract expansions arise spontaneously in A. flavus and other filamentous fungi.

Title: GenDiMug: a generic inclusive multigraph framework to analyze genomic organizations and -omics data at multiple scales
Authors: Teuliere, J.; Lopez, P.; Corel, E.; Llorente, B.; Bapteste, E.
Abstract: After decades of investigation, analyses of genome organization remain challenging. This is because genome descriptions are very information-rich and usually rendered as a linear map of genomic features corresponding to an ordered list of position intervals on a nucleic acid macromolecular backbone. This formalism, while accurate, is not fully optimized to mathematically analyze all genome structural properties, in particular the relations between genomic features, nor to integrate large amounts of -omics data, such as transcriptomes, epigenomes, proteomes, meltomes or chromatin accessibility data, which are increasingly available. We therefore developed GenDiMug, a tool that uses a network representation of the genome as a backbone, providing a natural framework to integrate spatial and ontogenetic relationships between genomic features and multi-omics data. We illustrate how this generic approach can be applied to all sorts of genomes, both to visualize genomic topology at contig and chromosomal scales at base-pair resolution, and to analyze genome positional effects using various graph metrics. Using GenDiMug, we further reveal clumping of genes with similar expression levels in eukaryotic genomes and their possible circadian regulation in a photosynthetic alga.

Title: Inferring ecDNA Evolution from Allele Frequency Spectra
Authors: Dameracharla, B.; Prasad, G.; Luebeck, J.; Amin, S.; Kirkland, J.; Chapman, O. S.; Chavez, L.; Verhaak, R.; Huang, W.; Mischel, P. S.; Werner, B.; Bafna, V.
Abstract: Extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) can arise early in the development of aggressive tumors or later upon progression, but the impact of chronology on patient outcome is not known. Currently, it is not possible to determine when an ecDNA arose in the course of tumor development and progression, based on genome sequencing data. Here, we develop an analytic method, ecEvol, to infer ecDNA emergence time, selection strength, mutation rate, and clonal dominance from allele frequency spectra in bulk whole-genome sequencing. EcEvol outperforms other methods and predicts parameters with high accuracy across a wide range of parameter values. Applying ecEvol to primary, treatment-naive tumors, we find that ecDNA typically emerges early and undergoes strong positive selection, albeit with substantial variation across cancer types. EcDNAs carrying known oncogenes emerge earlier and reach greater clonal dominance than ecDNAs lacking known oncogenes. In advanced and predominantly treated tumors, ecDNA emerges substantially later than in matched primary tumors, consistent with the generation and selection of new ecDNA during tumor progression and therapy. Longitudinal samples further support continued expansion of ecDNA-bearing lineages. Finally, earlier ecDNA emergence is associated with poorer overall survival. These results provide insight into the chronology of ecDNA formation from a single tumor biopsy taken at any point during the course of the disease, revealing that allele-frequency spectra encode the evolutionary history of ecDNA and provide a quantitative framework for reconstructing its emergence and expansion.

Title: In silico subtractive genomics and reverse vaccinology approach reveal outer membrane proteins OMP47 and LptD as dual-purpose drug and vaccine targets in Pasteurella multocida Pm70
Authors: Khan Chowdhury, A. R.; Islam, S.; Farid, A.; Lamia, F.; Ahmad, T. F.; Hossain, N. J.; Paul, A. R.; Afrin, T.; Elias, S. M.
Abstract: Drug targets and vaccines for bacterial diseases are challenging to develop.
