Computational subtractive genomics and reverse vaccinology offer a viable substitute for conventional drug and vaccine development approaches. In recent years, Pasteurella multocida, a Gram-negative pathogen responsible for severe infections in humans along with major diseases in livestock and poultry, has developed resistance to multiple drugs. As a result, there is an urgent demand for research into reliable, efficient, highly potent, and cost-effective strategies to combat the rise of Pasteurella multocida infections. To address this, the present study integrated an in silico subtractive genomics and reverse vaccinology workflow to pinpoint proteins with potential value as both drug and vaccine targets. From the complete Pasteurella multocida Pm70 proteome, we identified 446 proteins that had no similarities with human proteins, out of which 129 were found to be essential for the pathogens survival. These 129 proteins are therefore potential candidates for drug development. Further metabolic pathway analysis, virulence potential, subcellular localization, and structural analyses revealed two outer membrane proteins, namely, 47 kDa outer membrane protein and lipopolysaccharide-assembly protein LptD, as promising candidates for therapeutic development. Subsequent antigenicity analysis revealed both outer membrane proteins as potential vaccine targets, exhibiting highly favorable antigenicity scores. Candidate B- and T-cell epitopes were systematically mapped from these two targets based on antigenicity, immunogenicity, toxicity, and allergenicity potential and only high-confidence epitopes were assembled using adjuvants and class-specific linkers to construct the final multi-epitope vaccine (MEV). The designed MEV construct was demonstrated to be highly antigenic, non-toxic and non-allergenic to humans, while possessing favorable structural and physicochemical properties, and exhibited strong binding interactions with human toll-like receptors with minimal molecular deformability. Although further experimental validation is recommended to fully assess their efficacy, the present study establishes a solid foundation for the development of novel therapeutics and vaccine candidates against P. multocida, ultimately contributing to the reduction of its rising infections.

Title: Version-aware question answering over living oncology guidelines
Authors: Ravi Kumar, T.; Kaniyar Narayana Iyengar, A. I.; Khan, M. A.; Khakwani, K. Z. R.; Kathuria, K.; Sonbol, M. B.; Riaz, I.; Gupta, V.
Abstract: Living clinical guidelines revise recommendations as evidence emerges, so an AI answer can be faithful to a real guideline and still be out of date. Here we examine this failure using ASCOBench, 288 unique questions in 96 three-turn conversations grounded in versioned American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) breast and prostate cancer guidelines, with oncologist-reviewed reference answers. Oncologists corrected one in four version-sensitive answers drafted by a frontier model, against fewer than one in ten factual ones. Across the guideline corpus, 19 recommendations changed between versions, seven of them reversals, yet only 1 of 14 superseded documents states that it has been replaced. With a strong model, retrieval over several guideline versions made stale answers four times more frequent than answering without retrieval. SentryLine, a verification-first system, lowered incorrect answers to 4.2-5.2% from 9.7-22.9% for baselines across three models. Recognizing change before a guideline declares it remains an open problem.

Title: AI-Driven Design of Next-Generation Immunoinformatics Multi-Epitope Subunit Vaccine Targeting the Most Virulent Mpox Proteome: A Structural and Kinetic Validation Framework
Authors: Emon, M.; Siddiqque, N. H.; Haque, M. E.
Abstract: The resurgence of the Mpox virus (MPXV) highlights the urgent need for scalable, mutation-resistant countermeasures. Slow development timelines hinder traditional empirical vaccine discovery, while conventional vaccinology often yields high false-positive rates because it relies on static, linear sequence-based screening. These classical informatics filters consistently fail to predict physical structural stability or the dynamic presentation of immune cells under physiological conditions, creating a distinct translational gap between computational design and in vitro efficacy. To address these limitations, here we engineered an advanced, AI-augmented vaccine discovery pipeline targeting the most virulent components of the MPXV proteome. We systematically screened eight critical viral targets essential for replication, membrane morphogenesis, and host-cell entry to map highly conserved T-cell and B-cell epitopes. Moving beyond standard heuristic filtering, we implemented a high-fidelity deep learning validation layer: ESM-2 protein language models (pLMs) were deployed to calculate pseudo-perplexity scores across chimeric linker junctions (EAAAK, GPGPG) to guarantee structural naturalness, MHCflurry ensemble models successfully verified active intracellular antigen presentation, and structure-informed graph neural networks (GNNs) simulated the physical node-attention dynamics of the immune synapse. Finally, recurrent neural networks (RNNs)-driven mRNA kinetic modeling optimized translation initiation rates and minimum free energy profiles during in silico cloning. This multi-layered pipeline successfully yielded three structurally refined, multi-epitope vaccine constructs optimized for maximum global population coverage. ESM-2 structural validation confirmed exceptionally low perplexity scores at structural junctions, indicating that the engineered chimaeras have native-like stability and a minimized risk of proteolysis. GNN-based immune synapse modeling demonstrated highly stable binding kinetics and robust binding free energies between the target epitopes and human HLA alleles. Furthermore, RNN kinetic optimizations established that the cDNA sequences are optimized for high-yield expression in heterologous expression hosts without risk of ribosomal stalling or translational bottlenecks. This study establishes a deep learning-augmented framework that bridges the gap between theoretical sequence optimization and biopharmaceutical scalability. By validating the structural naturalness, real-world immunogenicity, and manufacturing kinetics of our vaccine chimeras, this framework presents a robust, proactive paradigm for rapid vaccine architecture against emerging orthopoxvirus threats.

Title: Transcriptional perturbation effects remain structured beyond the leading global trend
Authors: Liu, Q.; Zhang, Q.; Chen, Y.; Du, J.-H.; Zhao, S.; Wang, J.
Abstract: Prior work has described a global transcriptional response to gene perturbation, with many perturbations moving cells along a common direction. We find that perturbations contribute differently to this leading global trend and that substantial organization remains beyond it, including transferable perturbation-specific effects across datasets and a common hierarchy of responsive genes across perturbations. These patterns make simple strategies surprisingly competitive even in predicting effects beyond the leading global component.

Title: A multi-tissue transcriptome strategy for genomic resource development in  Pinus edulis
Authors: Macias, D. S.; Gyllenhaal, E. F.; Kleinkopf, J. A.; Pockman, W. T.; Marx, H. E.
Abstract: Premise:: Conifers comprise one-sixth of global forests and landscape genomic studies are urgently needed to understand their biology, yet relatively few conifer species have reference genomes. Targeted exon-capture is a practical alternative to whole-genome sequencing, but selecting loci without a reference genome remains a barrier. We developed a multi-tissue reference transcriptome for pi non pine (Pinus edulis) to ask how multi-tissue sampling improves probe design, and what is lost under a conventional single-tissue approach. Methods: We assembled a reference transcriptome from four diploid tissues (needle, phloem, root, vegetative bud) and one haploid tissue (megagametophyte), using the latter as a pseudo-guide. We designed a target-capture probe-set by prioritizing highly expressed P. edulis transcripts and transcripts matching a conifer exon database. Results: We recovered 76% of conserved plant genes with few duplicated transcripts. Filtering yielded 15,664 transcripts totaling 31.4 Mb, ~0.1% of the genome. Tissue-specific expression was substantial: 27.4% of transcripts occurred exclusively in non-needle tissues. Functional annotation confirmed complementary contributions, including seed-desiccation and germination genes from megagametophytes, and defense- and stress-associated genes from roots and phloem. Discussion: We built a transcriptome and efficient probe set using a roadmap suitable for other non-model plants with large genomes; keys to success were prioritizing complementary tissues and using expression-based filtering.

Title: From Sparse Visits to Continuous Molecular Trajectories with Flow Matching
Authors: Passban, P.; Gupta, S.; Guan, B.; Roosta, T.
Abstract: Longitudinal transcriptomic studies often capture only a few molecular snapshots of each patient over time. This makes it challenging to understand how patients are progressing, compare them when progression rates differ, and capture molecular changes between observed visits. We introduce CohortFM, a flow-matching framework that reconstructs continuous patient-specific molecular trajectories from sparse longitudinal observations and organizes them through an integrated mixture model into a compact set of cohort-level progression patterns. CohortFM separates molecular progression from calendar time, places patients on a shared progression scale, uses observed intermediate states to guide the learned trajectories, and maps the resulting patterns back to real patient samples for biological interpretation. We evaluated CohortFM across COVID-19, sepsis, influenza, and tuberculosis. Despite different sampling patterns, the method generalizes well and consistently produces meaningful trajectories. These trajectories capture biological differences between patients that cannot be explained by the observed samples alone. Compared with state-of-the-art trajectory baselines, CohortFM produces more biologically distinct trajectories and a more complete representation of the patient population. Its finer progression scale also reveals biological programs and temporal dynamics that are not captured by visit-level analysis. We further evaluated interpolation and true forward prediction to test whether CohortFM can accurately recover unobserved states. CohortFM remains competitive with strong interpolation baselines and is among the strongest learned predictors in the harder forecasting setting. Ablation experiments further show that flow matching is the core learning mechanism and that our design choices improve continuous trajectory learning. Our results support CohortFM as a practical framework for turning sparse molecular snapshots into continuous, biologically interpretable trajectories. By going beyond visit labels, CohortFM makes it possible to study disease progression and predict future molecular states even when patients are sampled only a few times.

Title: Autonomous AI agents discover reverse transcriptases with tandem repeat arrays
Authors: Yoon, P. H.; Athukoralage, J. S.; Ameisen, E.; Kauderer-Abrams, E.; Perry, N. T.; Durrant, M. G.
Abstract: Metagenomic databases hold vast quantities of unexplored genetic material that can seed tools for biotechnology and medicine, but discovery is limited by our ability to examine sequence data at scale. Here, we show that large language models (LLMs) in an autonomous harness can alleviate this bottleneck and surface novel molecular systems. We deployed Claude Code instances to survey reverse transcriptase (RT) loci across 1.9 billion protein clusters. Among the top candidates were array-associated RTs (ART), a novel family of jumbo-phage RTs coupled with an array of ~200-nucleotide units and a dedicated partner gene. Session transcripts show that Claude identified the ART family by directly examining its DNA sequences and recognizing the atypical repeats, a behavior attributable to specific Mythos 5 internal signals that respond to repeated DNA. ART arrays are highly expressed and appear as discrete units during Staphylococcus phage infection, suggesting an RT system directed by a repertoire of distinct RNAs. These findings indicate that LLMs can autonomously detect anomalies and drive analyses to initiate biological discoveries.

Title: kitAb: an automated framework for assay-specific antibody developability modeling and large-scale landscape analysis
Authors: Trofimova, E.; Shaburova, E.; Antonets, D.; Ramensky, V.
Abstract: Antibody developability is determined by multiple physicochemical properties, and the relevance of individual properties varies among experimental assays. Existing computational approaches, however, often provide fixed assessments or rely on computationally intensive descriptors. We present kitAb, an open-source framework for scalable physicochemical characterization of antibody Fv regions and assay-specific developability modeling. kitAb calculates 59 interpretable sequence- and structure-based descriptors and integrates them with automated feature selection and regression. We evaluated kitAb across ten public datasets comprising 46 experimental endpoints, using sequence-aware or predefined splits where feasible. Predictive performance was strongly assay-dependent. In nested evaluations with sequence-aware or predefined data splits, models using kitAb descriptors achieved predictive performance comparable on average to those using PROPERMAB descriptors, while outperforming models based on TAP or sequence-only features. In a single-structure CPU timing benchmark, kitAb descriptor calculation was approximately 11-fold faster than PROPERMAB. Predictive performance was similar across the three structure-generation backends, and broader AutoML searches did not substantially improve mean performance. We further applied the same descriptor representation to approximately 3.4 million paired natural antibodies and 706 Phase II or later therapeutic antibodies. Repertoire-scale analysis revealed systematic differences in surface charge, hydrophobic and aromatic organization, CDR length and germline-associated physicochemical profiles. The kitAb code and analysis workflows are openly available at https://github.com/katyachemistry/kitAb/.

Title: DeSPA uncovers genes with cross-state spatial pattern remodeling and coordinated spatial programs across multi-slice spatial transcriptomics atlases
Authors: Wen, H.; Shen, Q.; Yuan, Z.; Zhang, S.
Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics increasingly generates multi-slice atlases spanning developmental, regenerative, and disease-associated states. Identifying genes with spatial pattern remodeling across these states is essential for understanding tissue reorganization and the underlying gene programs, yet few existing methods systematically detect such changes while accounting for variation among replicate slices. Here we introduce DeSPA, a statistical framework that models gene-specific spatial variation within each slice using a linear mixed model, tests for cross-state remodeling by aggregating evidence across replicate slices, and organizes identified genes into interpretable spatial co-expression modules that reveal coordinated spatial programs. Simulations show that DeSPA achieves high power while controlling the false discovery rate under inter-slice heterogeneity. In mouse embryogenesis, it recovers programs linked to extracellular matrix organization, muscle formation, neural development, and erythrocyte development. In diabetic testis, it reveals disruption of a late-spermatid spatial program consistent with known spermatogenic dysfunction, while maintaining stable gene rankings under coordinate rotation. In axolotl brain, regeneration preserves a developmental-like biosynthetic backbone but reorganizes it into regeneration-specific modules. Across two mouse intracerebral hemorrhage models, DeSPA resolves a conserved spatial injury program alongside model-specific synaptic and tissue-response programs. Together, these findings establish DeSPA as a scalable and interpretable framework for detecting spatial pattern remodeling and resolving coordinated spatial programs across diverse biological states.

Title: Human Intestinal Absorption Revisited: The 1998 Descriptors Survive, and the Method Extends to Permeability
Authors: Muskal, S. M.; Wessel, M. D.
Abstract: In 1998 we predicted percent human intestinal absorption (HIA) for 86 drug and drug-like compounds from six molecular descriptors chosen by a genetic algorithm with a small neural network serving as the fitness function. That result rested on one division of the compounds into three sets: training, cross-validation and external prediction. Repeating the division shows it was a rather fortunate one. An extraction is one random draw from a wide distribution, so we repeat every experiment 250 times and report the result as a distribution. Across 250 stratified extractions, 14 match the published cross-validation error and only one matches the published external prediction error. Reconstructed this way, the published six descriptors give a mean extraction error roughly twice the external prediction value we reported in 1998 (Table 1). We then applied the same six descriptors to a larger set of 780 compounds from a public compilation. Under the 1998 network they give 22.50 %HIA units on training compounds against 25.77 on extracted compounds, whereas on the 86 they give 13.43 against 30.39. More compounds close the gap between fitting and prediction. Four datasets are modeled here: 780 small molecules with HIA measured in man, 3,771 small molecules and 1,281 cyclic peptides measured across Caco-2 cell monolayers, and 7,298 cyclic peptides measured across artificial membranes. Each is its own prediction problem, and one procedure is applied to all four. A genetic algorithm chooses which descriptors to use and how many, and a random forest grades each choice on compounds its own trees never saw. The descriptors chosen most often across the 250 extractions form one consensus set for each dataset. For absorption, 25 consensus descriptors under a random forest reach an extraction rms of 20.47 %HIA units at R 0.76. On the same compounds and the same extractions, the six 1998 descriptors under the 1998 network reach 25.77 at R 0.59. The four models are served at predicthia.ai, where a structure can be drawn or pasted, scored against its training set for similarity, and the training data with fitted models downloaded. Each model served is its fixed consensus set fitted on every compound in its dataset; the accuracy quoted beside a prediction comes from evaluating that same set across 250 extractions (Table 3). The fixed sets hold 25 descriptors for absorption, 55 for Caco-2 small-molecule permeability, 50 for Caco-2 peptide permeability and 25 for artificial-membrane permeability. Keywords: human intestinal absorption; QSPR; genetic algorithm; descriptor selection; cyclic peptides; membrane permeability; oral bioavailability; repeated extraction

Title: A prioritized medium-throughput screen identifies fibroblast growth factors as protective for human stem cell derived insulin secreting beta cells
Authors: Chu, C. M. J.; Kamal, S.; Huang, H.; Bayly, C. L.; Beletsky, M. J.; Mar, S.; Chen, S.-Y.; Omur, M. E.; Wasserman, W. W.; Lynn, F. C.; Johnson, J. D.
Abstract: Stem cell-derived {beta}-like cells (SC{beta} cells) are an alternative to cadaveric {beta} cells for replacement therapy in type 1 diabetes. However, SC{beta} cells face a multitude of stresses. Both {beta} cells and SC{beta} cells reside in complex microtissues and are modulated by hundreds of autocrine/paracrine signals. Here, we leveraged multi-omics data from late-stage SC{beta} cells and human islets to map ligand-receptor pairs and generate a prioritized list of ligands for high-content SC{beta} cell survival screening. Our medium-throughput screen tracked cell number, cell death, and INS production over several days using automated, high-content imaging. Members of the fibroblast growth factor (FGF) family significantly prevented cytokine-induced cell death, with the top validated hits being FGF4, FGF5, and FGF8F. With these results, there is the potential to improve SC{beta} cell survival in vitro via readily targetable pathways and to produce a more robust product for translation to the clinic.
